units.la: ASTROLOGIAM olim non nisi apud summos Reges in honore fuisse, nemo, qui temporum historias legit, ignorat, cum Astronomia vero esse ita semper conjunctam, ut tanquam altera soror ab illa divelli non possit. Sunt enim primaria scientia, quibus vera effectuum corporum cœlestium cognitio acquiritur, quamvis Astrologia sublimior semper & excelsior sit habita, quam ut vulgi humilitas ad eam ascendere unquam posset. Cum enim tam humanum nihil sit, tamq; jucundum nihil, quam ea cognoscere & scire, quæ natura inter arcana sua condidit, nihil tam præstans & magnificum, quam Dei maximum opus contemplari & intelligere, Astrologia autem comple-ctatur utrumq;, & futurorum arcanam notitiam, & cœlestis illius machinæ divinum & maximum opus, merito ab omnibus sapientibus præstantior semper & sublimior existimata est. Eos vero, qui tantum opus sunt aggressi, ut res mortalibus utilissimas invenirent, augerent, atque excolerent, antiquitas, Dei ignara, pro Diis venerata est. Qui error, si non omnino spreto divino & vero numine, irrepsisset, hoc ipso erat tolerabilis, quod dum Dei opera suspicimus, dum illius leges intelligimus, dum secreta percipimus, ejus magnitudinem ex operibus, sapientiam ex ordine, bonitatem ex concessa nobis sapientia veneramur. Quis enim, si opificem tantæ molis considerare velit, si æternas motuum leges, si secretorum nobis traditam scientiam, illico ejusdem potentiam non pertimescat, sapientiam non admiretur, bonitatem non diligat? Monuerat Philosophus ille Augustum, ut, cum facturus esset aliquid, prius Græcum Alphabetum revolveret, moram scilicet deliberationi interponendam docens, idque salubri consilio: sed salubriori certe, si quispiam moneat singulis noctibus semel stellas inspicere, illarumque splendorem, motum, ordinem, magnitudinemque considerare, indeque, quis tantus opifex ista condiderit. Simul enim, ut hæc diutius & frequentius quisquam secum reputaverit, illa occurrent, æternitatis memoria, conditionis nostræ fragilitas, ambitionis ineptia, scelerumque acerba recordatio, indeque contemtus tam brevis vitæ, quæ etsi centum annos duret, quid quaso porro ad æternitatis magnitudinem immensam? certe ut exiguum in circulo punctum. Et quid hæc tota felicitas humana, nisi ventus, fumus, somnium? Si quid vero in ea est, illud totum in divinorum operum contemplatione & admiratione repositum est. Quæ ambo cum Astrologia complectatur[?], totam etiam humanam felicitatem illam complecti verisimile est. Nec minus in adversis hæc æternitatis contemplatio nos confirmat, cum brevem onerosi ævi transitum consideramus, & fati impositam necessitatem, quæ eo est levior, quo assiduâ meditatione paulatim mitescit, & quasi fit familiarior. Verum his valere jussis, ad humanum commodum paululum sermo dirigatur. Quid utilius, quam scire futura? quid jucundius, quam divinitatis alicujus hac in parte esse particeps? Quidnam bonus Astrologus est aliud, quam consiliorum, quæ in cœlo fiunt astrifero, particeps? Et ut ille dicebat:
units.tr: No one who reads the histories of past ages is unaware that astrology was once held in honour only among the greatest kings. Astronomy has always been so closely joined to it that it cannot be torn away from it like a sister. For these are the chief sciences by which a true knowledge of the effects of the heavenly bodies is acquired, although astrology has always been regarded as too lofty and sublime for the humble common people ever to rise to it. For nothing is so natural to man, nothing so pleasing, as to know and understand the things that nature has hidden among her secrets; nothing is so noble and splendid as to contemplate and understand the greatest work of God. Astrology embraces both: the hidden knowledge of future events and the divine and mightiest work of that heavenly machine. Rightly, therefore, has it always been judged by all wise men to be the more excellent and sublime. Those who undertook so great a task, to discover, increase and cultivate things most useful to mortals, antiquity, ignorant of God, worshipped as gods. This error, if it had crept in without wholly scorning the divine and true godhead, would have been tolerable, in that while we admire God's works, while we grasp his laws, while we perceive his secrets, we venerate his greatness from his works, his wisdom from their order, and his goodness from the wisdom granted to us. For who, if he were willing to consider the maker of so great a mass, if he considered the eternal laws of motion and the science of secrets handed down to us, would not at once fear his power, admire his wisdom, and love his goodness? That philosopher had warned Augustus that when he was about to do anything he should first run through the Greek alphabet, teaching, that is, that a pause should be put between deliberation and action, and this was sound advice. But it would certainly be more sound if someone advised that once each night one should look at the stars and consider their brightness, motion, order and size, and from this consider what great craftsman made them. For as soon as anyone reflects on these things longer and more often, there come to mind the memory of eternity, the frailty of our condition, the foolishness of ambition, and the bitter recollection of crimes, and from these, contempt for a life so brief that, even if it lasts a hundred years, what is it, I ask, compared with the immense greatness of eternity? Surely it is like a tiny point in a circle. And what is all this human happiness, except wind, smoke, a dream? If there is anything of value in it, it lies entirely in contemplating and admiring the works of God. Since astrology embraces both of these, it is probably true that it embraces all that human happiness as well. Nor does this contemplation of eternity strengthen us less in adversity, when we consider the brief passage of a burdensome age and the necessity imposed by fate, which is lighter the more it gradually softens through constant meditation and becomes, as it were, more familiar. But, bidding these things farewell, let our discourse be turned for a little to human advantage. What is more useful than to know the future? What is more pleasant than to share in some measure of divinity in this respect? What else is a good astrologer than a partaker in the counsels that are carried out in the starry heaven? And, as that poet said:

units.la: Illic astra, polos, cœlum, septemque planetas Consulit Astrologus, terrisque reportat eorum Consilium, quo illas armat, firmatque caduca, Contra cœlestes iras, superumque furorem.
units.tr: There the astrologer consults the stars, the poles, the sky and the seven planets, and brings back to earth their counsel, by which he arms and strengthens frail mortals against the wrath of heaven and the fury of the higher powers.

units.la: Sed quod omnibus nobilioribus scientiis contingere semper solet, idem quoq; contigit & etiamnunc contingit Astrologia. Ut enim in illas, sic etiam in hanc innumerabilis turba nebulonum se conjecit, qui suis vanitatibus ita nobilissimam artem fœdarunt & conspurcarunt, ut ne quidem vestigium illius apparuerit. Verùm miserta generis humani divina bonitas, Ptolomæum unum pro tot millibus Sycophantarum est largita. Is artem in tenebris jacentem extulit, inq; lucem traduxit. Dignus certè Herculeis honoribus, atq; aliquanto etiam majoribus. Mira enim industria & arte, summa diligentia, maximis laboribus, magna fretus felicitate ac vitæ diuturnitate, non solum errantium & inerrantium syderum cursus, magnitudines, aliasq; illorum affectiones descripsit, sed & illorum decreta tanta ingenii subtilitate observavit & notavit, ut mortales omnes ab arte ipsa absterruisse, neminem accendisse videatur.
units.tr: But what has always happened to all the nobler sciences has also happened, and still happens, to astrology. For just as an innumerable crowd of scoundrels threw themselves upon those sciences, so they did upon this one, and by their follies so disgraced and defiled this most noble art that not even a trace of it appeared. But divine goodness, taking pity on the human race, gave us one Ptolemy in place of so many thousands of sycophants. He raised up the art, which lay in darkness, and brought it into the light. Certainly he deserves the honours of Hercules, and even somewhat greater ones. For with wonderful industry and skill, with the greatest diligence and labours, relying on great good fortune and a long life, he described not only the courses, magnitudes and other affections of the wandering and fixed stars, but also observed and noted their decrees with such subtlety of mind that he seems to have frightened all mortals away from the art itself, and to have kindled no one.

units.la: Maluit enim veritatem obscurè, quàm mendacia ac fabulas dilucidè scribere, sperans futuros tandem aliquos, qui hac sua monumenta possint explicare. Alii, ipsius artis planè ignari, non solùm non sincerè de illa sentiunt & loquuntur, ipsamq; tanquam κακοτεχνίαν [?] impugnant, & ad orcum usq; damnant, verùm etiam illius amatores, excultores, nec non admiratores calumniis impetunt, maledictisq; lacessunt. Quæ certè insania in bene constitutis scholis non ferenda, sed coercenda est, veterumq; ac recentium, ipsiusq; experientiæ armis, rationumq; ponderibus ac momentis corrigenda. Contra hos igitur, viri Amplissimi ac Consultissimi, præsenti discursu militabo, atq; ista in præclarissimam artem, ejusq; excultores invehendi rabie ac vesania dehortabor, idq; sobriè & modestè, non animo in personam illorum invehendi, aut privata illis objiciendi crimina, sed ipsam artem ut honestam & utilem ab injuriis vindicandi. Valdè enim ineptum est extra pomœria evagari, doctrinamq; aliquam vituperare, quæ simpliciter ignoratur.
units.tr: For he preferred to write the truth obscurely rather than lies and fables clearly, hoping that some men would eventually arise who could explain his records. Others, utterly ignorant of the art itself, not only do not speak or think of it sincerely, and attack it as [κακοτεχνίαν] and condemn it to the lower world, but also assail its lovers, cultivators and admirers with slanders and abuse. Such madness is certainly not to be tolerated in well-ordered schools, but must be restrained and corrected by the weapons of the ancients and moderns, by their own experience, and by the weight and force of reasons. Therefore, most distinguished and wise gentlemen, I shall wage war against these men in the present discourse, and I shall dissuade them from assailing this most splendid art and its cultivators with rage and frenzy. I shall do this soberly and modestly, not with the intention of attacking their persons or of charging them with private crimes, but to defend the art itself as honourable and useful against injuries. For it is very foolish to wander beyond the city walls and to disparage some doctrine that is simply not known.

units.la: Vos, Magnifici viri, enixè volo rogatos, ut hunc tractatum in sinum vestrum recipere, fovere, vestroq; patrocinio tueri contra Zoilorum rancidos morsus non gravemini. Quod enim eum nunc profero in lucem[?] sub Nominis vestri auspicio, duo sunt præcipuè, quæ me incitarunt: unum, quòd sciam, præter dignitatem, autoritatem, gloriæ splendorem, opesq;, quibus floretis, semper vos habuisse & coluisse viros tum in omni artium & disciplinarum genere, tum præcipuè in studio Mathematico & Astronomico excellentes: alterum, ut insignis vestra benevolentia ac humanitatis partem mihi aliquam conciliem atq; adjungam. Non igi-tur dubito, quin [?]Magnif. & Amplitudines Vestræ pro sua humanitate & bonitate hunc tractatum meum sint benigno animo acceptura, sere-no vultu respectura, & contra Sycophantas fortiter propugnatura. Deus Opt. Max. Amplitudines vestras diutissimè incolumes conservet ad nominis sui gloriam, multorumq; commodum & salutem. Marpurgi, è Musæo meo, xx. Maij, Anno MDCXI.
units.tr: You, magnificent gentlemen, I earnestly beg not to be reluctant to receive this treatise into your bosom, to cherish it, and to protect it under your patronage against the rancid bites of Zoilus. What has moved me above all to bring it forth into the light now under the auspices of your name is two things. First, because I know that, apart from your dignity, authority, splendour of glory and the wealth in which you flourish, you have always held in esteem and cultivated men excelling in every kind of art and discipline, and above all in the mathematical and astronomical study. Second, that I might win for myself and attach to myself some part of your remarkable kindness and humanity. I therefore do not doubt that your Magnificences and Honours, in keeping with your humanity and goodness, will receive this treatise of mine with a kindly spirit, will regard it with a calm countenance, and will bravely defend it against the sycophants. May God, most good and most great, keep your Honours safe for a very long time, to the glory of his name and the advantage and salvation of many. From Marburg, from my study, 20 May, in the year 1611.

units.la: VENUS τὲ admodum Euripides fingit Silenum atq; Satyrorum chorum Jovem & astra contemplari, hos vero ab hac contemplatione ferocientem Cyclopem dehortari cum increpatione, sic enim fingit Cyclopem eos affari:
units.tr: Euripides, for example, portrays Silenus and the chorus of Satyrs contemplating Jupiter and the stars, and the fierce Cyclops dissuading them from this contemplation with a rebuke. He has the Cyclops address them thus:

units.la: Τί φαλῖς[?], τὶ λέγεις, τύχαλις[?] ὑμῶν τῷ ξύλῳ[?]
units.tr: What are you saying, what are you talking about? Someone will soon make you shed tears with a club [Τί φαλῖς, τί λέγεις, τύχαλις ὑμῶν τῷ ξύλῳ].

units.la: Δάκρυα μεξήσει[?], βλέπεις ἄνω ἢ μὴ κάτω[?].
units.tr: You will weep, and you look up rather than down [Δάκρυα μεξήσει, βλέπεις ἄνω ἢ μὴ κάτω].

units.la: Quid loquimini, quid dicitis? celeriter quispiam vobis fuste lacrymas movebit; sursum videtis & non deorsum. At Silenum Cyclopi respondentem introducit, ut citra metum fateatur suam in contemplandis sideribus diligentiam, sic enim Cyclopem alloquitur:
units.tr: "What are you saying, what are you telling me? Someone will soon make you weep with a club; you look upward and not downward." But he introduces Silenus answering the Cyclops, so that he may confess without fear his diligence in contemplating the stars. For he addresses the Cyclops thus:

units.la: Ἰδὼ[?] ὡς ἐς αὐτὸν τὸν Δί[?] ἀνάκεκυφαμεν[?],
units.tr: Look, we have bent our gaze up to Zeus himself [Ἰδὼ ὡς ἐς αὐτὸν τὸν Δία ἀνάκεκυφαμεν].

units.la: Καὶ τ᾽ ἄστρα[?], τὴν ἀεὶ[?] ὠρίωνα[?] δέχομαι[?].
units.tr: And the stars, and Orion, which I always receive [Καὶ τ᾽ ἄστρα, τὴν ἀεὶ Ὠρίωνα δέχομαι].

units.la: Ecce ad ipsum Jovem oculos direximus, astraq; & Orionem aspicio. Quo quidem de duabus ingeniorum humanorum differentiis Poëta nos admonet, quarum alteram in Sileno, alteram proponit in Cyclope, fingit tamen neutram earum legibus, disciplinis aut assuefactione, seu humana societate institutam, sed sequi eas tantum motus à natura implantatos. Fingit Silenum in servitute degentem, quotidianis curis & voluptatibus deditum, nihilominus tamen quandoq; de divinis & rebus in natura bonis cogitare. Ac ejus personâ vult ostendere, esse quasdam naturas bonas, ac suæ conditionis memores, quæ licèt sint immersæ vel impeditæ quotidianis curis & voluptatibus, tamen quandoq; eas naturaliter incitari ad Dei, ejusq; operum considerationes, admirari propterea eas res bonas, atq; amore earum capi. Harumq; naturarum in Sileno spectandas imagines nobis proponit. At vero Cyclopem fingit austerum & ferocem, qui nec de Deo, nec de rebus bonis in natura fit sollicitus, nec capiatur amore earum, nec illis afficiatur, sed tantum sua curet, vel ea, quæ ad gulæ pertinent ganeæq; irritamenta, qui odio etiam prosequatur eos homines, qui vel Jovem, vel alias res bonas & honestas in natura admirantur, ac amplectuntur. Fingitq; simul, velle ipsum ejusmodi rerum bonarum admiratores ad suæ naturæ impetus cogere. Et quidem in hujus Cyclopis persona Poëta vult ostendere, esse etiam alias naturas & ingenia à prioribus longè dissidentia, quæ non modò naturaliter abhorrent à cogitationibus de Deo, & contemplatione divinorum operum, sed quæ interim honestas mentes, & quæ naturaliter, id est, sine assuefactione, ad bonarum rerum in natura feruntur contemplationem, minis [?] conantur à bonis motibus abducere. Harum naturarum exempla Poëta in Cyclope spectanda introducit, quem fingit suis minis velle cogere Silenum & Satyros, inter reliquas curas amantes Deum, ejusq; opera, ab hoc motu ad suæ naturæ monstrum, atque ideo velle eum illos dehortari, ut à siderum contemplationibus abstineant. Quemadmodum autem hæ sunt differentiæ in ingeniis humanis non informatis educatione aliqua, legibus aut disciplinis, ita similes sunt differentiæ in naturis humanis, hominum societate, artibus atque disciplinis excultis: quædam enim ad disciplinas artesq; naturaliter & proprio mentis motu, seu suopte nutu inclinantur, eas amant, discunt, exercent, earumq; admiratione capiuntur: quædam contra ita sunt affectæ, ut non solùm naturali quadam inclinatione artes oderint, easq; ludificentatq; concontemnant, sed etiam earum cultores insulsè derideant, co-nenturq; ab honestis suis motibus ad Cyclopicam ferociā atq; ignaviam eos deducere. Contra hæc monstra, si de universo genere humano nunquam melius & gloriosius mereri censendi sunt, nec Deo facere gratius quicquam, quàm,qui omni studio contentioneq; dant operam, ut pulcerrimæ ingenuæq; artes conserventur, & posteritati tradantur, quibus etiam merito nulli triumphi,nulla brabea, nulli arcus triumphales jure anteponi posse sapientissimi quiq; arbitrati sunt: Si,inquam, hoc ita est, ut certè est, non puto quenquam fore, qui & meos impetus conatusq; sit improbaturus, dum contra Cyclopicam illam & monstrosam barbariem, ad divinam scientiam Astrologiam illustrandam, ejusq; certitudinem atq; utilitatem demonstrandam, pro ingenii mei viribus, quas in me exiguas esse fateor, me accingo. Sunt enim non pauci, qui derogata ei omni veritate, artisq; detracto titulo, totam artium numero excluserunt, imò ex rerum natura relegârunt, tanquam quæ sese præstigiis ad veritatis quidem speciem confictis, scitèq; adornatis, sed alienis tamen à vero, venditet atq; insinuet: nonnulli contra eò prolapsi sunt amentiæ, ut omnium humanarū rerum publica & privata fata, quæq; quivis scire desideraret, in hoc oculis nostris obtenso coelo, illiq; affixis sideribus consignata tanquā tabella esse, indeq; depromi ac proferri ab eruditis posse affirmarint, nihilq; tentandum aut incoandum censuerint, nisi consultis astris, nec ea quæ gerenda susciperentur, procedere, fortiriq; optatos eventus, nisi astra annuerent ac suffragarentur. Utriq; autem decipiuntur vehementer. Illos permoverunt fortasse, ut in abjicienda arte progrederentur longius, cùm horum falsa & stolida promissa, quibus ad astra alligabant animos, ut exillis tanquam numinibus penderent, aut spe suspensi, aut metu capti, tum vatum crebræ aberrationes & judicia toto cœlo ab eveneventibus discrepatia, autorumq; quorundam veterum & recentiorum superstitiosa commenta nullis firmata rationibus, adq; usus nec veros nec legitimos, vel superstitione, vel uberioris lucri spe, vel studio novandae artis instructi Canones, quibus metas illi Physices egressi, adeo artem defoedarunt, ut inter acervos commentitiorum Canonum vix obscura physicae alicubi vestigia emicuerint. Hos vero ad praestigias coacervandas atq; excogitandas, artemq; in immensum extollendam, amplificandamq;, vel superstitio impulit, vel spes lucri & questus, vel ambitio & naturae vanitas. Hic tot Albumasares, Abenrageles, Alchabitii, Abubatres, Zaheles, Messahalaci. Sed ut in omni nobiliori ac difficiliori scientia semper majora contingunt vitia & errata, partim quidem per eos, qui cum eam non norint, se scire jactant, partim per eos, qui sciunt, sed male utuntur; ita in nobilissimam etiam astrorum scientiam pessima errata irrepserunt.
units.tr: "Behold, we have turned our eyes to Jupiter himself, and I look at the stars and Orion." In these two contrasting kinds of human temperament the poet reminds us, showing one in Silenus and the other in the Cyclops. Yet he imagines neither of them as formed by laws, teaching, habit or human society, but as following only the impulses implanted by nature. He imagines Silenus living in servitude, given over to daily cares and pleasures, and yet at times thinking about divine things and the good things of nature. Through his character he wishes to show that there are certain good natures, mindful of their condition, which, although they are immersed in or hindered by daily cares and pleasures, are nonetheless at times naturally stirred to consider God and his works, and so to admire those good things and be captivated by love of them. He sets before us the images of such natures to be seen in Silenus. But the Cyclops he imagines as harsh and fierce, one who is concerned neither with God nor with the good things of nature, is not captivated by love of them nor moved by them, but cares only for his own affairs, or for those things that serve the belly and the incitements of the throat. He even pursues with hatred those men who admire and embrace Jupiter or other good and honourable things in nature. And he imagines that he wishes to drive such admirers of good things by force toward the impulses of his own nature. Indeed, in the person of this Cyclops the poet wishes to show that there are also other natures and temperaments far removed from the former, which not only naturally shrink from thoughts of God and contemplation of divine works, but which also, when upright minds are naturally carried, that is, without habituation, toward the contemplation of good things in nature, try by threats to turn them away from good impulses. The poet introduces the Cyclops as an example of such natures to be observed, whom he imagines wanting by his threats to compel Silenus and the Satyrs, who among their other cares love God and his works, to turn from this motion toward the monster of his own nature, and therefore wanting to dissuade them from contemplating the stars. Just as these differences exist among human temperaments not shaped by any training, laws or teaching, so similar differences exist among human natures cultivated by human society, arts and disciplines. For some are naturally inclined to the disciplines and arts, by their own motion of mind or by their own accord; they love them, learn them, practise them, and are captivated by admiration of them. Others are so disposed that, by a certain natural disinclination, they not only hate the arts, mock them and utterly despise them, but also foolishly deride their practitioners, and try to lead them away from their honourable impulses into Cyclopean fierceness and sloth. Against these monsters, if those who devote all their zeal and effort to preserving the most beautiful and noble arts and handing them down to posterity are judged to deserve better of the whole human race than any others, and to do nothing more pleasing to God, and if the wisest men have judged that no triumphs, no laurel wreaths, no triumphal arches can rightly be placed above these things, then, I say, if this is so, as it certainly is, I do not think anyone will disapprove of my efforts and endeavours. I am girding myself, as far as the strength of my intellect allows (which I admit is slight in me), to illuminate astrology, a divine science, and to demonstrate its certainty and usefulness against that Cyclopean and monstrous barbarism. For there are not a few who, having denied it all truth and stripped it of the title of art, have excluded it from the number of the arts, and indeed banished it from the nature of things, as something that peddles and insinuates itself with deceptions devised to resemble the truth, skilfully dressed up, yet alien to the truth. Some have fallen into such madness that they have declared that the public and private fates of all human affairs, and whatever anyone might wish to know, are written in this heaven that lies open to our eyes, and in the stars fixed to it, as on a tablet, and can be drawn out and brought forth from it by the learned; and they have judged that nothing should be attempted or begun, nor should things to be undertaken proceed, unless the stars were consulted, nor should they obtain their desired outcomes unless the stars consented and favoured them. Both groups are gravely mistaken. The former were perhaps moved to go further in rejecting the art, since the false and foolish promises of the latter, by which they bound minds to the stars so that they hung upon them as on deities, held them either in suspense through hope or seized by fear. Also moving them were the frequent errors of the soothsayers and judgements wholly at odds with the events, and the superstitious inventions of certain ancient and recent authors, supported by no reasons, and canons neither true nor lawful in practice, devised either from superstition, or from hope of greater gain, or from a desire to alter the art. By these canons they, having passed beyond the bounds of natural science, so disfigured the art that amid the heaps of invented canons scarcely any obscure traces of physics shine forth anywhere. Superstition, the hope of profit and gain, ambition and the vanity of human nature drove these men to heap up and devise such juggleries and to extol and enlarge the art beyond measure. Here are so many Albumasares, Abenrageles, Alchabitii, Abubatres, Zaheles, Messahalaci. But just as in every nobler and more difficult science the greater faults and errors always arise, partly through those who claim to know it though they do not, and partly through those who know it but use it badly, so in the most noble science of the stars the worst errors have crept in.

units.la: Dolendum sane ac deplorandum, plurimos hoc seculo eruditos, inq; omni literarum genere exercitatos, adeo alienos esse ab hac doctrina, ut existiment aliud nihil in hac tradi, quàm quod vanum sit & impium, atq; Christiana caritate remotum, imo exterminatione dignos, qui huic illustrandae atq; amplificandae operâ insumserunt. Hodie enim quàm excolatur, quanto in honore habeatur, imo quàm tractetur diligenter, maledicendi quorundam libido orta ex mera ignorantia, imo verò publica quorunda contra eam evibrata spicula satis demonstrant.
units.tr: It is truly to be lamented and deplored that so many learned men of this age, practised in every kind of literature, are so alien to this doctrine that they think nothing is taught in it but what is vain and impious, and far removed from Christian charity; indeed, that those who have devoted their labour to illustrating and extending it deserve banishment. For how much it is cultivated today, how highly it is esteemed, or indeed how diligently it is handled, the spite of certain people, arising from pure ignorance, and certain public shafts hurled against it by some, sufficiently demonstrate.

units.la: Non enim sentiunt nec intelligunt male isti feriati, quantum detrimenti rebus humanis afferat rerum coelestium ignorantia, & quantum utilitatis earundem cognitio. Naturae enim, hoc est, coelestium & elementarium harmonian & consensum ignorare, extremę est miserię & cęcitatis, ob quam in eam mentis delabuntur etiam infirmitatem & hallucinationem, ut, quae non intelligunt, nec assequi ratione possunt, insulse contemnant, nant, Astrorumq; scientiam, & coelestium influentiarum doctrinam, quàm[?] in naturæ theatro nihil excellentius, nihil sublimius, nihil utilius, & ad vitæ actiones conservandas, dirigendas atq; moderandas, nihil illustrius, ad mores quoq; regendos atque componendos, animiq; impetus vehementiores refrenandos, torpidiores vero & segniores accendendos, nihil præstantius atq; commodius, superba quadam ac superciliosa fatuitate explodant. Hanc antiquissimos Patriarchas, Græciæ sapientes, Indorum Gymnosophistas, cæterosq; Græciæ Philosophos sinceriores coluisse, aliosq; plurimos multorum seculorum viros sanctissimos, literatissimosq; Reges ac Principes in maximo semper pretio & honore habuisse, tum divina, tum profana literarum testantur monimenta. Sublimiorem tamen hanc doctrinam semper fuisse habitam, quam ut vulgi humilitas ad eam ascendere posset unquam, nemo qui temporum historias legerit, inficiabitur. Nam nascendi moriendiq; causam ex cœlorum provenire motu, tanquam occasum ab ortu, aut finem ab initio, à non nisi summis ingeniis satis percipitur. Quin etiam universa illa rerum natura quid est aliud, quàm ordinata quædam sibiq; semper constans immutatio atq; conversio? quid vita & mors animantium, quàm quidam ab initio ad finem usq; motus? quid præterea motus ille cœli, stellarumq; irradiationes mortalium generi præstent, docet Astrologia, cujus qui principia, à quibus orditur, quibusq; sefundat[?] ac stabilit, ac metas intra quas continetur, novit, sponte à convitiis abstinebit. Hanc igitur nobilissimam fati partem convitiis oppressam, in tenebris jacentem, & ludificari denuò cœptam, dum à calumniis vindico, pristino nitori restituo, & in lucem, quantum quidem in me est, reduco, rogo, ut perbenigne audiar. Ac primò quidem ut originem Astromantiæ demonstrem, quibusq; nitatur principiis & demonstrationibus, clarius innotescat, non ignotum esse arbitror, duas esse doctrinæ de astris partes, quarum una certissimas motuum cœlestium leges in stellis ostendit, & dicitur Astronomia, altera siderum monstrat effectus & significationes, ac dicitur divinatrix seu μαντικὴ[?]. Prior, motus siderum varios, horumq; distantias, altitudines, progressus & regressus Mathematica quadam ratione mensurat atque investigat. Et licet ex manifestis sit demonstrationibus extructa, & utilitatem hanc insignem, & omnibus necessariam ac notam contineat, ut scilicet ex motu Solis & Lunæ certas anni, mensiumq; metas, discrimina & partes, partiumq; anni justam descriptionem, notatis æquinoctiis & solstitiis, teneamus, & propterea ab omnibus fere eruditis tanquam certa, nunquam satis laudata, vereq; cœlestis ars commendetur; tamen plurimi ex Cyclopica prosapia inveniuntur, qui eam susq; deq; facientes, suis exemplis alios etiam ab ea retrahere omnibus modis contendunt. Verum horum judicia divinis statim testimoniis refutantur. Scriptum enim est, & erunt lumina in signa, tempora, dies, annos, ubi certe motuum aspectio & observatio præcipitur. Ac certe annos quod attinet, ego quidem nullos unquam Cyclopes tam fuisse feros puto, neq; ullam tam horridam barbariem, quæ non annorum, mensiumq; intervalla notârit, posteritatiq; tradiderit, ut turpe sit in literarum & musarum quarumcunque etiam castris militanti, hanc artem negligere, vituperare, & committere, ut insulsissimis indoctorum judiciis superbè derideatur, cum de Deo, ipsiusq; admirânda sapientia & bonitate nos commonefaciat, quem ita prope monstrat, ut Paulus dicat, pene manibus contrectari posse Deum, ostendentem se nobis in admirando hoc suo artificio, in quo tanquam lucidissimo speculo quasi ipsum Deum aspicimus, ut rectè etiam dixerit Alcinous Platonicus c. 6. In Astronomiam incumbentes, ab iis quæ oculis percipiuntur, ad inaspectabilem & intelligibilem essentiam dedudeducimur. Proponamus exempli loco ex luminibus cœli Solem & Lunam, quorum motu viribusq; perspectis facilis postea erit transitus ad Astromantiam. Sol enim non semper easdem & æquales in corporibus nostris excitat qualitates & vires, sed pro ea regione cœli, quam peragrat, dum aut est propinquior, aut remotior à conspectu nostro, agere, suoq; accessu & recessu efficere diversas, & qualitatibus differentes anni partes, mani-feste quotidiana comprobant documenta. Nam quid quæso manifestius, quàm calorem aëris, fervoremq; æstivum à Sole, radiisq; solaribus & eorundem reflexione provenire, frigus aë-ris nocturnum, humoresq; roscidos generari à Luna, quod te-stantur noctu, cum Luna est pernox, iter facientes: quis ignorat solaris caloris affluxu ver & æstatem, frugum ac florum amoe-nitate, veluti copiæ cornu exuberare, infecta quoq;, muscas, angues, ranas, hirundines, quæ brumali frigore semimortuæ ta-bularum rimis, medullis sambuci, cavernis littorum, ac intra arborum caudices sese illatebrarunt, reviviscere? ut ita manife-stum sit, non tantum à Sole, sed etiam in Sole calorem esse, seu ingenitam quandam & peculiarem virtutem calefactivam, testante Ptolomaeo, i. quadripart. c. 3. cui etiam consentiunt eruditiores Philosophi nostri seculi. Sic enim inquit inter alios Tau-rellus contra Cæsalpinum lib. 3. pag. 569. Naturali astrorum vir-tute calorem & frigus, ut & alias complures qualitates manifestas occultasq; in corpora sublunaria vibrari profitemur. Et certè nulla firma & solida ratione probari potest, cur stellæ (cùm sint corpora lucida, & velut candelæ in mundo accensę, cœloq; à Deo impiætæ[?], ut rationalis creatura ad divinæ Trinitatis ex-emplar facta, ex periodicis earundem motibus & diurnis con-versionibus, quibus à divina sapientia sunt prævisæ, futura in-telligeret, & quæ sub mobili sphæræ Lunaris vertigine agitan-tur, ad generationem suscitarent) non sint habitualiter dicen-dæ cadæ calidæ. Omnes enim calidæ, quia lucidæ, & quò quid lucidius, eò calidius; unde Sol omnium maximè calefactivus, quia omnium maximè lucidus: quæ tamen intelligenda sunt de luce cœlesti, cujus primum effectum est suâ naturâ calefacere atque vivificare; nam lumen in crystallo & glacie non est calidum, ideoq; non calefacit, quoniam non habet principium in se calefactionis. Quòd verò Saturnus dicitur frigidus, Luna frigida, comparatè accipiendum est, pro leviter calida. Licèt enim Saturnus sit calidus, quia lucidus; quoniam tamen frigus magis efficit quàm calorem, frigidus etiam dicitur, nam Soli junctus calorem ejus minuere deprehensus est, & propter hunc effectum frigidus dicitur: cur autem non calefaciat terras, ratio est, quòd in eo sunt aliæ qualitates & facultates abstrusiores, infrigidantes, propter quas calor descendere ad terram prohibetur; tum etiam, quòd lucida cœli corpora ex propinquitate aut remotione magis vel minus calefaciant, Luna excepta, quæ, licèt utriusq;, cœlestis & sublunaris regionis particeps, frigida tamen magis deprehenditur & humida, quàm calida. Vanum igitur est dicere, Solem non esse calidum, & nihilominus calefacere virtute scilicet & effectivè, non secus ac vinum, quod calefacit, & tamen actu calidum non est, sed δυνάμει tantum. Nunquam enim radiis suis lucidis posset Sol calefacere, si insito calore non calefaceret, radiiq; caloris in se haberent principium, nec Luna posset refrigerare aut humectare unquam, nisi nativa quadam eaq; infrigidante virtute id efficeret; ut ita ineptius aut absurdius nihil excogitatum sit, aut excogitari possit, quàm calorem, humorem, frigus, siccitatem & alias qualitates proprias esse elementorum corruptibilium, in cœlo verò esse nullas. Ipse Aristoteles 1. meteor. cap. 3. astra vocat calida: & 2. de ort.animal.c.3. ait, calorem, qui in animantibus est, neq; ignem esse, neq; ab igne habere principium, sed à diviniore, quàm sint eleelementa, corpore provenire, id autem est elementum a-ftræum. Sic & alias qualitates in cœlo reperiri, ut raritatem, densitatem, lœvitatem, mollitiem & perspicuitatem, certa experientia habetur compertum, licet non sint elementaris conditionis & cognationis; nam omnium seculorum memoria idem cœlum, eœdemq; stellœ in eadem magnitudine, colore & distantia in hunc usque diem incorruptæ perstiterunt, nec ulla tanto temporum intervallo labes cœlestibus corporibus accidit. Unde vere dictum ab Aristotele est, cœlum secundum naturam suam nulli ortui, nulli interitui, nulli incremento, nulli decremento, nulli alterationi obnoxium esse, adeoq; omnis gravitatis & levitatis expers, idq; firmis rationibus demonstrat, 1. de cœl.cap.3. Corruit igitur, & in nihilum abit generalis axiomatis veritas: Omne materiatum est corruptibile, cùm de materia sublunarium id intelligendum sit, quæ interitus, divortii, & divisionis causa est, propter adjunctam privationem, quæ cœlesti materiæ non inest, ob quam etiam causam cœlum non est corruptionibus & alterationibus subjectum. Cæterùm inter qualitates cœlestes sensu & effectu illustres sunt calor, qui excellit in Sole, & frigiditas, quæ in Luna & Saturno. Cum lucidis radiis Solis produci & effundi calorem Sole clarius est: à luce Lunæ per effusum radium sublunaribus infundi frigiditatem & humiditatem, quotidianis experimentis habetur patefactum: ut autem calor Solis, & humiditas Lunæ in diversis oriatur locis, & terris, motus requiritur, qui lucem circumvehat. Quemadmodum enim quotidianâ Solis circa terram vertigine, ortu, obituq;, adq; Medium seu culmen cœli delatione, quo motu alias atque alias stellas subinde secum defert, alias è regione sub occasum urget & præcipitat, aut turbari aërem videmus, obnubilariq;, aut serenescere atque inclarescere plus nimio, aut contra perfrigerari, humectari aut arefieri, aliterq; atque aliter mutamutari pro stellarum cooriuntium, occumbentium, vel ad Solem radios ejaculantium natura, positu, & conditione, ita Luna terris proxima manifestissime in terrena influit, crescens humiditates commovet, corporibusq; affundit, quas marcescens & decrescens resorbet. Pleno lucente orbe plantae & animalia liquoribus exuberant, deficiente minuuntur, interlunio vero, cum scilicet ipsa lumen omne a terris aversum coelo regerit, arent: eadem supra horoscopum conscendente maria tanquam vi sideris impulsa exaestuant atque affluunt, decumbente de-fluunt rursus paulatim, donec consideant & acquiescant. Hæc cum usu didicissent agricolæ, aptissima tempora sationum, ad-missionis pecudum ad coitum, incubationis avium domestica-rum, sectionis lignorum vel urendorum, vel ad structuras adhi-bendorum distribuerunt. Etsi vero præcipui & illustriores sunt ef-sectus & significationes influentiaeq; Solis & Lunae, quod ille & mole corporis antecellens cæteris, & nativæ lucis copia, fulgo-re atq; efficacia (unde præses diei, Gen. 1. vas admirabile, opus excelsi, Eccles. 43. rector orbis terrarum, Sapient. 3. dux, princeps & moderator luminum reliquorum a Cic. & cor mundi appel-latur a Ptolom.) accessuq; & conjectu radiorum reliquas stel-las aut moderatur, aut extimulat, aut obtundit, aut comburit, hæc vero & Solis luce imbuitur, & ut terris proxima, quicquid a cæteris derivatur excipit, colligit, atq; acervatim demittit, ta-men cæterarum tam errantium quam fixarum stellarum longa experientia deprehensus influxus, non est parvipendendus, cum fixarum natura effectiones pariat statis anni temporibus recur-rentes, & tunc sese promunt vel maxime, cum Soli orienti vel assistunt, vel cadunt ex adverso, aut cum occumbente Sole se condunt, prodeuntq; illo abeunte. Solem enim vires stellarum fixarum, quas adit, & diurnas sumit itineris comites, quasve adverso ferit pulsatq; radio, excitare, planetarum contra influxum obtundere sua præsentiâ, radiorum verò inflictu acuere, minimè obscurum est ei, qui diligentiùs est astra perscrutatus: ac valdè illustre est testimonium & exemplum in fabrica itine-ris motusq; solaris per zodiacum. Solem, cum obliquo circuitu oporteret 4. anni cardines distinguere & temperare, variareq; illos qualitatibus toti sublunari naturæ necessariis, eamq; va-rietatem sua vi solus efficere nequiret; Deus naturæ conditor totum ejus iter ex diversarum naturarum stellis non confusis sine ordine & discrimine, sed miranda sapientiâ alternatim dis-tributis construxit, & huic vicinos utrinq; tractus similium na-turarum stellis complevit, ut extimulatæ à vicino Sole promerent sese atq; exererent, convenientemq; vicissitudinem præ-starent. Frigidam cœli intemperiem & constitutionem, squalli-dam, inimicam nascentibus affert Sol, ubi limitem sui à nobis recessus occupat remotissimum in Capricorno, quę durat, dum & hoc signum, & aquarii primam faciem pervagatur. Inde Sep-tentriones versus cursu inverso procedens circa mediam pi-scium regione, quod signum humidius est, & naturæ flatuosæ, cùm directiorum in subjectas terras radiorū allifu, tum stella-rum, & in piscium signo consistentium, ac coöriuntium Pegasi, Persei, Andromedæ adjumento, teporem afflat aëri blandio-rem, fusisq;, qui constiterant, humoribus, laxataq; terra, & illis diluta, aut ex nivibus pluviisvé liquore asperso, fœcundorum-favoniorum crebriores elicit & producit flatus, quibus terram vegetat & fœcundat. Ubi signum piscium emensus transiit in-arietem, superata Zodiaci & æquatoris sectione, propiùs subjectæ terræ incumbens radiis eam suis premit urgetque fortius, acuentibus vim eorum signi stellis calidioribus naturâ. Quare tum redundantes noxiosq; terræ humores depascitur atq; ab-sorbet, reliquos cum aridioribus terris miscet exactiùs, tum-subsolanos ventos aridiores commovet, qui superfluum hu-morem morem absumant ac dissipent, ut proscindi terra, conseri possit & occari. Nam & inundati aquis agri exerceri non possent, & innatans aquarum copia cum mandata terræ femina, tum fœ-tus arborum fuisset enectura. Rursus ne caloribus continuis & flatibus arefacta terra semina destituat, & plantas humore, ple-iadum, hyadumq; in tauro & à septentrione hædorum, à meri-die vicini Orionis, atque ex adverso decumbentes Arcturi vires extimulat, quæ sidera turbulenta natura tum austrinos humi-dosq; flatus exuscitant, tum aliquot dierum continuis pluviis & condita semina, & enata frugem, plantasq; universam omnes rigant. Quoniam vero absq; calore fovente & digerente hu-mor putresceret, è vestigio è tauro progredientem Solem exci-piunt geminorum stellæ, quæ cum eo calorem non urentem & consumtivum, sed temperatum, fœcundum & convenientem nascentibus atq; augescentibus rebus procreant. Postquam creverunt in festucam herbæ, jamq; aristas exerunt, & granorum formant initia, cumq; arborum flores in fructum abierunt paulatim grandescentem, humore rursus opus est, qui si deficeret, iustam nunquam assequerentur magnitudinem. Eum cancri pluviosæ stellæ quasi Solis accessu excitatæ, promunt & suppeditant. Ne vero his omnibus absolutis maturatio deesset, (quæ enim si non accederet, perirent naturæ opera quantumvis exquisitè elaborata) ideò Cancro Leonis æstuans urensq; succedit sidus, cui ceu Satellites præsto sunt canis utriusq; flammeæ stellæ, quæ vibratu radiorum Solis ictæ incensæq; exardescunt, augentq; & intendunt Solis ex propinquo verticibus imminentis fervores. His quicquid est reliquum superflui humoris in terra ipsa, & terra natis exugitur ac discutitur, reliquum maturatur. Hi ipsi ardores luxuriem minuunt vitium, uvasq; excoquunt, siq; sunt exuperantes, exustis ceu quodam uredinis carbone vitibus infligunt malum, quod carbunculationem vocant: Unde canicula, ut decretorium uvis sidus, carbuncu-lare dicitur. Ne vero animantium corpora nimium urantur, provocat Sol Etesias ventos, qui cum ipso nascentes atque aspi-rantes, leniunt interdiu æstus moderato & frigidiusculo flatu, Soleq; rursus abeunte desinunt. Post demessas & reconditas fruges tempus appetit satiionis leguminum, milii, panici, item raporum & hujusmodi aliorum, ac vindemiæ in regionibus ca-lidioribus. Verum quia præcedentibus æstibus terra torrefacta, siararetur, non cohæreret, sed comminueretur & spargeretur in pulverem, injectaq; semina aut non admitteret, aut admissa contectaq; non vegetaret, exucca enim esset & retorrida, iccirco extremo à Leone digressu mox commovet Sol virginis astrum, stellasq; sua natura ventosas aquosasq;, tum arcturi vicinum sidus, tempestuosis effectibus celebre & insigne, ac de congregatis horum siderum virtute nubibus fundit aquas, quibus pulverulenta terra pennadescens glutinatur, & arentes ac corrugatæ uvæ reficiuntur atq; augescunt. Confitis leguminibus calore temperato opus est, ut germinent & maturescant, in frigidioribus regionibus eodem vina indigent & fructus, in ca-lidioribus enim fructuū alii citius, & propemodum sub ipsam messem ad maturitatem perveniunt. Talem præstat Sol evoca-tis flatibus fœcundis, & temperatis librae stellis in auxilium ac-citis, mox ubi alteram utriusq; circuli sectionem conscenderit, atq; medium ejus accesserit. Excipit postmodum leguminum messem, & tardiorem vindemiam hiberna satio, cui terram fa-tigatam, atque æstivis laboribus exhaustam, multoq; æstu defic-catam, emolliunt, subigunt ac præparant cum Sole Scorpionis stellæ, & contrarii atq; orientis Solis adversis radiis depressę sub occasu irritataeq; Hyades, plejades, & orionis, hædorumq; aste-rismi: nec vero subruta occultataq; femina repentinu frigus ob-ruat & perimat, auxilio calidi sagittarii Sol id arcet & suspendit, donec actis firmatisq; radicibus contra coeli & frigoris injurias sese muniant. Adeo est evidens & certum ab his stellis Sole extimulatis, hanc, quam annuatim experimur vicissitudinem, effici, ut colonis etiam, agricolis & nautis observationes temporum ex Plejadum, hyadum, orionis, hoedorum & Arcturi ortu vel occasu sint cognitae. Quemadmodum igitur Sol est πηγὴ[?] τῆς ζωϊκῆς δυνάμεως, sic Luna τῆς φυσικῆς[?] & naturalis. Primo enim menstruo suo ambitu excitis, atque in auxilium assumtis stellis insignes ac notabiles parit vicissitudines. Efficacissima tamen est in Tauro, & Cancro, haec namque sidera perambulans, nisi validiores causae obstiterint, educit, cogit & densat nubes, indeque pluvias aquas extillat. Eadem à conjunctione, vel oppositione, vel quadraturis discedens, si feratur ad Saturnum, imbres ut plurimum excitat, aeremq; turbulentat. Sed quàm variè mutatis subinde sedibus, & in alios atq; alios aliorum Planetarum radios incurrens terrena afficiat omnia, primo monstrat dierum Criticorum ratio, deinde maris fluxus atq; refluxus, tertio Lu-natici, id est, sidere[?] certo afflati seu tacti. Ac Criticos quod attinet dies, quaesitum semper fuit, qui fiat, quod in ipsis pene articulis dierum septimorum accidant in aegris subitae morborum cōverfiones, quae aut oppressos eos perimant, aut solutos morbos profligent? Cur qui praecedunt quarti, secuturam septimo conditionem declarent? Causam certe huius rei in Lunae motum Hippocrates pariter atque Galenus retulerunt, quos plaerique etiam recentiores sequuntur, licet alii non tam in astra, quam naturam morborum, corporumq; atq; humorum qualitatem, conditionemac copiam dierum criticorum rationem referri posse existimarunt. Cùm enim Crisis sit subita in mor-bo mutatio, vel ad salutem, vel ad interitum, humorisq; precantis excretio, illa autè quarto, 7. nono deniq; atq; undecimo, decimoque quarto soleat terminari, non immerito quaesitum semsemper fuit, ad quam causam ejusmodi effectus sint referendi? Causam recte Lunæ motui assignari quotidianis experimentis patefactum habetur. Septimo namq; quovis die defertur ad signum illi adversum, in quo fuit constituta, cùm morbus coepit. Sicq; hoc posito morbo quoq; adversatur, cæterorumq; Planetarum consentientia, seq; roborantia nancisci tur suffragia, na-turam ægri contra morbum incitat, instruitq; validissimè, cum-que ea morbum discutit evincitq;, si vero cum morbo consen-tit, ceu in naturæ conspirans perniciem, acuit illum, ut fractam debilitatamq; extinguat. Quartū septimi prænunciare statum & conditionem similiter observatum est, quod eo fere de signo, aliqua ex parte contrario primo (in quo scilicet erat tempore morbi invadentis) transit in aliud cognatius ac familiarius, siq; illud, ut signo primo, sic morbo contrarium fuerit, nec in eo transitu infestum ipsa Luna aliquid aut hostile perpessa fuerit, auget naturæ robur morbi viribus attenuatis, idq; se promit quarto, quo sedem mutat, die. Sic si morbū armatin naturam, aut debiliori præsidio naturæ subvenit, contrariū accidit. Hinc Gal.3.de diebus crit. Luna, inquit, significat dies, quibus erit dispositio hominis in ægritudine sua vel sanitate, nam si applicentur Lunæ stellæ erraticæ fortunatæ, erunt illi dies homini convenientes, & terminabitur crisis ut plurimùm in salutem, si vero infortunatæ, in malum. Ad exactè autem inveniendum dies criticos diligenter locus Lunæ observandus est tempore decu-bitus seu invasionis morbi. Cùm enim Lna est in signo, quod quadrato aspicit illud, in quo fuit in principio ægritudinis, movet crisin, quod plerunq; fit 7. à principio invasionis morbi die, quoniam tunc Luna pervenit ad signum contrarium ei, in quo erat in principio morbi: decimaquarta deinde die communiter venit ad signum oppositum, unde & hæc dies critica dici-tur, 21. vero die iterum attingit quadratū aspectum secundum, & 28. revertitur ad signum, in quo fuit in morbi principio. Ex-emplo res tota evadet manifestior. Invasit aliquem morbus 6. Martii die, post meridiem, Luna peragrante 25. gradum Gemi-norum, quarto die ab invasione morbi pervenict[?] Luna ad 3. si-gnum, hoc est, sextilem Leonis, & tunc indicabit, quid futurum sit in die septima; unde medici hunc diem indicativum dixere, & praesignabitur crisis post meridiem illius diei horaII. quando scilicet Luna perveniet ad 25. Leonis. Cùm autem Luna perve-niet ad quartum signum, hoc est, 25. Virginis, quod fit die 7. ab hora invasionis morbi, movebit crisin, quoniam Luna pervenit ad signum contrarium ei, in quo erat tempore & hora invasionis morbi: quod si vero attigerit quintum signum, 25. scilicet li-brae, quod signum cum eo, in quo Luna erat initio aegritudinis, est in triquetra radiatura, nunciabit tunc, quid futurum sit 14. die, cùm scilicet perventura est ad signum oppositum Geminis, in quibus Luna erat tempore morbi invadentis, unde concitabit maximè naturam contra morbum, quartusq; decimus inde dicitur Criticus. Sic igitur facilè dies critici ex motu Lunae in-vestigari possunt in quocunq; morbo acuto & febrili. Quem-admodum enim Sol mutationes excitat per motum suum in-quatuor quadraturis circuli signorum, id est Zodiaci in morbis Chronicis & diuturnis, sic Luna mutationem operatur in acu-tis motu suo per quatuor Zodiaci quadrantes, dies enim qui numerantur in morbis acutis, imitantur motum Lunae, qui in-chronicis, motum Solis. Sed vehementer erratur circa dies criti-cos, qui imitantur motum Lunae. Non enim semper 7. 14. & 21. sunt critici, qui secundum Lunae motum variant: motus enim Lunae in suo epicyclo, cùm interdum fit velocior, conficiatque saepe uno die 15. fere gradus, interdum tardior, & tunc 13. motu diurno gradus conficit, fit ut & Criticorum dierum ratio non-semper sit una & eadem. Luna namq; motu velox pervenit ad aspeaspectum quadratum primum post 6. dies à principio morbi: tarda verò cursu non pervenit ad quadratum, nisi post diem 7. cum dimidio feré. Quare sæpius decipiuntur Medici Astrono-miam ignorantes, quoniam aliter judicant crisin quàm sit even-tura, non animadvertentes ad applicationem Lunæ cum reliquis Planetis, ejusq; transitum per 12. Signiferi signa, quamvis non adeò sollicitè ac superstitiosè illis inhærendum censeam, sed aliis etiam observationibus innitendum, quæ scilicet eruuntur ex natura morborum, corporumq; atque humorum qualitate, dispositione, copia. Interim tamen astrorum signa non negligenda. Experientia enim certa habetur compertum, Lunam sæpè, cùm pervenit ad signum, quod quadrato radio infestat illud, in quo reperiebatur ægritudinis initio, inter naturam & morbum luctam excitare, in qua illa hunc excutere laborat, cumq; in retundeda[?] morbi sævitia torpescat, invalidior scilicet reddita, primo quoque tempore, nempe vel 7. vel 14. conflictus terminatur. Simile enim quiddam iis corporibus evenit, quod urbi arctissima obsidione oppressæ, quæ, cùm non satis instructa sit commeatu, aliisque ad hostibus resistendum præsidiis, post unam atque alteram oppugnationem deficit atque labascit, ita & in acutis morbis usuvenit, in quibus morbi vim ac insultum observamus, ut tempestates & sæviores ventos nunc consile-scere, nunc tanta violentia renovari atq; intendi, ut natura vix subsistat, nec vita in 7. usq; diem produci posse videatur. Quare Septenarii numeri vis & facultas, cùm in multis naturæ rebus sit animadversa & deprehensa, viri etiam eruditi fere omnes magnam illi virtutem subesse persuadeant, Medicorum præcipuè interest accurate eum observare atq; pensitare. Non enim in secunda tantùm, sed & valetudine adversa, inque dierum, mensium, annorumq; decursu, & morborū indiciis magnum obtinere momentum, quotidiana documenta commonstrant, sic etiam, ut, qui inedia conficiuntur, septimo demum die mor-tem oppetant, aut ægrè, si aliquid lambant ac deglutiant, in no-num vitam producant. Decet igitur Medicum in omni morbo acuto observare diem præcipuè 7. tum etiam, in quo signo exi-stat Luna, cùm morbus primò invadit. Experientia enim habe-tur compertum, Lunam, si in principio morbi inventa fuerit de-bilis & infortunata, in signo unius ejusdemq; cū morbo naturę, ægrotum magis inquietare, si verò fuerit in signo morbo con-trario, ægro afferre levamen: & posset plura ejusmodi experi-menta proferre, nisi ad homines eruditissimos haberetur ser-mo. Nunc in vastum pelagus navigandum, fluxuumq; ac reflu-xuum maris causæ inquirendæ, hic enim utriusque luminis vis evidentissimè deprehenditur. Vos auditores benevolentiæ ve-stræ aurâ benignè me prosequimini. Magnam autem inter Phy-sicos video controversiam extitisse de causa efficiente commo-tionis & æstus marini. Quidam enim causam affcribunt vio-lentæ maris intra angusta terræ loca compressioni, & exiis eru-ptioni, tum violentæ ejusdem ad littora vel alia terræ loca, re-pulsioni, ajunctq;, mare angustis terræ locis compressum violen-tia quadam quærere exitu, & sic celeri prolapsu effundi: idemq; allisum suis fluctibus ad objectas terras, insulas, promontoria, tunc violenter repelli, & sic cum fragore & tumore ingenti ad littora accedere, idq; probatur exemplo fluminum, quæ modò ad hoc, modò ad illud littus fluctibus suis allidunt: cujus mo-tus nullam existimant subesse aliam causam, quàm fluctuum validus ac violentus, qui ad unum ripæ littus alliduntur, ad al-terum latus repulsus. Alii ad terræ motum referunt, quem di-cunt fundum maris concutere: quidam salsedinem, vel potius spiritum quendam maris causam esse prodiderunt, cujus scili-cet vi ipsum mare in æstum agatur: quidam rarefactionem ma-ris, ejusq; condensationem, & illius quidem vi attolli & afflue-re, re, hujus vero refluere: quidam continuam ebullitionem maris & fervorem, vi caloris tum nativi, tum solaris excitatam: quidam ad ventorum impulsum & remissionem causam hujus motus retulerunt: alii ad multorum fluviorum & ingentium in mare influxum: alii ad Solem, quatenus suis radiis calefaciendo attenuat aquas marinas, unde in mari excitatur ebullitio ac fervor, cujus vi attollitur, & ad littora violenter recurrit, unde similem dicunt hunc motum marinum fervori aquae ad ignem ebullientis: alii deniq; referunt ad Lunam, quatenus videlicet vel motu suo locali, vel luminis incremento & decremento, vel naturali quadam sympathia aquas marinas commovet. Etsi autem in tanta opinionum varietate difficile sit veritatem astruere, & prima ratio videatur omnium probabilissima, fatendum tamen cum Magistra experientia est, & pro confesso habendum & indubitato, quoties Luna cum mundo se attollit ad coeli culmen, id est, ab horizonte ad Meridianum ascendit, toties maria impelli, insurgere atq; intumescere: quoties à meridiano ad horizontem descendit, mare à littoribus refluere, ac se contrahere atq; recipere quasi resorptum. Unde patet æstum maris esse fluxionem reciprocam, qua statò tempore mare ad littus accedit & recedit. Etsi vero multiplex sit, ac secundum cujusq; regionis situm naturamq; variet, genuina tamen causa dependet à coelo, potissimum vero à Luna, quamvis non parum juvetur à Sole. Animadversum enim est, interlunio & plenilunio, cum scilicet Luna Soli vel subjicitur, vel è diametro objicitur, maria incitari vehementius, diffundique ac ruere impetuosius, ternis diebus ante, & totidem post, languescere vero æstum, ac velut lentescere circa Lunæ quadraturas & dimidiationes. Plures observationes tradit ex Poßidonio Strabo, & Plinius, videlicet quòd tolerabiliores contingant fluxus atq; refluxus, Luna pererrante signa tropica, instabiliores contra ac incertiores, permeante signa æquinoctialia: ingrave-scere quoq; æstus atq; intendi, cùm Luna in Austrum digressa propiore nisu atq; conatu vim suam exercet, & ab æquinoctiis ad solstitia, id est, ab ariete in cancrum, itemq; à libra in capricornum, & contra à solstitiis ad æquinoctia, id est, à cancro in libram, & à libra in capricornum: leniri verò maris æstum atq; mitescere, cùm Aquilonia est, & in Septentriones evagata. Ut-plurimum autè semis[?] cum quadrante horis mare accrescit, sum-maq; littora premit, totidemq; decrescit, reditq; in altù, qua in-reciprocatione Lunæ motum plane sequitur: prope enim hori-zonte existente littora plena redundant, & maria obvia flumina retrudunt, eádem meridianù conscendente, hoc est, cœli fasti-gium tenente, aquæ recedunt, littoraq; cernuntur inania. Estq; eò plenior æstus, quò facies Lunæ major, unde plenilunio vehe-mentior est. Ergo hæc ratio est, cur mare singulis horis semis[?] vel affluat, vel defluat, cùm totidem horis Luna quadrantem sui motus diurni conficiat, singulis verò vicenis quatuor horis bis intumescat, bisq; resideat, ut Venetis & Mediterranei maris ac-colis notum est. Indici maris refluxus Alexandri Magni bellis innotuit, cujus incautum exercitum, naturæq; freti ignarum repente invaserat. Ad caput Rubrum Africæ diversus est, nam quaternis horis affluit tanto impetu, ut navigia plenis velis cur-rentia retrò urgeat, octonis autem recurrit, quò enim celerius accrescit, hoc lentius recedit. Sentiunt hunc quoq; maris, ceu aperientis atq; expandentis se, impetum retroacta, inhibita & detenta flumina: Ad Hamburgum quidem Albim 18. ab Ocea-no milliaribus: Ad Antuerpiam Scaldim, itidem 18. fere millia-ribus, regurgitari, augescere & effluere mari accedente, eo-demq; reciprocante diminui & relabi intra alveos, iisdem, qui-bus mare, vicibus, accolis notum est. Vehementissimos habet æstus Oceanus, mitiores mare mediterraneum: nullos Hellefpontus, & pontus Euxinus, Ligusticum item, Balthicum, & Caspium maria. Bis die noctéq; effusum resorptumq; alternat Siculum mare ad Scyllae & Charybdis cavernosos scopulos. Septies Chalcidicum ad Euboeam, Euripi alternantibus refluxibus celebre & insigne. Sed & praeter aestum alio, sed minus tamen evidenti motu, eoq; perpetuo, agitari maria, nautae comperenerunt, nimirum Oceanum ipsum, qui late fusus alluit, interluit & ambit terram universam, tum mediterraneum mare, quod per angustias freti Herculei infusum amplo patentiq; alveo orbis habitati medium inundat. Experiuntur quoq; nautae, si solverint à Nerito promontorio Hispaniae, & vela fecerint Britanniam versus ad orientem Solem, longè se tardius provehi, quàm si in Hispaniam revertantur. Idem contingit iis, qui ex Hispania in insulas recens à Columbo Genuensi in Oceano Occidentali inventas vela dirigunt, iter enim illud 24. dierum spacio in accessu, secundis ventis devecti conficiunt, quibus Hispaniam repetentibus vix trium quatuorq; mensium spacium sufficit, etiamsi aura flatusq; nullus adversetur. Et Lusitani, qui Africae oram & promontorium Bonae Spei praeternavigant, ut Taprobanem insulam ingrediantur allatum inde merces Indicas, etiā secundis aspirantibus ventis tardius & difficilius multò accedunt, quàm inde domum revertuntur. Causa hujus rei nulla alia datur, nisi quòd Oceanus perpetuo & continente, rapidissimoque orbium coelestium ab ortu in occasum circumactu, in eandem impellitur, cogitur & contorquetur partem, non quidem evidenter & manifestè, sensibiliter tamen. Hunc occurrentis ex coeli impulsu maris renixum, inhibere ajunt & retardare vel concitatissimarum navium impetum. Eodem coeli impulsu mare mediterraneum, quod angustioribus litto-rum repagulis coërcetur, in gyrum circumagi observatum nostra memoria est. A Palaestinae enim scopulis, qui orientem Solem respiciunt, incitatum, & fecundùm Phœniciæ, Pamphiliæ, Hellefponti, & Græciæ oras, littora lambendo provolutum, dehinc Dalmatiæ, Histriæ & Illyridis alluit continentem, atque in intimo recessu maris Adriatici eum angulum, in quo Venetiæ sitæ sunt, obiens, in oppositum littus Italiæ Flaminiam versus reflectitur, indeq; per Piceni, Apuliæ, Magnæ Græciæ & Siciliæ limites ad orientem Solem revolutum, moxq; & Tyrrheni maris oram universam circumiens, & Narbonensis Galliæ, Beticam Hispaniæ, provincias, fretiq; Herculei angustias præterfluens, & Mauritaniæ, Africæ & Ægypti littora perlabens, redit ad ortum. Exæstuationis hujus etsi obscurior ratio sit, tamen in Sole & Luna causa est. Cùm enim Horizon & Meridiannas[?] mu-tuis interfectionibus totum cœlum in 4. plagas divellant, quarum duabus contrariis vecta lumina affluxus faciunt accessuf-que inundantibus aquis, ab exortu ad cœli culmen, & ab occa-su ad cœli imum seu angulum terræ: duabus verò aliis recessus ac reflexus. Utriusq; igitur sideris circumactu quotidiano effectuq; maria cōmoventur, & mutantur hæ commotiones congressibus ipsorum inter se, aspectibusq; mutuis, incessuq; per diversos zodiaci tractus, & ad ipsos marium tractus dissimili inclinatione. Lunæ tamen potiorem esse vim inde patet, quòd hac exoriente æstus incipiunt, tantoq; tardius incipiunt, quanto longius provectailla, serius prodit. Sed qua vi trahat, moveatq; maria, an solo radiorum vibratu & emissione, an verò alio quopiam medio interveniente, non ineptè[?] quæritur? Etsi enim mirando consensu vim radiorum Solis Lunæq; in terrenis corporibus humores afficere & agitare, tota hæc inferior natura luculenter demonstrat, tamen cùm videantur æstus marini similes esse fervori calentis ad ignem aquæ, qua ratione potest hoc Lunæ imputari? Peucerus in lib. de divinat. hanc recte subdit causam, sicut aqua fervet, cùm resolutorum ardoris vehevehementia tenuiorum halituum copia, & levitate ac tenuitate sua, & vi caloris impulsa diffusaq; exitum quærit, quem, nisi turbatis & agitatis aquis, & ab imo ad summum, à medio ad extremos aheni ambitus dispulsis, non invenit: sic maria exæstuare, cum virtute radiorum magna copia extenuati, impulsi aut tracti ab imo maris fundo, marini terreniq; halitus, luctantes cum circumfusis aquis, atq; erumpere, exitu patefacto, anniten-tes, displodunt, discerpunt, ac veluti distorquent aquas, quæ, dum urgentibus halitibus concedunt exitum, dehiscendo ac discedendo adiguntur ad littora & fluminum ostia, ubi his repressa flumina primo sistunt, mox retrovertunt cursus, elevataq; ex reciprocatione effunduntur, & proxima quæq; inundant atque integunt, & quidem ad littora ab imo ipsa maria res varias ceu excrementa revomunt atq; expuunt. Oceanus æstus habet sæviores, leniores mediterrancum mare, quod isthic aperta magnitudo siderum vim laxè & latè grassantium efficacius sentit, hic eandem arcent angustiæ: unde & Balthicum, & reliqua maria angustis coarctata alveis, atq; à radiorum efficaci projectu longius dissita, & propter profunditatem radiis lumi-nū minus pervia, æstus nullos experiūtur, ut & propter easdem causas mare Ligusticum, tum etiam quod fundus saxeus in halitus resolvi nequit agitationi accommodos. Sed nec maria solum, verum & cæterae hujus inferioris & sublunaris mundi partes experiri se fatentur Lunæ vim & efficaciam, cum perpessarum mutationum edunt notas, agris sterilescentibus, rubigine vel uredine fruges, carbunculo occupante vites, floribus decidentibus, proveniente ubiq; erucarū diversorumq; vermium & infectorum copia, tum venenatis in aërem expirantibus halitibus. In Pleniluniis, quibus supra terram totas noctes eminet, æstate, gelida aura impressum aëri arcet atq; elidit fervorem, lenitque ex æstu contractas molestias, quod certè experimento hocanno1611. didicimus, cùm totum ver à Martio in 20. usque Maji irregulari plane, & vix hominum memoria observato, æ-stu premeretur: hyeme verò tepidiore aura mitigat frigoris ri-gorem, quia æstivis pleniluniis procul abit adversa Soli, hibernis per æstivum circulum propius accedit, Deo ita constituente & ordinante. Lunatici quoq; sideris vim manifesto experiuntur: laborant enim furore certis intervallis recurrente, indeq; id mali genus nomen accepit, quod iis qui ipso interlunio nati sunt, familiare esse consueverit, sive quod statis Lunæ ratione intervallis soleat reverti. Julius Firmicus 4.Math.idipsum confirmans ait: Luna male collocata aut Spasmaticos facit, aut Lunaticos, aut caducos. Est in exemplis quidam, qui, quoties intueretur Lunam, toties in morbum caducum incidisse fertur. Et experiuntur id noctu peregrinantes sub Luna plena. Ubi tamen hoc notandum, effectus quandoque diversos & varios eventus Lunam ciere pro diversis reliquorum errantium fide-rum cum ipsa congressibus & configurationibus, prout scilicet vel faustis se mutuo, felicibusq; radiis complectuntur, vel minacibus ac hostilibus se feriunt ac infestant, proq; habitudine & positu ad subjectas terras, cumque iisdem familiaritate & congruentia ratione signorum, in quibus consistunt, quæ omnia & singula bonum Astrologum considerare diligenter decet, ad nativitatum judicia juxta artis præcepta, recte informanda. Ex hactenus dictis patet, cùm aër ita diversimode ab astris cœli afficiatur, variosq; cœlestium luminum influxus ac vires suscipiat, præcipuè verò tum, cùm existunt in signis tropicis, ut cancro & capricorno, & æquinoctialibus, ut ariete & libra, in quibus insignes fiunt mutationes aëris, & temporum conversiones, non tantum temperamenta mutari, & actiones quæ temperamentum seu justam humorum contemperationem sequuntur, verùm etiam diversis cœli constitutionibus aliter atq; aliter affici principes corporum nostrorum partes, quiq; his af-sistunt & serviunt, humores & spiritus. Hinc fit, ut quandoque langueamus, aut contra rectius valeamus, lætemur, aut subito in mœstitiâ labamur: celerius, expeditius & alacrius, in quo ela-boramus, conficiamus, nec sine difficultate exerceamus, sensi-bus vigeamus, & cùm ad cogitandum animum dirigimus, faci-le inquisita percipiamus, imò abundemus copia bonarum co-gitationum, aut contra intendamus omnes ingenii vires, desu-demus, ringamur, nihil quicquam tamen, quod sit aptum, propositoq; conveniens, efficimus, eaq; omnia absq; conspicuâ aliqua & evidente causa contingere fatemur, scilcet, quod diversi fiderum positus, nobis non advertentibus, alias effectiones im-primunt, vel concitatis turbatisq; humoribus, vel spiritibus se-datis, perpurgatis ac collustratis, vel excitatis ac roboratis principalium membrorum facultatibus. Hinc fit, ut excitatis spiriti-bus, vigenteq; mente rectius circumspiciantur omnia ac decer-nantur, provideaturq;, quid intercidere aut obsistere possit, quam eadem languente aut turbata. Ab astris igitur oriri, ut a-liâs simus ad cogitandum, faciendumq; alacriores & expeditio-res, aliâs minus idonei, qui negat, veratro expurgandus potiùs quàm demonstrationibus convincendus est. Confessi sunt hoc ipsum Clarissimi Medicorum Hippocrates & Galenus. Et licet temperamenta multum sumant à materia & femine, tamen plurimùm immutari, alterari, & temperari quandoq; fiderum vi & impulsu fatendum est. Divinaturo autem ex fiderum positu, quoniam stellarum omnium naturæ & qualitates, diligenter sunt exigendæ & explorandæ priùs, quàm ad Prognosticum ipsum perveniatur, præmittenda necessario sunt, vel potiùs præ-struenda fundamenta quædam, quæ ipsum prognosticum ordine naturæ antecedunt, quibus non cognitis, vel malè intelle-ctis, illud protinus labitur. Ordienda autem contemplatio & cognitio est ab illis stellis fixis, quæ constituunt 12. zodiaci signa, quorum etiam præcipua vis deprehenditur, ut & eorum, quæ minori his utrinq; intervallo assistunt, ut Orionis, arcturi, Procyonis, Sirii, &c. Hic igitur maxime inserviunt judiciis Astrologicis dictorum signorum cognitæ differentiæ, quæ scilicet constituant trigonum igneum, quæ aqueum, quæ terreum, & quæ aërium: item quæ æquinoctialia, quæ solstitialia, quæ mobilia, quæ fixa, & quæ communia, quæ masculina, quæ fœminina, quæ rectè ascendant, & quæ obliquè ascendant, quæ fœcunda, quæ sterilia, quæ septentrionalia, quæ meridionalia, quæ præcipientia seu alta, quæ obedientia, quæ ascendentia, quæ descendentia, quæ muta, quæ rationalia, quæ invicem sibi amica, quæ inimica, quæ aliena & non conjuncta, & quæ invicem devincta, quæ sint ingenii, facundiæ & eloquentiæ, &c.
units.tr: For those idle fellows do not perceive or understand how much harm ignorance of celestial things does to human affairs, or how much benefit knowledge of them brings. To be ignorant of nature, that is, of the harmony and agreement of the heavenly and elemental bodies, is the extreme of wretchedness and blindness. It leads minds into such weakness and delusion that they foolishly despise what they do not understand and cannot grasp by reason. With a kind of proud and haughty folly they reject the science of the stars and the doctrine of celestial influences, which in the theatre of nature has nothing more excellent, nothing more sublime, nothing more useful, nothing more distinguished for preserving, directing and regulating the actions of life, and nothing more outstanding and suitable for ordering and shaping morals and for restraining the more violent impulses of the mind and kindling the more sluggish and lazy ones. The monuments of both sacred and secular letters bear witness that the most ancient patriarchs, the wise men of Greece, the Gymnosophists of the Indians, and the other more sincere philosophers of Greece cultivated it, and that many most holy men and most learned kings and princes of many ages always held it in the highest esteem and honour. Yet no one who has read the histories of the times will deny that this doctrine has always been regarded as too lofty for the lowly crowd ever to rise to it. For that the cause of birth and death comes from the motion of the heavens, as the setting follows the rising and the end follows the beginning, is grasped only by the highest intellects. Indeed, what is that whole nature of things but a certain orderly and always constant change and transformation? What is the life and death of living creatures but a certain motion from beginning to end? Furthermore, astrology teaches what that motion of the heavens and the rays of the stars bring to the human race. Whoever knows its principles, from which it starts and on which it is founded and stabilised, and the limits within which it is contained, will of his own accord refrain from abuse. Therefore, while I defend this most noble part of fate, which has been crushed by reproaches, lies in darkness, and has begun to be mocked again, from calumnies, restore it to its former lustre, and bring it back into the light as far as lies in me, I ask that you hear me most kindly. And first, so that the origin of astromancy may be shown more clearly, and so that it may become plain on what principles and demonstrations it rests, I think it is not unknown that there are two parts of the doctrine of the stars. One of them shows in the stars the most certain laws of celestial motions and is called astronomy; the other shows the effects and significations of the stars and is called divinatory, or mantic [μαντικὴ]. The former measures and investigates by a certain mathematical method the various motions of the stars, their distances, heights, advances and retrogradations. And although it is built on manifest demonstrations, and holds this remarkable and necessary and well-known usefulness, namely that from the motion of the Sun and Moon we may keep the fixed limits, divisions and parts of the year and of months, and a just description of the seasons of the year, with the equinoxes and solstices marked, and therefore it is commended by almost all learned men as a certain art, never praised enough, and truly a heavenly art; nevertheless very many are found of the Cyclopean stock who make light of it and by their examples try in every way to draw others away from it too. But their judgments are at once refuted by divine testimonies. For it is written: "And let them be for lights in the signs, the seasons, the days and the years" (Gen. 1.), where surely the observation and watching of the motions is enjoined. As for the years, I certainly do not think that any Cyclopes were ever so savage, nor any barbarism so harsh, as not to have noted the intervals of years and months and handed them down to posterity. So it is shameful for anyone serving even in the camp of letters and the Muses to neglect and disparage this art, and to allow it to be proudly mocked by the most foolish judgments of the unlearned, since it reminds us of God and of his wonderful wisdom and goodness. It shows him so nearly that Paul says God can almost be handled with the hands (Acts 17.), revealing himself to us in this wonderful workmanship of his, in which, as in a most bright mirror, we look almost upon God himself. So Alcinous the Platonist rightly said (ch. 6): "Those who apply themselves to astronomy are led from things perceived by the eyes to an invisible and intelligible essence." Let us take as an example the Sun and Moon among the lights of heaven. Once their motion and powers have been clearly seen, the passage to astromancy will afterwards be easy. For the Sun does not always stir up the same and equal qualities and powers in our bodies, but according to the region of the heavens through which it passes, and whether it is nearer to or further from our sight, it acts and by its approach and recession produces different parts of the year that differ in their qualities. Daily experience plainly proves this. For what, I ask, is more evident than that the heat of the air and the summer warmth come from the Sun, by its rays and their reflection, and that the cool night air and the dewy moisture are produced by the Moon, as travellers who journey by night under a full Moon bear witness? Who does not know that with the influx of solar heat the spring and summer, like the horn of plenty, overflow with the sweetness of crops and flowers, and that insects too, flies, snakes, frogs and swallows, which were half-dead in the cold of winter and hid themselves in the cracks of boards, in the pith of elder, in the caverns of the shore and within the trunks of trees, come back to life? So it is plain that the heat is not only from the Sun but in the Sun itself, or an innate and peculiar heating power, as Ptolemy testifies (Tetrabiblos, bk 1, ch. 3). Our more learned philosophers of this age agree with him too. For among others Taurellus, against Cesalpinus (bk 3, p. 569), says: "We profess that by the natural power of the stars heat and cold, as well as many other qualities, manifest and hidden, are shaken into sublunary bodies." And indeed no firm and solid reason can prove why the stars should not be called hot in their nature. For they are bright bodies, and like candles lit in the world, and set in the heaven by God, made as a rational creature to be an image of the divine Trinity, so that from their periodic motions and daily revolutions, which divine wisdom foresaw, they might understand the future, and by stirring up the things that are carried along by the whirling of the lunar sphere, they might bring about generation. All bright things are hot, because they are bright, and the brighter a thing is the hotter it is. Hence the Sun, being the brightest of all, is the greatest heater of all. Yet these things must be understood of celestial light, whose first effect is by its nature to heat and to quicken. For light in crystal and ice is not hot, and therefore does not heat, because it has no principle of heating in itself. As for the claim that Saturn is called cold and the Moon cold, this must be taken comparatively, as slightly warm. For although Saturn is hot, because it is bright, yet because it produces more cold than heat it is also called cold. For when joined to the Sun it has been observed to diminish the Sun's heat, and for this effect it is called cold. The reason why it does not warm the earth is that in it there are other more hidden qualities and powers, which cool, and because of which the heat is prevented from descending to the earth. Also, the bright bodies of the heavens heat more or less according to their nearness or distance, except the Moon, which, though it shares in both the celestial and the sublunary region, is found to be cold and moist rather than hot. It is therefore vain to say that the Sun is not hot and yet heats, namely by power and effectively, just as wine heats and yet is not actually hot, but only potentially [δυνάμει]. For the Sun could never heat by its bright rays if it did not heat by an innate heat, and the rays of heat would not have their principle in themselves. Nor could the Moon ever cool or moisten unless it did so by a natural and cooling power. Thus nothing more foolish or absurd has been, or can be, thought of, than that heat, moisture, cold, dryness and the other proper qualities belong to corruptible elements, while in the heavens there are none. Aristotle himself (Meteorology, bk 1, ch. 3) calls the stars hot, and (On the Generation of Animals, bk 2, ch. 3) says that the heat which is in living creatures is neither fire nor derived from fire, but comes from a body more divine than the elements, and that this body is the starry element. In the same way, that other qualities too are found in the heavens, such as rarity, density, lightness, softness and transparency, is known by sure experience, even though they are not of elemental condition and kinship. For by the memory of all ages the same heaven and the same stars have remained uncorrupted to this day, in the same size, colour and distance, and in so long a span of time no blemish has fallen on the celestial bodies. Hence Aristotle rightly said that the heaven, by its nature, is subject to no birth, no death, no increase, no decrease, no alteration, and so is free of all heaviness and lightness, and he proves this by firm arguments (On the Heavens, bk 1, ch. 3). So the general axiom falls and vanishes into nothing: "Whatever is made of matter is corruptible." For this must be understood of the matter of the sublunary things, which is the cause of decay, separation and division, because of the privation attached to it, which is not in celestial matter; and for this reason too the heaven is not subject to corruptions and alterations. Moreover, among the celestial qualities the most conspicuous to sense and to effect are heat, which excels in the Sun, and coldness, which is in the Moon and Saturn. That heat is produced and poured out by the bright rays of the Sun is clearer than the Sun itself. That coldness and moisture are poured into the sublunary things by the light of the Moon through its outflowing ray is known from daily experiments. But for the heat of the Sun and the moisture of the Moon to arise in different places and lands, motion is required, which carries the light around. For just as by the daily whirling of the Sun about the earth, by its rising and setting and its passage across the middle or summit of the heavens (by which motion it carries along now one star and now another, and now drives down and casts out one that lies under the setting), we see the air either disturbed and clouded over, or excessively cleared and brightened, or on the contrary chilled, moistened or dried, and changed now this way and now that according to the nature, position and condition of the stars that rise, set, or shoot their rays at the Sun; so the Moon, being nearest the earth, most plainly flows into earthly things. Waxing, it stirs up moistures and pours them into bodies, and waning, it sucks them back again. When the orb is full and shining, plants and animals overflow with liquids; when it wanes they diminish; at new Moon, when it turns all its light away from the earth back to the heaven, they dry up. Again, when it climbs above the horizon, the seas, as if impelled by the force of a star, swell and flow in; when it goes down, they ebb, and little by little they subside and become quiet.
