Farmers learned these things by experience and assigned to them the most suitable times for sowing, for bringing livestock together to mate, for setting domestic birds to brood, and for cutting timber to be burned or used for building. Although the effects and significations and influences of the Sun and Moon are the most important and conspicuous (because the Sun surpasses the rest in the bulk of its body and the abundance of its native light, in brilliance and efficacy, whence it is called the president of the day (Gen. 1.), "a wonderful vessel, the work of the Most High" (Ecclus 43.), "ruler of the world" (Wisd. 3.), leader, prince and governor of the other lights, as Cicero calls it, and "the heart of the world," as Ptolemy calls it; and by its approach and the falling of its rays it either moderates, or stirs up, or dulls, or burns the other stars), and although these are also steeped in the light of the Sun, and as nearest to the earth they receive whatever is derived from the others, gather it and send it down in heaps, nevertheless the influx of the other stars, both wandering and fixed, which long experience has detected, is not to be made light of. For the natures of the fixed stars produce effects that recur at fixed seasons of the year, and these show themselves most strongly when the stars rise with the Sun or stand in opposition to it, or set opposite, or hide themselves when the Sun goes down and come forth when it departs. It is no obscure matter to anyone who has searched the stars more diligently that the Sun takes the powers of the fixed stars it approaches, and takes them as companions of its daily course, or strikes and drives back those that lie opposite with its ray; that by its presence it dulls the influence of the planets, but by the falling of its rays sharpens it. There is a very clear testimony and example in the construction of the Sun's path and motion through the zodiac. Since the Sun, by its oblique circuit, must mark and temper the four cardinal points of the year and vary them with qualities necessary to the whole sublunary nature, and since the Sun alone could not bring about this variety by its own power, God, the Creator of nature, built its whole course from the stars of different natures, not jumbled together without order or distinction, but distributed alternately with wonderful wisdom. He filled the tracts on either side of it with stars of kindred natures, so that, stirred up by the nearby Sun, they might put forth and show themselves and provide the fitting change. The Sun brings the cold, unpleasant and squalid disposition of the heavens, harmful to things being born, when it occupies the furthest point of its withdrawal from us in Capricorn, and this lasts as long as it wanders through that sign and the first face of Aquarius. From there, proceeding towards the north with a reversed course, around the middle region of Pisces, a sign that is moister and of a windy nature, it breathes a milder warmth into the air, both by the striking of the more direct rays on the lands beneath and with the help of the stars of the Pisces sign, and those rising together with it, Pegasus, Perseus and Andromeda. It melts the humours that had stood still, loosens the earth, dissolves them within it, or sprinkles moisture from snows or rains, and draws out and produces the more frequent breaths of the fertile west winds, by which it quickens and fructifies the earth. When the Sun, having passed through the sign of Pisces, enters Aries, past the intersection of the zodiac and the equator, it bears down more closely on the earth below and presses and urges it more strongly with its rays, the stars of that sign, which are hotter by nature, sharpening their force. Therefore it then feeds on and absorbs the superfluous and harmful humours of the earth, mixes the rest more thoroughly with the drier lands, and stirs up the drier east winds, which carry away and disperse the excess moisture, so that the earth may be broken up, sown and harrowed. For fields flooded with water could not be worked, and the floating abundance of waters would have destroyed both the seed entrusted to the earth and the fruit of the trees. Again, lest the earth, dried by continual heats and blasts, should be left without seed, it stirs up the moisture of the plants by the forces of the Pleiades and Hyades in Taurus, of the Kids to the north, and of Orion, which lies near them to the south, and of Arcturus, which sets opposite. These stars, of turbulent nature, then stir up the southern and moist winds and water with continual rains for several days, and water all the sown seed, the sprouted grain and all the plants. But since moisture would rot without a warm and digesting heat, the twins' stars receive the Sun as soon as it leaves Taurus, and with it they produce a heat that does not burn or consume, but is temperate, fertile and suited to things that are being born and growing. When the grasses have grown into stalks and now put forth ears and begin to form the grains, and the flowers of the trees have gradually turned into fruit that grows larger, moisture is again needed, and if it failed they could never reach their proper size. The rainy stars of Cancer, roused as if by the approach of the Sun, bring it forth and supply it. And lest, when all these things are finished, ripening should be lacking (for if it did not come, the works of nature, however exquisitely wrought, would perish), therefore the glowing and burning star of Leo follows Cancer. Around it, like attendants, are the two flaming stars of the Dog, which, struck and kindled by the vibration of the Sun's rays, blaze up and increase and intensify the heats of the Sun as it hangs near the zenith. By these, whatever superfluous moisture is left in the earth and in the things grown from it is drained off and dispersed, and what remains is ripened. These same heats lessen the vice of luxuriance and bake the grapes, and if they are excessive, they inflict a disease on the vines, as if with a burnt coal of mildew, which they call carbunculation; hence the Dog Star, as the sign that decides the grapes, is said to carbuncle them. But lest the bodies of living creatures be burned too much, the Sun calls up the Etesian winds, which, rising and blowing with it, soften the heat by day with a moderate and somewhat cool breeze, and cease again when the Sun departs. After the crops have been reaped and stored, the time comes for sowing pulses, millet, panic grass, also turnips and other things of this kind, and in the warmer regions for the vintage. But because in the preceding summers the earth, parched by the heat, would not cohere when ploughed but would be crushed and scattered into dust, and would either refuse the seed thrown into it or, if admitted and covered, would not sprout, for it would be dry and parched, therefore, as soon as the Sun has left Leo, it stirs the star of Virgo, and the stars of Libra, windy and watery by nature, and the neighbouring star of Arcturus, famous and remarkable for its stormy effects. From the clouds gathered by the power of these stars it pours down water, by which the dusty earth is made wet and clammy, and the dried and wrinkled grapes are restored and grow. The sown pulses need a temperate heat in order to sprout and ripen; in the colder regions the vines and fruits need the same, but in the warmer ones some of the fruits ripen sooner, almost at harvest time. Such heat the Sun provides when it has called up fertile winds and brought in the temperate stars of Libra as helpers, as soon as it has climbed the other intersection of the two circles and reached its middle. After the harvest of the pulses, the winter sowing follows, and the later vintage. The stars of Scorpio prepare and soften the land, exhausted by summer labours and dried by much heat, and the Hyades, Pleiades, Orion and the Kids are roused by the Sun's opposed rays as it rises in the setting sign. Nor should the buried and hidden seed be overwhelmed and destroyed by a sudden cold; the warm Sagittarius helps, and the Sun keeps this off and holds it back until the sown seed has firmed its roots and defended itself against the injuries of sky and frost. So plain and certain is it that this annual change we experience is brought about by these stars when the Sun has stirred them up, that the rising and setting of the Pleiades, Hyades, Orion, the Kids and Arcturus are known to farmers, husbandmen and sailors as signs of the seasons. Therefore, just as the Sun is the fountain of the vital power [πηγὴ τῆς ζωϊκῆς δυνάμεως], so the Moon is that of the natural [τῆς φυσικῆς]. For in each of its monthly courses it stirs up and, taking in the aid of the stars, brings about remarkable and noticeable changes. Yet it is most powerful in Taurus and Cancer, for, wandering through these stars, unless stronger causes stand in the way, it draws out, gathers and thickens clouds, and from these squeezes out rainwater. Departing from conjunction, opposition or the quadratures, if it is carried to Saturn it generally stirs up storms and disturbs the air. But how variously, by changing its seats from time to time and running into this or that ray of the other planets, it affects all earthly things, is first shown by the reckoning of the critical days, then by the flow and ebb of the sea, and thirdly by lunatics, that is, those who are touched or struck by a certain star. As for the critical days, it has always been asked how it comes about that sudden changes of diseases occur in the sick almost at the very joints of the seventh days, which either carry off those oppressed or put an end to the diseases that have been loosened. Why do the days that come before the fourth announce the condition that will follow on the seventh? The cause of this, indeed, Hippocrates and Galen alike referred to the motion of the Moon, and most of the more recent writers follow them, although others have thought that the reason for the critical days may be referred not so much to the stars as to the nature of the diseases, and to the quality, condition and quantity of the bodies and humours. For since a crisis is a sudden change in a disease, either to health or to death, and an excretion of the morbid humour, and since it usually ends on the fourth, seventh, ninth, eleventh or fourteenth day, it has not without reason always been asked to what cause such effects should be referred. That the cause is rightly assigned to the motion of the Moon is held to be plain from daily experience. For on every seventh day it is carried to the sign opposite that in which it was placed when the disease began. So, when the disease has begun, the Moon too is opposed to it, and when it finds the support of the agreeing and strengthening stars of the other planets, it stirs up the nature of the sick person against the disease and arms it most strongly. And when it does so, it shakes off and overcomes the disease. But if it agrees with the disease, as if conspiring with nature to destroy it, it sharpens the disease so that it extinguishes the broken and weakened nature. That the fourth day after the seventh similarly announces the state and condition has also been observed, because from a sign partly opposed to the first (namely the one in which the Moon was at the time the disease attacked), it passes into another more akin and familiar; and if that sign is opposed to the disease as the first sign was, and the Moon has suffered nothing hostile or harmful in that passage, it increases the strength of nature as the force of the disease is weakened, and this shows itself on the fourth day, when it changes its seat. Thus, if the disease has taken arms against nature, or nature comes to the aid of the disease with a weaker defence, the opposite happens. Hence Galen (On Critical Days, bk 3): "The Moon, he says, signifies the days on which a man's condition in his sickness or health will be. For if the fortunate wandering stars are applied to the Moon, those days will be suitable for the man, and the crisis will generally end in health; but if the unfortunate, in harm." To find the critical days exactly, the place of the Moon must be carefully observed at the time of the decumbence, or onset of the disease. For when the Moon is in the sign that looks at the one in which it was at the beginning of the illness with a square aspect, it moves the crisis, which usually happens on the seventh day from the beginning of the attack, because then the Moon reaches the sign opposite to that in which it was at the beginning of the disease. Then, on the fourteenth day, it commonly comes to the opposite sign, whence this day too is called critical; on the twenty-first day it again touches the second square aspect, and on the twenty-eighth it returns to the sign in which it was at the beginning of the disease. The whole matter will become clearer by an example. A disease attacked someone on the 6th of March, in the afternoon, while the Moon was passing through the 25th degree of Gemini. On the fourth day from the onset of the disease the Moon came to the third sign, that is, the sextile of Leo, and then it indicates what will happen on the seventh day; whence physicians have called this day indicative, and the crisis will be signalled for the afternoon of that day at the second hour, when the Moon will have reached the 25th of Leo. But when the Moon reaches the fourth sign, that is, 25 Virgo, which happens on the seventh day at the hour of the onset of the disease, it will move the crisis, since the Moon has come to the sign opposite to that in which it was at the time and hour of the onset of the disease. But if it has touched the fifth sign, namely 25 Libra, which sign, being in a triangular ray with the one in which the Moon was at the beginning of the sickness, then it will announce what is going to happen on the fourteenth day, when it is about to reach the sign opposite to Gemini, in which the Moon was at the time of the attack. From this it especially stirs up nature against the disease, and the fourteenth day from there is called critical. So critical days can easily be found from the motion of the Moon in any acute and febrile disease. For just as the Sun brings about changes, by its motion through the four squares of the circle of signs, that is the zodiac, in chronic and long diseases, so the Moon works changes in acute ones by its motion through the four quadrants of the zodiac. For the days that are counted in acute diseases imitate the motion of the Moon, as those in chronic ones imitate the motion of the Sun. But people are greatly mistaken about the critical days that imitate the motion of the Moon. For the 7th, 14th and 21st are not always critical, though they vary according to the Moon's motion. The Moon's motion in its epicycle, when it is sometimes faster, often covers nearly 15 degrees in one day, and sometimes slower, when it covers 13 degrees by its daily motion; so the reckoning of the critical days is not always one and the same. For the Moon, moving quickly, reaches the first square aspect after six days from the beginning of the disease; but when its course is slow it does not reach the square until about the seventh day and a half. Therefore physicians who are ignorant of astronomy are often deceived, because they judge the crisis otherwise than it is going to happen, not noticing the application of the Moon to the other planets and its passage through the twelve signs of the zodiac. Yet I do not think we should cling to these so anxiously and superstitiously, but should rely on other observations too, which are drawn from the nature of the diseases and the quality, disposition and quantity of the bodies and humours. Meanwhile, nonetheless, the signs of the stars are not to be neglected. For it is held by sure experience that when the Moon comes to the sign which strikes with a square ray the sign in which it was found at the onset of the sickness, it stirs up a struggle between nature and disease, in which nature labours to shake the disease off; and while the disease, grown fierce, grows sluggish in being beaten back, the struggle ends at the first opportunity, either on the seventh or the fourteenth day, because the disease has become weaker. Something similar happens to those bodies which, pressed by a very tight siege of a city, which is not well supplied with provisions and other means of resisting the enemy, after one or two assaults fail and weaken; so it happens in acute diseases, in which we observe the violence and attack of the disease: at one time the storms and fiercer winds subside, at another they are renewed and intensified with such violence that nature can hardly hold on, and life seems unlikely to be carried on to the seventh day. Therefore, since the power and efficacy of the number seven has been noticed and detected in many things in nature, and almost all learned men persuade themselves that a great virtue lies in it, it is especially the business of physicians to observe and weigh it carefully. For daily examples show that it has great weight not only in health but also in sickness, and in the course of days, months and years and in the signs of diseases; so too, those who are worn out by hunger die only on the seventh day, or, if they lick or swallow something, with difficulty they prolong life to the ninth. Therefore the physician should observe in every acute disease especially the seventh day, and also in what sign the Moon stands when the disease first attacks. For experience shows that if the Moon is found weak and unfortunate at the beginning of the disease, in a sign of the same nature as the disease, it disturbs the patient more; but if it is in a sign opposed to the disease, it brings relief to the sick. I could bring forward many more such experiments, were it not that my talk is for most learned men. Now we must sail into the vast sea and inquire into the causes of the flow and ebb of the sea, for here the power of each light is most clearly perceived. You, listeners, kindly accompany me with the breeze of your goodwill. I see that among the natural philosophers there has been a great controversy about the efficient cause of the motion and swell of the sea. For some ascribe it to the violent compression of the sea within the narrow places of the land and its eruption from them, and also to its violent repulsion from the shores or other places of the land. They say that the sea, pressed into narrow places of the land, seeks an exit with a certain violence and so pours out with a swift fall; and that when it is struck back by its own waves against the lands, islands and headlands that lie opposite, it is then violently driven off, and so comes to the shore with a crash and great swelling. This they prove by the example of rivers, which at one time strike this bank with their waves and at another that one. They think this motion has no other cause than the strong and violent waves, which are dashed against one bank of the river and repelled to the other side. Others refer it to earthquakes, which, they say, shake the bed of the sea. Some have declared that the saltiness, or rather a certain spirit of the sea, is the cause, by whose power the sea itself is driven into motion. Some have held that it is the rarefaction and condensation of the sea, rising and flowing in by the power of the one, and flowing back by that of the other. Some have assigned it to the continual boiling and fervour of the sea, stirred up by the force of heat, both native and solar. Some have referred the cause of this motion to the pushing and withdrawing of the winds; others to the influx of many great rivers into the sea; others to the Sun, insofar as by its rays it heats and thins the sea-water, whence boiling and fervour arise in the sea, by whose force the water is lifted up and violently runs back to the shores, so that they say this motion of the sea is like the fervour of water boiling over a fire. Finally others refer it to the Moon, insofar as it moves the sea-waters either by its local motion, or by the increase and decrease of its light, or by some natural sympathy. Yet although in such a variety of opinions it is difficult to establish the truth, and the first explanation seems the most probable of all, we must nevertheless admit with experience, the teacher of all things, and hold as confessed and undoubted, that whenever the Moon rises with the world to the summit of the heaven, that is, ascends from the horizon to the meridian, the seas are driven, rise and swell; and whenever it descends from the meridian to the horizon, the sea recedes from the shores, and contracts and draws back as if it had been sucked back in. Hence it is plain that the flow of the sea is a reciprocal flowing, by which at fixed times the sea comes to the shore and withdraws from it. And although it is manifold, and varies according to the position and nature of each region, its genuine cause depends on the heaven, chiefly on the Moon, though it is not a little helped by the Sun. For it has been observed that at new Moon and full Moon, when the Moon is either placed under the Sun or set opposite to it along a diameter, the seas are stirred more violently and pour out and rush forward more impetuously; for three days before and as many after they grow calm, and the swell becomes slack, as if it grew sluggish, about the quadratures and halvings of the Moon. Strabo and Pliny, drawing on Posidonius, hand down more observations: namely that the flows and ebbs are more moderate when the Moon wanders through the tropical signs, and more unstable and uncertain when it passes through the equinoctial signs. The swell also grows heavier and intensifies when the Moon, having gone off towards the south, exerts its force with a nearer effort and push, and from the equinoxes to the solstices, that is from Aries to Cancer, and likewise from Libra to Capricorn, and conversely from the solstices to the equinoxes, that is from Cancer to Libra, and from Libra to Capricorn. And the swell of the sea is softened and becomes calmer when the Moon is in the north and has wandered toward the Septentriones. For the most part the sea rises for six and a half hours, and presses hardest on the shores, and falls for as many hours, and returns to the deep; in this reciprocation it plainly follows the motion of the Moon. For when it is near the horizon the shores overflow full, and the seas push back the rivers that meet them; but when it climbs to the meridian, that is, holds the summit of the heaven, the waters recede, and the shores are seen empty. And the swell is the fuller the greater the face of the Moon, so it is stronger at full Moon. Therefore this is the reason why the sea flows in or ebbs every six or so hours, since the Moon completes a quarter of its daily motion in those hours, but at every twenty-four hours and fifty minutes the sea swells twice and subsides twice, as is known to the inhabitants of Venice and the Mediterranean. The backflow of the Indian sea became known in the wars of Alexander the Great, whose army, unwary and ignorant of the nature of the strait, he suddenly attacked. At the Red Cape of Africa it is different, for it flows in for four hours with such force that it drives back ships running with full sails, and it ebbs for eight; for the faster it rises, the more slowly it recedes. The rivers, held back and detained, also feel this impetus of the sea, as if it were opening and spreading itself. At Hamburg the Elbe, eighteen miles from the ocean, and at Antwerp the Scheldt, about eighteen miles too, are driven back and swell and overflow as the sea comes in, and diminish and fall back within their channels as it recedes, by the same alternations as the sea, as the inhabitants know. The ocean has the most violent swells; the Mediterranean, milder ones. The Hellespont and the Black Sea have none, and likewise the Ligurian, Baltic and Caspian seas. Twice a day and night the Sicilian sea pours out and draws back, alternating around the hollow rocks of Scylla and Charybdis. Seven times a day the Chalcidian sea alternates around Euboea, famous and remarkable for the back-and-forth flows of the Euripus. But sailors have also found that the seas are stirred, apart from the swell, by another motion, less evident but continuous. Namely, the ocean itself, which spreads out widely and washes, flows between and surrounds the whole earth, and the Mediterranean, which pours in through the narrows of the Pillars of Hercules and floods the middle of the inhabited world with its wide, open bed. Sailors also find that if they set off from the promontory of Nerium in Spain and set sail eastward towards Britain, with the Sun, they make their way much more slowly than if they turn back to Spain. The same happens to those who sail from Spain to the islands recently discovered by Columbus the Genoese in the Western Ocean: they complete that journey in twenty-four days when going out, carried along by favourable winds; but when they return to Spain, scarcely three or four months suffice, even though no breeze or wind opposes them. And the Portuguese, who sail past the coast of Africa and the Cape of Good Hope to enter the island of Taprobane, and bring from there the Indian goods, even with favourable winds reach it much more slowly and with more difficulty than they return home. No other cause for this is given except that the ocean, being continually and most rapidly turned by the heavenly bodies from east to west, is driven, forced and twisted in the same direction, not indeed plainly and manifestly, but still perceptibly. They say that this backward push of the sea, caused by the impulse of the heavens, slows down and retards even the impetus of the swiftest ships. By the same impulse of the heavens, the Mediterranean, which is held in by narrower barriers of its shores, has been observed in our own memory to be driven round in a circle. For set in motion from the rocks of Palestine, which face the rising Sun, and rolled along the coasts of Phoenicia, Pamphylia, the Hellespont and Greece, lapping at the shores, it then washes the continent of Dalmatia, Istria and Illyria, and in the innermost recess of the Adriatic Sea it goes round that corner in which Venice lies, and is turned back towards the opposite shore of Italy, towards Flaminia; thence, by the borders of Picenum, Apulia, Magna Graecia and Sicily, it is turned back to the rising Sun, and then, circling the whole shore of the Tyrrhenian Sea and flowing past the provinces of Narbonese Gaul and Baetica in Spain, and the straits of Hercules, and washing the shores of Mauritania, Africa and Egypt, it returns to its rising. Although the reason for this stirring is more obscure, it is nonetheless caused by the Sun and Moon. For since the horizon and the meridian, by their mutual intersections, divide the whole heaven into four quarters, the lights carried in two opposite quarters produce a flowing and an approach of the flooding waters: from the east to the summit of the heaven, and from the west to the lowest point of the heaven, that is the angle of the earth. In the other two quarters they produce a withdrawal and a return. Therefore the seas are moved by the daily circuit and effect of each of these bodies, and these motions are changed by their meetings with each other, by their mutual aspects, by their progress through the various parts of the zodiac, and by their dissimilar inclinations towards the tracts of the seas themselves. But it is plain from this that the Moon has the greater power, since the tides begin when it rises, and begin so much the later as it has advanced further and comes late. But whether it draws and moves the seas by the mere vibration and emission of its rays, or by some other medium intervening, is not an inept question. For although the whole of this lower nature clearly shows that the rays of the Sun and Moon affect and stir the humours in earthly bodies by a wonderful agreement, nevertheless, since the swells of the sea seem similar to the boiling of water heated over a fire, by what reasoning can this be imputed to the Moon? Peucer in his book On Divination rightly adds this cause: just as water boils when the great heat of its dissolving ardour, with a quantity of thinner vapours, and by their lightness and tenuity, impelled by the force of heat and spread out, seeks an exit, which it does not find unless the waters are disturbed and stirred, and driven from the bottom to the top, from the middle to the outer edges of the bronze vessel; so the seas, when the power of the rays has thinned a great quantity of the marine and earthly vapours, drawn or pulled from the bottom of the sea, struggle with the surrounding waters and strive to break out, and when they open an outlet they burst and tear apart and, as it were, twist the waters, which, while the pressing vapours give way for an exit, are driven by the opening and parting to the shores and mouths of rivers; there the rivers, held back, first stand still, then soon turn their courses back, and being lifted by this reciprocation they pour out, flood and cover whatever lies nearby; and indeed at the shores the seas themselves vomit and spit out various things as excrements from their depths. The ocean has fiercer swells, and the Mediterranean gentler ones; there the open vastness allows the stars, which act loosely and widely, to be felt more effectively, while here the narrowness keeps off the same power. Hence the Baltic and the other seas, confined within narrow beds and far removed from the efficacious projection of the rays, and because of their depth less open to the light, experience no swells; and for the same causes the Ligurian Sea too, and also because its rocky bed cannot dissolve into vapours suited to agitation. But not only the seas, but the other parts of this lower and sublunary world also confess that they feel the power and efficacy of the Moon, when they show the marks of the changes they have suffered: fields become barren, grain is spoiled by rust or mildew, vines are seized by blight, flowers fall, and everywhere there is an abundance of caterpillars and various worms and insects, and also of poisonous vapours breathed into the air. At full Moon, when it rises above the earth through whole nights, in summer a cool breeze impressed on the air holds back and breaks the heat, and softens the troubles drawn from the heat; this we certainly learned by experience in the present year 1611, when the whole spring, from March to the twentieth of May, was observed to be quite irregular, and almost without precedent in human memory, and was oppressed by heat. In winter, on the other hand, its milder breeze softens the harshness of the cold, because in summer full Moons it moves far from the Sun, and in winter, during the summer circle, it comes closer, God so arranging and ordering it. Lunatics also plainly experience the power of this star. For they suffer from a madness that returns at fixed intervals, and from this the kind of illness took its name; it is customary for those born at new Moon to be subject to it, or because it usually returns at regular intervals of the Moon. Julius Firmicus, confirming this very point (Mathesis, bk 4), says: "A Moon badly placed makes people spasmodic, or lunatic, or epileptic. There is an example of a man who, whenever he looked at the Moon, was said to fall into the falling sickness. And travellers at night under a full Moon experience it." But it must here be noted that the Moon sometimes produces diverse effects and various outcomes according to the different conjunctions and configurations of the other wandering stars with it, namely whether they embrace each other with favourable and happy rays, or strike and attack each other with threatening and hostile ones; and according to their aspect and position towards the lands beneath, and their familiarity and agreement with them, by reason of the signs in which they stand. All and each of these an astrologer ought to consider carefully, to inform his judgments of nativities correctly according to the precepts of the art. From what has been said so far it is plain that, since the air is affected in such different ways by the stars of heaven and receives various influxes and powers of the celestial lights, especially when they stand in the tropical signs, such as Cancer and Capricorn, and in the equinoctial ones, such as Aries and Libra, in which the air undergoes remarkable changes and the seasons turn, then not only do the temperaments change, and the actions that follow the temperament or the just mixing of the humours, but also the principal parts of our bodies are affected differently and in different ways by the different dispositions of the heavens, and the humours and spirits that attend and serve them. Hence it happens that we sometimes languish or, on the contrary, feel better; we rejoice, or suddenly slip into sadness; what we work at we finish more quickly, easily and cheerfully, and perform without difficulty; our senses are vigorous, and when we direct our minds to thinking we easily grasp what we have sought, and indeed we abound in a stream of good thoughts; or on the contrary we strain all the powers of our wit, and yet fail, grow dull and get nowhere, achieving nothing that is fitting and suited to our purpose. And we admit that all these things happen without any visible and evident cause, namely because the different positions of the stars, unnoticed by us, impress different effects, either by stirring up and disturbing the humours, or by calming, purging and clearing the spirits, or by exciting and strengthening the faculties of the principal members. Hence it happens that, with the spirits roused and the mind alert, everything is looked at more carefully and decided more rightly, and what may fall or hinder is foreseen better than when the mind is languid or troubled. Therefore whoever denies that from the stars we are made more lively and quicker to think and act, and at other times less fit, is to be purged with hellebore rather than convinced by demonstrations. Hippocrates and Galen, the most famous of physicians, have confessed this very thing. And although temperaments take a great deal from matter and seed, yet it must be admitted that they are very much changed, altered and tempered at times by the force and impulse of the stars. But for one who would divine from the position of the stars, since the natures and qualities of all the stars must be carefully demanded and explored before one comes to the prognostic itself, certain foundations must necessarily be laid first, or rather laid beforehand, which precede the prognostic itself in the order of nature, and without knowing or rightly understanding them, the prognostic straightway falls. The contemplation and knowledge must begin with those fixed stars which make up the twelve signs of the zodiac, whose chief power is also detected, as well as that of those which stand a smaller distance on either side of them, such as Orion, Arcturus, Procyon, Sirius and so on. Here, then, the known differences of the said signs serve especially the astrological judgments: namely which constitute the fiery triplicity, which the watery, which the earthy and which the airy; likewise which are equinoctial, which solstitial, which movable, which fixed and which common; which masculine and which feminine; which rise straight and which rise obliquely; which are fruitful and which barren; which northern and which southern; which are commanding or high, which obedient, which ascending, which descending; which are mute and which rational; which are friendly to each other and which hostile; which are alien and not conjoined, and which are mutually bound; which are of talent, eloquence and fluency, and so on.

units.la: Igneum trigonum constituunt Aries, Leo, & Sagittarius, in cono est Leo, in basis parte dextra Sagittarius, in sinistra Aries: hujus trigoni Domini sunt Sol de die, Jupiter de nocte, particeps autem est Mars.
units.tr: The fiery trigon is made up of Aries, Leo and Sagittarius. Leo is at the apex, Sagittarius is on the right of the base, and Aries on the left. The lords of this trigon are the Sun by day and Jupiter by night, and Mars shares in it.

units.la: Aries primum in zodiaco signum, exaltatio Solis, domus secundaria Martis, naturæ calidæ & siccæ: ex membris humanis habet caput, faciem, oculos, aures, & horum membrorum infirmitates. In eo exaltatur Sol id ingrediens mense Martio, ex austrina mundi plaga septentriones versus se attollens, omnibusq; sublunaribus frigoris rigore fere emortuis vitam & calorem reportans.
units.tr: Aries is the first sign of the zodiac. It is the exaltation of the Sun and the secondary house of Mars, and its nature is hot and dry. Among the parts of the human body it governs the head, face, eyes and ears, and the diseases of these parts. The Sun is exalted in it when he enters it in March, rising from the southern region of the world toward the north and restoring life and warmth to everything beneath the moon, which has almost died under the rigour of cold.

units.la: Leo quintum in zodiaco signum, domicilium SOLIS[?], naturæ calidæ & siccæ, habet cor, stomachum, dorsum, latera, costas, horumq; membrorum morbos, ut febres, apostemata, pestilentiam, in hoc nullus Planetarum exaltatur.
units.tr: Leo is the fifth sign of the zodiac, the domicile of the Sun, and its nature is hot and dry. It governs the heart, stomach, back, sides and ribs, and the diseases of these parts, such as fevers, abscesses and plague. No planet is exalted in this sign.

units.la: Sagittarius 9. in zodiaco signum, domus principalis Jovis, naturæ calidæ & siccæ, habet coxas, femora, nates, horumque membrorum morbos. In hoc nullus Planetarum exaltatur.
units.tr: Sagittarius is the ninth sign of the zodiac, the principal house of Jupiter, and its nature is hot and dry. It governs the hips, thighs and buttocks, and the diseases of these parts. No planet is exalted in this sign.

units.la: Aqueam triplicitatem constituunt Cancer, Scorpius, Pisces, in cono est Cancer, in basis parte dextra Scorpius, in sinistra pisces: Dominus hujus trigoni est Mars, participesq; assumit Venerem & Lunam, illam de die, hanc de nocte.
units.tr: The watery triplicity is made up of Cancer, Scorpio and Pisces. Cancer is at the apex, Scorpio is on the right of the base, and Pisces on the left. The lord of this trigon is Mars, and he takes Venus and the Moon as partners, Venus by day and the Moon by night.

units.la: Cancer 4. in zodiaco signum est, domus Lunæ, exaltatio Jovis, naturæ frigidæ & humidæ, habet pulmonem, epar, splenem, mammillas, horumq; membrorum infirmitates, ut tussim, pthisin, pleuresin.
units.tr: Cancer is the fourth sign of the zodiac. It is the house of the Moon and the exaltation of Jupiter, and its nature is cold and moist. It governs the lungs, liver, spleen and breasts, and the infirmities of these parts, such as cough, consumption and pleurisy.

units.la: Scorpius 7.in zodiaco signum est, domus principalis Martis, naturæ frigidæ & humidæ, habet pudenda, testiculos, vesicam, anum, oculorumq; ægritudines à 20. gradu usq; in 24. ex morbis cancrum, lepram, fistulas.
units.tr: Scorpio is the seventh sign of the zodiac. It is the principal house of Mars, and its nature is cold and moist. It governs the private parts, testicles, bladder and anus, and diseases of the eyes from the twentieth to the twenty-fourth degree. Among diseases it governs cancer, leprosy and fistulas.

units.la: Pisces, ultimum in zodiaco signum, Jovis domus secundaria, exaltatio Veneris, qualitatis frigidæ & humidæ, ex morbis habet paralysin, podagram, ex membris pedes cum talis.
units.tr: Pisces, the last sign of the zodiac, is the secondary house of Jupiter and the exaltation of Venus, and its quality is cold and moist. Among diseases it governs paralysis and gout, and among the parts of the body the feet with the ankles.

units.la: Aëriæ triplicitatis signa sunt, gemini, libra, aquarius, in basis dextro est libra, aquarius in sinistro, gemini in cono. Domini ejus sunt Saturnus de die, Mercurius de nocte, Jupiter particeps est.
units.tr: The signs of the airy triplicity are Gemini, Libra and Aquarius. Libra is on the right of the base, Aquarius on the left, and Gemini at the apex. Their lords are Saturn by day and Mercury by night, and Jupiter shares in it.

units.la: Gemini tertium in zodiaco signum sunt, domus secunda ria Mercurii, naturæ calidæ & humidæ, ex membris habent humeros, brachia, manus, & horum membrorum ægritudines ex sanguine.
units.tr: Gemini is the third sign of the zodiac. It is the secondary house of Mercury, and its nature is hot and moist. Among the parts of the body it governs the shoulders, arms and hands, and the diseases of these parts that arise from the blood.

units.la: Libra 7. in zodiaco locum occupat, domus principalis Veneris, exaltatio Saturni, naturæ calidæ & humidæ, ex membris habet lumbos, renes, vesicam, & inferiora ventris, ex morbis dysenteriam, dysuriam, dolores dorsi.
units.tr: Libra occupies the seventh place in the zodiac. It is the principal house of Venus and the exaltation of Saturn, and its nature is hot and moist. Among the parts of the body it governs the loins, kidneys, bladder and lower belly. Among diseases it governs dysentery, dysuria and pains of the back.

units.la: Aquarius 11. in zodiaco signum est, domus secundaria Saturni, naturæ aeriæ, calidæ & humidæ, ex morbis habet icteritiam nigram, Scorbutum, & oculorum ægritudines à 20. in 25. gradum.
units.tr: Aquarius is the eleventh sign of the zodiac. It is the secondary house of Saturn, and its nature is airy, hot and moist. Among diseases it governs black jaundice, scurvy, and diseases of the eyes from the twentieth to the twenty-fifth degree.

units.la: Terreæ triplicitatis signa sunt taurus, virgo, capricornus, conum tenet taurus, basis partem dextrā virgo, sinistram capricornus. Domini hîc sunt Venus de die, Luna de nocte, particeps est Saturnus.
units.tr: The signs of the earthy triplicity are Taurus, Virgo and Capricorn. Taurus holds the apex, Virgo the right side of the base, and Capricorn the left. The lords here are Venus by day and the Moon by night, and Saturn shares in it.

units.la: Taurus domus secundaria Veneris; exaltatio Lunæ, naturæ frigidæ & siccæ, ex morbis habet illos, qui collum, cervicem & guttur infestant. In hoc signo Luna est maximarum virium.
units.tr: Taurus is the secondary house of Venus and the exaltation of the Moon, and its nature is cold and dry. Among diseases it governs those that afflict the neck, nape and throat. The Moon is of greatest strength in this sign.

units.la: Virgo domus principalis & exaltatio Mercurii, naturæ terreæ, habet ventrem, intestina, diaphragma, & horum membrorum infirmitates: in hoc signo Mercurius non afflictus, est efficacissimus.
units.tr: Virgo is the principal house and the exaltation of Mercury, and its nature is earthy. It governs the belly, intestines, diaphragm and the infirmities of these parts. In this sign Mercury, if not afflicted, is most effective.

units.la: Capricornus domus principalis Saturni, exaltatio Martis, naturæ terreæ, melancholicæ, ex membris habet genua, horumque ægritudines, necnon oculorum impedimenta à 22. in 25. gradum.
units.tr: Capricorn is the principal house of Saturn and the exaltation of Mars, and its nature is earthy and melancholic. Among the parts of the body it governs the knees and their diseases, and also impairments of the eyes from the twenty-second to the twenty-fifth degree.

units.la: Ex his porrò enumeratis signis quædam sunt æquinoctialia, in quibus fiunt æquinoctia, ut sunt aries & libra, quædam solstitialia, ut cancer & capricornus, in his enim fiunt Solis stationes.
units.tr: Of the signs enumerated so far, some are equinoctial, those in which the equinoxes occur, such as Aries and Libra; some are solstitial, such as Cancer and Capricorn, for in these the Sun makes his stations.

units.la: Quædam mobilia, ut aries, cancer, libra, & capricornus: quædam fixa, ut taurus, leo, scorpius, & aquarius, reliqua sunt communia & bicorporea, ut gemini, virgo, sagittarius & pisces.
units.tr: Some are movable, such as Aries, Cancer, Libra and Capricorn; some are fixed, such as Taurus, Leo, Scorpio and Aquarius; the rest are common and double-bodied, such as Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius and Pisces.

units.la: Masculina sunt aries, gemini, leo, libra, sagittarius, aquarius: fœminina taurus, cancer, virgo, scorpius, capricornus & pisces.
units.tr: The masculine signs are Aries, Gemini, Leo, Libra, Sagittarius and Aquarius; the feminine are Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, Capricorn and Pisces.

units.la: Rectè ascendentia sunt, quorum latitudo est major longitudine: seu rectè oriuntur illa signa, cum quibus major æquatoris quàm zodiaci pars ascendit, id est, cùm plures quàm 30. æquatoris gradus supra horizontem emergunt. Obliquè contra. Quo autem obliquius horizon intersecat zodiacum ascenden-te signo, eo citius & obliquius, minoriq; cum æquatoris arcu id signum emergit, & vicissim, quo rectius horizon zodiacum di-vidit, eo rectius & tardius id signum emergit, id est, majori cum æquatoris arcu.
units.tr: Those are called right-ascending whose breadth is greater than their longitude, or those signs rise right, with which a greater part of the equator than of the zodiac rises, that is, when more than thirty degrees of the equator emerge above the horizon. The reverse holds for oblique signs. Moreover, the more obliquely the horizon cuts the zodiac as a sign ascends, the more quickly and obliquely that sign emerges, and with a smaller arc of the equator; and conversely, the more directly the horizon divides the zodiac, the more directly and slowly the sign emerges, that is, with a greater arc of the equator.

units.la: Sterilia signa sunt, gemini, leo, virgo: fœcunda, cancer, scorpius, pisces: mediocria, taurus, aries, sagittarius, capricor-nus, libra, pisces.
units.tr: The sterile signs are Gemini, Leo and Virgo; the fruitful are Cancer, Scorpio and Pisces; the middling are Taurus, Aries, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Libra and Pisces.

units.la: Septentrionalia sunt, quæ in parte zodiaci septentriones versus declinante conspiciuntur, ut aries, taurus, gemini, can-cer, leo, virgo: Meridionalia, quæ in meridionalem mundi pla-gam declinant, ut libra, scorpius, sagittarius, capricornus, aqua-rius, pisces.
units.tr: The northern signs are those which are seen in the part of the zodiac that inclines toward the north, such as Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo and Virgo. The southern signs are those which incline toward the southern region of the world, such as Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces.

units.la: Præcipientia & alta signa sunt, quæ sunt in medietate zo-diaci æstivali: obedientia & infima, quæ sunt in medietate zo-diaci hyemali: tortuosè quoq; ascendentia obediunt signis re-ctè ascendentibus, sic gemini obediunt cancro, taurus leoni.
units.tr: The preceding and high signs are those in the summer half of the zodiac; the obedient and low signs are those in the winter half. Signs that rise obliquely also obey the signs that rise right; thus Gemini obeys Cancer, and Taurus obeys Leo.

units.la: Ascendentia sunt capricornus, aquarius, pisces, aries, tau-rus, gemini, in his enim Planetæ decurrentes dicuntur in zodia-co ascendentes. Descendentia, cancer, leo, virgo, libra, scorpius, sagittarius.
units.tr: The ascending signs are Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces, Aries, Taurus and Gemini, for in these the planets running through the zodiac are said to ascend. The descending signs are Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio and Sagittarius.

units.la: Quædam sunt muta & voce carentia, ut scorpius, cancer, pisces: quædam rationalia & humana, ut gemini, virgo, libra & aquarius: reliqua sunt bestialia, ut aries, taurus, leo, capri-cornus.
units.tr: Some signs are mute and lack voice, such as Scorpio, Cancer and Pisces; some are rational and human, such as Gemini, Virgo, Libra and Aquarius; the rest are bestial, such as Aries, Taurus, Leo and Capricorn.

units.la: Invicem sibi amica sunt, quæ trigono vel sextili aspectu se vibrant: trigono, ut aries, leo, & sagittarius, taurus, virgo, & capricornus, gemini, libra, & aquarius, cancer, scorpius, & pisces: Sextili, ut aries & gemini, taurus & cancer, gemini & leo, cancer & virgo, leo & libra, virgo & scorpius, libra & sagittarius, scorpius & capricornus, sagittarius & aquarius, capricornus & pisces, aquarius & aries, pisces & taurus. Invicem vero inimica sunt, quae quadrato vel oppositο radio se feriunt: quadrato, ut aries & cancer, taurus & leo, gemini & virgo, cancer & libra, leo & scorpius, virgo & sagittarius, libra & capricornus, scorpius & aquarius, sagittarius & pisces, capricornus & aries, aquarius & taurus, pisces & gemini.
units.tr: Signs are friendly to one another when they strike each other by trine or sextile aspect. By trine: Aries, Leo and Sagittarius; Taurus, Virgo and Capricorn; Gemini, Libra and Aquarius; Cancer, Scorpio and Pisces. By sextile: Aries and Gemini, Taurus and Cancer, Gemini and Leo, Cancer and Virgo, Leo and Libra, Virgo and Scorpio, Libra and Sagittarius, Scorpio and Capricorn, Sagittarius and Aquarius, Capricorn and Pisces, Aquarius and Aries, Pisces and Taurus. Signs are hostile to one another when they strike each other by square or opposition: by square, Aries and Cancer, Taurus and Leo, Gemini and Virgo, Cancer and Libra, Leo and Scorpio, Virgo and Sagittarius, Libra and Capricorn, Scorpio and Aquarius, Sagittarius and Pisces, Capricorn and Aries, Aquarius and Taurus, Pisces and Gemini.

units.la: Peregrina, non conjuncta & divisa sunt, quae nullo radio concordant, ut sunt quae distant invicem per 30. vel 60. gradus.
units.tr: Foreign, unconnected and divided signs are those that agree by no ray, such as those that are distant from one another by thirty or sixty degrees.

units.la: Signa deniq; boni ingenii & facunditiæ sunt, gemini, virgo, libra, capricornus & aquarius: In horum enim signorum aliquo Mercurius cum Luna constitutus, ingeniorum præstantiam largitur, & ad actiones obeundas felicitatem ac promtitudinem insignem. In reliquis est mediocris, nisi Lunæ vel Jovis radiis juvetur, tunc enim ingenium acuit.
units.tr: Finally, the signs of good wit and eloquence are Gemini, Virgo, Libra, Capricorn and Aquarius. For when Mercury is placed with the Moon in one of these signs, he bestows excellence of mind and a remarkable felicity and readiness for carrying out tasks. In the other signs he is of middling quality, unless he is aided by the rays of the Moon or Jupiter, for then he sharpens the mind.

units.la: Non autem sufficit has dictas signorum zodiaci differentias observasse, sed inquirendæ ulterius sunt proprietates quaedam eorum & significationes naturales, quas in elementarem hunc mundum promunt, quæ cognitio non parum habet momenti tum ad statum anni, tum ad temperamentorum etiam nostrorum causas & differentias, inveniendum.
units.tr: However, it is not enough to have observed these differences of the signs of the zodiac; certain of their properties and natural significations must be investigated further, which they bring forth in this elementary world. This knowledge is of no small importance both for determining the state of the year and for discovering the causes and differences of our own temperaments.

units.la: Arietis signum, Ptolomæo judice & teste, experientiaque suffragante, in primis partibus, hoc est, à 1. gradu in 10. propter æquinoctium in illis contingens, & stellas etiam fixas iis subjectas, ut plurimum pluviosum est & procellosum, intemperatæ igitur complexionis: media vero ejus pars, hoc est, à 10. in 20. usque gradum temperata est, extrema, hoc est, à 20. in 30. gradum sæpe funesta, & mortalibus inimica.
units.tr: The sign of Aries, according to the judgement and testimony of Ptolemy, and with experience supporting it, is for the most part rainy and stormy in its first parts, that is, from the first to the tenth degree, because of the equinox which occurs in those parts, and also because of the fixed stars subject to it; it is therefore of intemperate complexion. Its middle part, that is, from the tenth to the twentieth degree, is temperate; its last part, that is, from the twentieth to the thirtieth degree, is often deadly and hostile to mortals.

units.la: Tauri primæ partes procellosæ sunt & tempestuosæ, pars media infrigidat & humectat, postrema citra Aldebaram, & oculum tauri ignea est & fulminans. Septentrionales autem ejus stelstellæ, quæ scilicet vergunt ad polum nostrum, temperati influxus sunt, meridionales intemperati.
units.tr: The first part of Taurus is stormy and tempestuous; the middle part chills and moistens; the last part, on this side of Aldebaran and the eye of the Bull, is fiery and thundering. Its northern stars, that is, those which lean toward our pole, have a temperate influence, and its southern stars an intemperate one.

units.la: Geminorum totum signum generaliter temperaturam præstat: Specialiter tamen pars ejus prima multum humectat, media efficit temperiem, postrema mixturam quandam propter stellas diversarum naturarum ibidem concurrentes. Septentrionales vero partes aërem turbulentant, meridionales æstuant.
units.tr: The whole sign of Gemini generally gives a temperate quality. Specifically, however, its first part greatly moistens, its middle part produces temperateness, and its last part a certain mixture, because stars of different natures meet there. Its northern parts disturb the air, and its southern parts make it hot.

units.la: Cancri pars prior aërem turbat & obscurat, media temperata est, postrema ventosa. Partes septentrionales & meridionales æstuant & incendunt.
units.tr: The earlier part of Cancer disturbs and darkens the air, the middle part is temperate, and the last part is windy. Its northern and southern parts are hot and inflame.

units.la: Leonis pars prior calet, aëremq; turbat & corrumpit: pars media æstum temperat, pars postrema plane intemperata. Partes ejus septentrionales urunt & incendunt, meridionales humectant. Ratio est, quoniam aër calidus congruit cum virtute Solis, unde prior Leonis pars tempore Ptolomæi habebat naturam Solis & Martis, pars media Jovis, & finis Saturni: Septentrionales vero ejus partes erant de natura Martis, meridionales de natura Mercurii & Veneris, unde etiam humectare deprehendebantur.
units.tr: The earlier part of Leo is hot, and it disturbs and corrupts the air; the middle part tempers the heat, and the last part is wholly intemperate. Its northern parts burn and inflame, and its southern parts moisten. The reason is that hot air agrees with the power of the Sun; hence in the time of Ptolemy the earlier part of Leo had the nature of the Sun and Mars, the middle part that of Jupiter, and the end that of Saturn. Its northern parts were of the nature of Mars, and its southern parts of the nature of Mercury and Venus, which is why they were also found to moisten.

units.la: Virginis pars prior intemperata est, media temperata, postrema aquosa: partes septentrionales ventosæ, meridionales temperatæ, quia de natura Jovis.
units.tr: The earlier part of Virgo is intemperate, the middle temperate, and the last watery. Its northern parts are windy, and its southern parts temperate, because they are of the nature of Jupiter.

units.la: Libræ pars prima, & media, temperaturam præstant, postrema aquosa est: Septentrionales partes aquosæ, meridionales funestè humectantes.
units.tr: The first and middle parts of Libra produce a temperate quality; the last part is watery. Its northern parts are watery, and its southern parts moisten to the point of harm.

units.la: Scorpionis pars prima siccat & obnubilat, media temperata, postrema turbulentans. Partes septentrionales sunt Martiæ naturæ, meridionales Saturninæ, pars autem ejus media, quæ temperata est, Jovialis naturæ est.
units.tr: The first part of Scorpio dries and clouds over, the middle part is temperate, and the last part stirs up storms. Its northern parts are of the nature of Mars, its southern parts of the nature of Saturn; the middle part, which is temperate, is of the Jovian nature.

units.la: Sagittarii pars prima humectat, media temperat, postrema ob caliditatem incommodat: partes septentrionales sunt ventosæ, meridionales fortiter humectantes & turbantes.
units.tr: The first part of Sagittarius moistens, the middle part tempers, and the last part is troublesome because of its heat. Its northern parts are windy, and its southern parts moisten strongly and disturb.

units.la: Capricorni priores partes sunt destruentes, mediæ Jovia-les & temperatæ, extremæ pluviosæ: partes septentrionales & meridionales corrumpentes & destruentes.
units.tr: The earlier parts of Capricorn are destructive, the middle parts are Jovian and temperate, and the last parts are rainy. Its northern and southern parts corrupt and destroy.

units.la: Aquarii pars prior multum humida, media temperata, postrema ventosa: Partes septentrionales in caliditate immo-derata, meridionales nebulosæ & grandinosæ.
units.tr: The earlier part of Aquarius is very moist, the middle part temperate, and the last part windy. Its northern parts are immoderately hot, and its southern parts misty and hail-bearing.

units.la: Piscium pars prior est temperata, media multum hume-ctans, extrema adurens: partes ejus septentrionales sunt ven-tosæ, meridionales aquosæ.
units.tr: The earlier part of Pisces is temperate, the middle part greatly moistens, and the last part scorches. Its northern parts are windy, and its southern parts watery.

units.la: His autem viribus signorum zodiaci exploratis non acquiescere debet divinaturus ex illis, sed collatio instituenda ac investiganda, habitudoq; & affectio erga Planetas, cumprimis Solem & Lunam. Diligenter igitur hic inquirendum, Planetæ, in quibus signi partibus ambulent, signiq; stellæ an unà cum Sole vel Luna emergant aut occumbant, vel orientem Solem aliquantum antecedant, vel exortum mox insequantur? aut Sole oriente è regione condantur, aut culminante vel eve-hantur, vel sub occasum præcipitentur, vel ipsi assistant, vel sub imo jaceant terræ, vel in culmine cœli emineant? Intenduntur enim vires radiorum, qui ex cardinibus rectiori trajectu appul-si figuntur fortius: & efficacius longè imminentes vertici stellas, & vel coörientes, vel è regione se abscondentes, aut in cœli constitutis angulo summo, Sol ferit incitatq; fortius quàm cæteras. Et eadem ratio Planetarum est cæterorum, quorum in zodiaco motus ad Solem & Lunam semper referendus est & conferendus: idq; longo usu observatum est, si mediocriter ad Solis motus attendimus, & momenta orientium vel occidentium stellarum observamus. Quâ quidem observatione singulorum dierum qualitates, diurnæq; intensiones & remissiones (ut loquar cum Ptolom.) dignoscuntur, ubi fixarum stellarum eæ, quæ sunt insigniores & maximè illustres cœlo, matutinis aut vespertinis, ortusq; aut occasus sui fulgoribus conspicuæ fuerint, convertunt enim illæ particularem statum plerumque ad modum suarum naturarum. Proderit autem hujus observa-tionis proferre exempla. Nonas circa Aprilis, id est 5. Vergiliæ occidunt occasu vespertino: tempore autem Ptolomæi Sol erat circa 12. partem arietis, Vergiliæ verò circa 5. tauri, quare occidente Sole ilico post crepusculum, quod durat, donec descendant 16. aut 18. partes cœli, Vergiliæ occidunt, id est, quæ jam prius videbantur occidente Sole post occasum ejus, nunc primùm Sole appropinquante incipiunt latere, ideoq; immutant statum aëris, cùm aër privetur tali lumine illarum stellarum, vocaturq; hic occasus vespertinus, quando scilicet in occidente, quæ prius solebant videri, Solis lumine quasi abreptæ, desinunt apparere, & tunc Africus flat die sequente. Sic eadem Vergiliæ nonis Maji, id est 7. exoriebantur ortu matutino, id est, incipiebant apparere ante Solis ortum propter Solem recedentem: nam nonis Maji Sol erat circa 16. partem tauri, Vergiliæ circa 5. tauri partem, ideò illa stella, quæ plus habet latitudinis, incipit apparere. Ubi primò notandum, si plures sunt stellæ, exortum intelligi, cùm una earum primò prodit, occasum, cùm prima illarum, qualiscunque fuerit, abscondítur[?]. Exquo patet, quòd plus distent stellæ à Sole, quando abscondúntur[?], si sint plures, quàm quando oriuntur. In occasu enim Vergiliæ distabant à Sole 23. gradibus, vel paulò minus, in ortu gradibus 11. Et causa tota consistit in eo, quia ortus atque occasus à diversis su-muntur[?] stellis, exortus à prima, quæ apparet, occasus à prima, quæ occultatur. At quia pars horizontis occidua contraria est orientali, ideò duabus hisce causis contingit varietas. Deinde observandum, ortum talem & occasum in stellis pluribus durare per plures dies, scilicet à prima, quæ oritur, ad ultimam earum durat ortus, & similiter occasus, à prima, quæ occidit, ad ultimam, & perseverat ejusmodi effectus plerumque non solum toto tempore intermedio, sed in ortu etiam per aliquot dies, postquam omnes apparere cœperint. Sed in occasu alia est ratio, quia non durat effectus, nisi ab occasu primæ ad occasum ultimæ: ubi autem omnes occiderint, die sequente effectus cessat. Quod si vero fit una tantum stella illustris, puta Arcturus, vel Sirius, tunc ortus fit in una die, effectus autem durat in dies plures, adeò, ut caniculæ ortus duret 30. diebus, & secundum quosdam 40. Arcturi vero 8. vel 10. Occasus autem contingit in una die, & effectus etiam finitur eâdem. Tertiò attendendum, ortum & occasum unius & ejusdem stellæ non fieri in eadem distantia à Sole, sed magnam esse diversitatem & varietatem, tum propter obliquitatem vel rectitudinem signorum, tum propter latitudinem australem vel borealem, facit enim latitudo borealis, ut oriantur celerius matutino, & vespertino ortu tardius, australis autem facit ad occasum tam vespertinum quàm etiam matutinum. Ergo boreales stellæ, ut Arcturus oritur utroq; ortu in minori à Sole distantia, quàm occidat: canicula contrario modo. Quartò: licèt ortus stellarum insigniorum per plures dies duret, ut & effectus earum, mutatio tamen aëris non fit, nisi in prima ortus die, sicut etiam in occasu fit mutatio die illa solùm. Quintò: ortus & occasus earundē non fieri apud omnes gentes temporibus iisdem, propter diversam poli altitudinem, & horizontis varietatem, propter quam etiam causam necessarium fuit conficere tabulam ortus & occasus siderum tam vespertini quàm matutini, pro cujuscunque regionis conditione, per totum annum. Sextò: ortum & occasum siderum eorundem non solùm in diversis regionibus diversa operari propter naturam ventorum, & qualitatum aëris diversam, tum etiam propropter situm. Septimò: exortus majorem facere mutationem quàm occasus, & matutinos vespertinis esse validiores, ut ita sint quatuor ordines, matutinus validissimus, ortus vespertinus huic in ordine succedens, postea occasus matutinus, postremò occasus vespertinus. Unde nil mirum, quod Ptolomæus libro de ortu siderum scribens, circa nonas Aprilis Plejades occidere, vespertino occasui nihil asscripserit, sed sequenti die flatum Africum, qui effectus cùm sit debilissimus, quia fit ab occasu vespertino, differtur in diem sequentem. Sed nonis Maji, cùm scribit Vergilias seu Plejades oriri ortu matutino, effectum assignavit, seu futurū ait die eodem, & spiraturum Favonium. Octavò: stellas fixas exoriri in parva à Sole distantia, hoc est, videri Sole etiam ipsis propinquo, tum propter altitudinem illarum eximiam, qua fit, ut lumen earum minus à Sole præpediatur, tum etiam propter insignem quarundam latitudinem, ut Arcturi & caniculæ, quæ licèt non tantum efficiat quantū lon-gitudo, quia circulus latitudinis multum convenit cum horizonte, adeò, ut stella aliqua possit distare 25. gradibus & plus ab ipso Sole, & tamen simul exoriri cum Sole, & ab eo obscurari, quod fieri non potest in distantia 25. graduum secundum longi-tudinem, nihilominus magna distantia secundum latitudinem facit, ut plerumq; stella Soli proxima secundum longitudinem apparet ante ortum Solis, & hoc contingit nobis in latitudine boreali, tam in ortu matutino, quàm vespertino. Hæc ideò dif-fusè dicenda fuerunt, quoniā plurimum momenti afferunt ad qualitates aëris rectè cognoscendas, tum etiā ipsas nativitates & genituras dijudicandas: multum enim refert aliquē nasci ipsa die exortus matutini vel vespertini, stellamq; ipsam orientem cardinem orientis, occidentis vel meridiei possidere. Nunc re-vertor ad exempla. Matutinus occasus intelligitur, cùm Sole o-riente stella ex adverso occidit, ut pridie Idus Octobr. id est 14. ejusdem, Vergiliæ occidunt occasu matutino, id est, Sole oriente ex adverso occidunt, & dicitur occasus matutinus Plejadum. Sic Heliace dicitur oriri astrum, quod mane oritur paulò ante Solem, & hic modus est nobilissimus, cùm scilicet stella radiis solaribus aliquandiu occultata, iterum emergit, inq; conspe-ctum nostrum prodit. Chronice autem stella oritur, quæ Sole occidente emergit in oriente, ut mense Novembri, Sole peragrante Scorpionis signum, & quidem occidente cum extremis ejusdem gradibus, Plejades in oriente emergunt. Occasu deniq; Chronico astrum occidit, cùm Sol accedit ad astrum occidens, illudq; occultat. Sed heliacè stella occidit, quæ manè ante Solis exortum conspecta, postea radiis ipsius correpta occultatur. Vespertinus igitur Plejadum occasus fit in principio Aprilis, ortus matutinus heliacus 7. die Maji, exortus vespertinus in Novembri, occasus heliacus matutinus in Octobri: mutatio autem temporis fit eâ horâ, cùm Sol aut Luna, aut stella oriens vel occidens matutino aut vespertino ortu heliacè ad angulí sive cardinis apicem properat, ipsumq; attingit, ut ita, quicquid ad temporum pertinet mutationes, aërisq; immutationes & corruptiones, id totum ad siderum motus & naturas debeat referri, atq; ex his præcognosci. Sic igitur fixarum natura, signorumque zodiaci differentiæ & divisiones ex Ptolomæo, aliisque auctoribus perquisitæ sunt; nunc errantes quoque considerandæ, sine quibus totus hic discursus mancus foret & imperfectus. Hic enim fores rerum aperiuntur, & regia ad ipsam Astrologiam via præsternitur.
units.tr: But once these powers of the signs of the zodiac have been investigated, the one who is going to divine must not rest content with them. He must also institute and examine a comparison, and the relation and disposition of the planets toward them, above all the Sun and the Moon. Here one must inquire carefully: in what parts of a sign the planets are moving, and whether they rise or set together with the Sun or the Moon, or precede the rising Sun by some distance, or follow soon after it rises; whether they are hidden in the region opposite the rising Sun, or rise to the meridian or are carried up, or are cast down at sunset, or stand near the Sun, or lie beneath the lowest part of the earth, or stand out at the summit of the heavens? For the force of the rays is intensified when they strike more strongly after reaching the cardinal points by a more direct passage. And stars that hang close above the vertex, whether rising together with the Sun or hidden in the region opposite it, or stars placed at the highest angle of the heavens, the Sun strikes and stirs more strongly than the others. The same reasoning applies to the other planets, whose motion in the zodiac must always be referred and compared to the Sun and the Moon. This has been observed through long experience, if we attend moderately to the motions of the Sun and observe the moments when stars rise and set. By this observation the qualities of individual days, and their daily intensifications and remissions (to use Ptolemy's words), are discerned, when the fixed stars that are the more prominent and most brilliant in the sky are seen in the morning or evening, in their rising or setting splendour; for these generally turn the particular state of things toward the mode of their natures. It will be useful to set out examples of this observation. Around the nones of April, that is the 5th, the Pleiades set with an evening setting. In Ptolemy's time the Sun was about the 12th degree of Aries, while the Pleiades were about the 5th degree of Taurus. So when the Sun sets, immediately after twilight, which lasts until 16 or 18 degrees of the heavens have descended, the Pleiades set; that is, the stars which were visible before the Sun set now, as the Sun approaches, begin to lie hidden after its setting. Thus they change the state of the air, since the air is deprived of the light of those stars. This is called the evening setting, namely when the stars that used to be seen in the west disappear, as if snatched away by the light of the Sun. And then the south-west wind blows on the following day. Likewise the same Pleiades rose with a morning rising on the nones of May, that is the 7th, that is, they began to appear before the rising of the Sun, because the Sun was receding from them. For on the nones of May the Sun was about the 16th degree of Taurus, and the Pleiades about the 5th degree of Taurus; therefore that star which has more latitude begins to appear. Here first it must be noted that, where there are several stars, the rising is understood to occur when the first of them appears, and the setting when the first of them is hidden, whatever it may be. From this it is clear that when several stars are hidden they are farther from the Sun than when they rise. For at the setting of the Pleiades they were 23 degrees, or a little less, from the Sun, while at the rising they were 11 degrees away. The whole cause lies in this: the rising and the setting are taken from different stars, the rising from the first that appears, the setting from the first that is concealed. But because the western part of the horizon is opposite the eastern, the variation arises from these two causes. Next it must be observed that such a rising and setting in several stars lasts for several days: the rising lasts from the first star that rises to the last of them, and likewise the setting from the first that sets to the last. Such an effect generally persists not only through the whole intervening time, but in the rising also for some days after all of them have begun to appear. But in the setting the case is different, because the effect lasts only from the setting of the first to the setting of the last; and when all have set, the effect ceases on the following day. But if only one bright star is concerned, such as Arcturus or Sirius, then the rising takes place in a single day, yet its effect lasts for many days, so that the rising of the Dog Star lasts 30 days, and according to some 40, and that of Arcturus 8 or 10. The setting, however, occurs in one day, and its effect also ends on the same day. Thirdly, it must be noted that the rising and setting of one and the same star do not occur at the same distance from the Sun. There is great diversity and variety, both because of the obliquity or straightness of the signs and because of southern or northern latitude. For northern latitude makes stars rise more quickly in the morning and set more slowly in the evening, while southern latitude makes them set both in the evening and in the morning. Therefore northern stars, such as Arcturus, rise at either rising at a smaller distance from the Sun than that at which they set; the Dog Star does the opposite. Fourthly: although the rising of the more notable stars lasts for many days, and likewise their effect, the change of the air does not occur except on the first day of the rising, just as in the setting the change occurs on that day alone. Fifthly: the rising and setting of these same stars do not happen at the same times among all peoples, on account of the different height of the pole and the variety of the horizon. For this reason too it was necessary to draw up a table of the rising and setting of the stars, both evening and morning, for the condition of any region whatever, for the whole year. Sixthly: the rising and setting of the same stars not only produce different effects in different regions, on account of the nature of the winds and the differing qualities of the air, but also on account of their position. Seventhly: the rising produces a greater change than the setting, and the morning risings are more powerful than the evening ones. So there are four orders: the most powerful is the morning rising, followed in order by the evening rising, then the morning setting, and last the evening setting. Hence it is no wonder that Ptolemy, writing in his book on the rising of the stars, ascribed no effect to the evening setting of the Pleiades around the nones of April, but said that the south-west wind would blow the following day, an effect which, since it is very weak because it comes from the evening setting, is deferred to the next day. But on the nones of May, when he writes that the Vergiliae, or Pleiades, rise with a morning rising, he assigned an effect to it, or said that it would happen on the same day, and that the west wind would blow. Eighthly: fixed stars rise at a small distance from the Sun, that is, they are seen even when the Sun is near them. This is due partly to their great height, by which their light is less hindered by the Sun, and partly to the notable latitude of certain ones, such as Arcturus and the Dog Star. Although latitude does not produce as much as longitude, since the circle of latitude agrees much with the horizon, a star may be 25 degrees or more distant from the Sun itself, and yet rise together with the Sun and be obscured by it. This cannot happen at a distance of 25 degrees in longitude; nevertheless a great distance in latitude causes a star that is close to the Sun in longitude to appear, for the most part, before the Sun rises. This happens to us in northern latitude, both in the morning and the evening rising. These matters have been set out at length here because they contribute very much to recognising rightly the qualities of the air, and also to judging the nativities and births themselves. For it makes a great difference whether someone is born on the very day of a morning or evening rising, and whether the star rising at that moment holds the cardinal point of the east, west or south. Now I return to examples. A morning setting is understood when a star sets opposite the rising Sun, as on the day before the Ides of October, that is the 14th of that month, the Pleiades set with a morning setting; that is, they set opposite the rising Sun, and this is called the morning setting of the Pleiades. Thus a star is said to rise heliacally when it rises a little before the Sun in the morning, and this mode is the most noble, since the star, having been for some time hidden by the solar rays, emerges again and comes forth into our sight. A star rises cosmically, however, when it emerges in the east as the Sun sets, as in November, when the Sun is travelling through the sign of Scorpio, and indeed when the Sun is at the last degrees of that sign, the Pleiades emerge in the east. Finally, a star sets cosmically when the Sun approaches a setting star and hides it. But a star sets heliacally when it is seen in the morning before the rising of the Sun and afterwards, seized by its rays, is hidden. Thus the evening setting of the Pleiades occurs at the beginning of April, their heliacal morning rising on the 7th of May, their evening rising in November, and their heliacal morning setting in October. The change of season occurs at that hour when the Sun, or the Moon, or a star rising or setting in a morning or evening rising or setting heliacally, hastens to the summit of an angle or cardinal point and touches it. So whatever pertains to the changes of seasons, and to the changes and corruptions of the air, must all be referred to the motions and natures of the stars and foreknown from them. In this way, then, the nature of the fixed stars, and the differences and divisions of the signs of the zodiac, have been sought out from Ptolemy and other authors. Now the wandering stars must also be considered, without which this whole discourse would be maimed and imperfect. For here the doors of things are opened, and the royal road to astrology itself is laid down.

units.la: Saturnus Planetarum supremus, firmamento proximus, coloris est pallidi, naturæ & influentiæ frigidæ & siccæ: dicitur ab Astronomis infortuna major, quoniam suâ influentia adversatur vitæ: ex membris habet aurem dextram, splenem, ossa & dentes: ex morbis, frigidos & siccos, catarrhos, paralysin, hydrodropisin, scorbutum, podagram, chiragram, lepram & cancrum: ex metallis, plumbum: ex regionibus Clima primum, Orientis dextrum, Saxoniam, Stiriam: ex lapidibus pretiosis bruces, lapides nigros, obscuros: ex regionibus Clima primum, Orientis dextrum, ex metallis plumbum, ex plantis frigidas & siccas, stipticiq; saporis & astringentis. Frigidum eum esse & siccum antiqui Astrologi sic probârunt: Cùm viderent Solem existentem in Leone terras adurere, aliquando autem id factum non esse observatum sit, inquisiverunt, quænam hujus sit frigiditatis causa? repererunt autem Saturnum cum Sole, unde concluserunt, ipsum Solis calorem imminuisse. Licet enim sit calidus, tamen sunt in eo aliæ qualitates reconditæ, propter quas calor non est potis ad nos descendere. Non enim frigefacit per lucem, quæ sua natura calefacit, sed per qualitatem insensilem infrigidantem, quam lumen non potest rejicere ac vincere. Sphæra ipsius est amplissima: quò enim Sphæra aliqua est firmamento propior, eò amplior, unde longiori etiam ambitu cursum suum absolvit, 30. enim annorum fere spacio, vel secundum alios annis 29. diebus 162. horis 7. minutis 36. centrum epicycli ejus totum zodiacum percurrit motu æquali seu medio, unde motus Saturni dicitur tardissimus. Motus ejus diurnus est 57. minut. tantum enim singulis diebus in epicycloitineris conficit: totam vero epicycli revolutionem 3 7 8. diebus, id est anno, & 13. diebus, qui motus dicitur periodicus. Apogæum ejus, id est, maxima à terra distantia, tempore Ptolomæi, id est ante 1400. annos fuit in 23. scorpionis, nostro in 23. sagittarii gradu. Latitudo vero ejus maxima septentrionalis in epicyclo est 3. graduum, totidemq; meridionalis, si centrum epicycli extiterit in nodorum umbilico, & ipse Saturnus in epicycli parte ima: si enim extiterit in summo epicycli fastigio, maxima latitudo septentrionalis est 2. graduum, totidemq; meridionalis. In eccentricoautem terminus maximæ latitudinis septentrionalis est 7. grad. scorpionis, meridionalis 7. gr. tauri. Arcus visionis in Saturno est 11. grad. magniq; interest scire, quanti sint arcus visionis, hoc est, in qua distantia singulæ stellæ radiis Solis occultatæ denuò prodeant in nostrum conspectum: hi autem arcus aliàs majora, aliàs minora occupant in Ecliptica spacia, propter obliquitatem zodiaci & horizontis. 15. annis cum dimidio est septentrionalis, reliquis 14. meridionalis.
units.tr: Saturn, the highest of the planets, nearest the firmament, is pale in colour, cold and dry in nature and influence. Astronomers call him the greater misfortune, since his influence works against life. Among the body parts he rules the right ear, the spleen, the bones and the teeth. Among diseases he rules cold and dry ones: catarrhs, paralysis, dropsy, scurvy, gout in the feet, gout in the hands, leprosy and cancer. Among metals he rules lead. Among regions he rules the first clime, the eastern right side, Saxony and Styria. Among precious stones he rules bruces and dark, obscure stones.
