Among plants he rules cold and dry ones, with a styptic and astringent taste. The ancient astrologers proved that Saturn is cold and dry in this way. They saw that the Sun, when in Leo, scorches the earth, yet it was observed that this did not always happen. So they inquired what the cause of this coldness was, and they found Saturn together with the Sun. From this they concluded that Saturn diminishes the heat of the Sun. For although Saturn is hot, there are in him other hidden qualities, because of which his heat cannot descend to us. For he does not chill by light, which by its nature warms, but by an insensible chilling quality that light cannot repel or overcome. His sphere is very large, for the nearer a sphere is to the firmament, the larger it is, and so it completes its course in a longer circuit. In about thirty years, or according to others in 29 years, 162 days, 7 hours and 36 minutes, the centre of his epicycle traverses the whole zodiac with uniform or mean motion, whence Saturn's motion is called the slowest. His daily motion is 57 minutes, for he covers only that much in his epicycle each day. The full revolution of the epicycle is 378 days, that is a year and 13 days, and this is called the periodic motion. His apogee, that is his greatest distance from the earth, was in the time of Ptolomy, that is 1400 years ago, at 23 degrees of Scorpio; in our time it is at 23 degrees of Sagittarius. His greatest northern latitude in the epicycle is 3 degrees, and his southern latitude is the same, if the centre of the epicycle is at the node's navel and Saturn himself is in the lowest part of the epicycle. For if he is at the highest summit of the epicycle, his greatest northern latitude is 2 degrees, and the southern the same. On the eccentric, the limit of his greatest northern latitude is 7 degrees of Scorpio, and of his greatest southern latitude 7 degrees of Taurus. The arc of visibility for Saturn is 11 degrees. It matters greatly to know how large the arcs of visibility are, that is, at what distance each star, hidden by the rays of the Sun, reappears in our sight. These arcs occupy now larger, now smaller spaces on the ecliptic, because of the obliquity of the zodiac and the horizon. For 15 and a half years he is north of the ecliptic, and for the other 14 years south of it.

units.la: Stationes Saturni fiunt in quadrato, id est, distantia à Sole 90. & aliquot graduum. Stationum puncta nosse, exploratumque habere, utrum Planeta fit in statione prima vel secunda, plurimùm momenti affert & lucis ad dexterius ex astris divinandum. Est autem statio punctum in epicyclo, in quo Planeta fit vel retrogradus vel directus. Estq; prima vel secunda. Prima est illud epicycli punctum, in quo Planeta fit retrogradus, quod fit, si Planeta à suprema epicycli parte ad inferiorem in latere orientali velociter descendit, & tunc aliquantum videtur subsistere, ac dicitur stationarius statione prima, fitq; in hujus stationis principio retrogradus, donec ad imam epicycli partem devenerit, indeq; in fine retrogradationis per alterum epicycli latus, occidentale scilicet, ascendens fit iterum stationarius statione secunda, quæ tantisper durat, donec summum epicycli fastigium assecutus fit. Ubi sciendum arcum stationis primæ non semper esse ejusdem quantitatis, quanto enim centrum epicycli terræ centro fuerit vicinius, eò minor est arcus stationis primæ, regressioq; minor: ii quoq; Planetæ qui majorem habent epicyclum, majorem quoque obtinent stationem primam, sed arcum regressionis minorem, ut in Marte & Venere apparet.
units.tr: Saturn's stations occur in quadrature, that is, at a distance of about 90 and some degrees from the Sun. To know the points of the stations, and to have it established whether a planet is in its first or second station, contributes greatly to light and to divining from the stars more accurately. A station is a point in the epicycle at which the planet becomes either retrograde or direct. There is a first and a second station. The first is that point of the epicycle at which the planet becomes retrograde. This happens when the planet descends swiftly from the highest part of the epicycle to the lower part on the eastern side, and then it seems to stand still for a while, and is said to be stationary in the first station. It becomes retrograde at the beginning of this station, until it reaches the lowest part of the epicycle. Then at the end of the retrogradation, it ascends by the other side of the epicycle, namely the western, and becomes stationary again in the second station. This lasts only until it reaches the highest summit of the epicycle. Here it should be noted that the arc of the first station is not always of the same size. The nearer the centre of the epicycle is to the centre of the earth, the smaller the arc of the first station and the smaller the retrogression. Those planets which have a larger epicycle also have a larger first station, but a smaller arc of retrogression, as appears in Mars and Venus.

units.la: Cæterum Saturnus celerius fertur in suo epicyclo quàm Jupiter, & hic velocior est rursus Marte, Sol enim tardissimum quemq; ex his suo cursu celerrimè assequitur, quare necesse est
units.tr: Moreover, Saturn moves more quickly in his epicycle than Jupiter, and Jupiter is in turn faster than Mars. For the Sun, the slowest of these, overtakes each of them most quickly in its course, so it is necessary that

units.la: Planetam, qui in suo eccentrico movetur tardius, suum in epi-cyclo cursum accelerare, ut Sole accedente ad conjunctionem ipse in fastigio sui epicycli reperiatur. Tres enim Planetæ supe-riores ita se in epicyclo Soli accommodant, ut, quoties Soli iis con-jungitur, toties summum epicycli sui occupent fastigium, cum vero iis opponitur, imam teneant partem. Semper quoque su-periores, Saturnus, Jupiter, Mars, circa medium directionis tempus Soli conjunguntur, circa vero medium regressionis, ei-dem opponuntur.
units.tr: the planet which moves more slowly on its eccentric should speed up its course in the epicycle, so that, as the Sun approaches conjunction, the planet itself is found at the summit of its epicycle. For the three superior planets accommodate themselves to the Sun in the epicycle in such a way that whenever they are in conjunction with the Sun, they occupy the summit of their epicycle, but when they are in opposition to it, they hold the lowest part. The superior planets, Saturn, Jupiter and Mars, are also always in conjunction with the Sun around the middle of the time of direct motion, and in opposition to it around the middle of retrogression.

units.la: Longissimè deniq; Saturnus à terris distat hac nostra æta-te ratione eccentrici, cùm epicyclus ejus currit per postremas sagittarii partes, unde minoris est efficaciæ, quàm cùm est in ge-minis, ut anno 1441. sub Imper. Friderico proavo Caroli V. veri-simile est, eum sua ad terram propinquitate effecisse immanissi-mum illud frigus, & plane inusitatum, quod adeo fuit sævum & diuturnum, ut illa hyemis nostra ætate hominum memoriâ facta sit celebris: hæc remotio & propinquitas Saturni (ut & reliquorum) etiam magnitudines & colores nonnihil mutat, ut hoc anno Saturnus & minor paulò & obscurior apparet, quoniam Apogæo vicinior est quàm Perigæo.
units.tr: Finally, in our age, Saturn is furthest from the earth by this arrangement of the eccentric, when his epicycle passes through the last parts of Sagittarius. Hence his power is weaker than when he is in Gemini. It is likely that in the year 1441, under the Emperor Frederick, great-grandfather of Charles V, he caused by his proximity to the earth that immense and quite unusual cold, which was so fierce and lasting that the winter became famous in the memory of men of our time. This remoteness and nearness of Saturn (and of the other planets) also alters their sizes and colours somewhat. Thus this year Saturn appears a little smaller and dimmer, because he is nearer to apogee than to perigee.

units.la: Jupiter Planeta est Saturno proximus, lucidus maximè, [illegible, ~7 letters] & temperatus, generiq; humano salutaris: ex membris habet venas aurem sinistram, pulmones, epar, & horum membrorum infirmitates: ab Astrologis dicitur fortuna major. Ex gemmis habet smaragdum, sapphyrum, amethystum: ex metallis stannum: ex regionibus Clima secundum, Septentrionem; Babyloniam, Persiden, Hungariam, Hispanias: ex plantis calidas & humidas moderatè, dulcisq; saporis, ac odoris boni.
units.tr: Jupiter is the planet next to Saturn, very bright, [illegible], temperate, and wholesome for the human race. Among the body parts he rules the veins, the left ear, the lungs, the liver, and the illnesses of these parts. Astrologers call him the greater fortune. Among gems he rules the emerald, the sapphire and the amethyst. Among metals he rules tin. Among regions he rules the second clime, the North, Babylonia, Persia, Hungary and Spain. Among plants he rules those that are moderately warm and moist, with a sweet taste and a good smell.

units.la: Centrum epicycli ejus totum zodiacum percurrit 12. ferè annis: motus diurnus est 54. minutorum: periodicus unius an-ni, & 34. ferè dierum.
units.tr: The centre of his epicycle traverses the whole zodiac in about 12 years. His daily motion is 54 minutes, and his periodic motion is one year and about 34 days.

units.la: Apogæum ejus tempore Ptolomæi erat in ii.[?] gradu virgi-nis, nuncin 6. libræ: Perigæum in 6. arietis, unde cum per primos arietis gradus incedit, Soli oppositus, fulgentissimus appa-ret, ut quandoq; etiam umbram spargat, quoniam tunc epicy-clus in ima eccentrici parte versatur.
units.tr: His apogee in the time of Ptolomy was at the second degree of Virgo; now it is at 6 degrees of Libra. His perigee is at 6 degrees of Aries, so that when he passes through the first degrees of Aries, opposite the Sun, he appears most brilliant, so that he sometimes even casts a shadow, since then the epicycle is in the lowest part of the eccentric.

units.la: Terminus & punctum maximæ latitudinis septentriona-lis est 27. gradus libræ, meridionalis 27. gr. arietis: maxima vero elongatio seu latitudo Jovis in epicyclo, & quidem apogæo & parte septetrionali est unius gr. 6. min. in perigæo 2. gr. & 5. min. Meridionali vero & apogæo unius gr. 4. min. In perigæo 2. grad. 8. min.
units.tr: The limit and point of his greatest northern latitude is 27 degrees of Libra, and his greatest southern latitude is 27 degrees of Aries. The greatest elongation or latitude of Jupiter in the epicycle, namely at apogee and on the northern side, is 1 degree 6 minutes; at perigee it is 2 degrees 5 minutes. On the southern side at apogee it is 1 degree 4 minutes; at perigee 2 degrees 8 minutes.

units.la: Arcus visionis est 10. grad. Stationes ejus fiunt in trigono, hoc est, distantia à Sole 120. grad. Sexannis cum dimidio fere septentriones versus deviat, quinq; cum semisse versus meridiē.
units.tr: The arc of visibility is 10 degrees. His stations occur in trine, that is, at a distance of 120 degrees from the Sun. For about six and a half years he deviates towards the north, and for five and a half towards the south.

units.la: Mars Planeta in ordine tertius, coloris semper rutilantis, naturæ calidæ & siccæ vehementer. Zodiacum interdum egre-ditur, & quidem cum est in opposito augis, sed tamen raro, ut anno 1529. quo per dies 40. fere in mense Julio habuit latitudi-nem 7. graduū. Ex membris habet, fel, venas & renes: ex morbis tertianas, & calidiores omnes, vulnera item faciei: ab Astrologis dicitur infortuna minor. Ex lapidibus habet Jaspidem & Hæmatitem. Ex metallis ferrum: ex plantis calidas & siccas immoderatè, saporisq; fellei & acris. Ex climatibus, tertium, Septen-trionem, Gothiam, Longobardiam, Ferrariam. Motus ejus pe-riodicus est 2. annorum, & 67. dierum: motus diurnus 27. mi-nut. Zodiacum percurrit motu proprio biennio fere. Apo-gæum ejus tempore Ptolomæi erat in 25. grad. Cancri, hodie in 27. Leonis. Maxima latitudo septentrionalis Martis est in 27. Leonis, meridionalis in 27. Aquarii. Extrema latitudo epicycli in septentrione & apogæo est unius gr. 6. min. in perigæo 2. gr. 5. min. In meridie vero & apogæo, 0. gr. 2. min. In perigæo 7. gr. 30. 30. min. Arcus visionis est 11. graduum & dimidii. In perigæo existens, peragransq; extremas æquarii partes, Solíq; oppositus, inusitata plane magnitudine, & horrendo rubore fulget.
units.tr: Mars is the third planet in order. He is always of a ruddy colour, very hot and very dry in nature. He sometimes leaves the zodiac, and this happens especially when he is in opposition to the apogee, but rarely; for instance in the year 1529, when for about 40 days in July he had a latitude of 7 degrees. Among the body parts he rules the gall, the veins and the kidneys. Among diseases he rules tertian fevers and all the hotter ones, and likewise wounds of the face. Astrologers call him the lesser misfortune. Among stones he rules jasper and haematite. Among metals he rules iron. Among plants he rules those that are immoderately hot and dry, with a bitter and sharp taste. Among climes he rules the third, the North, Gothia, Lombardy and Ferrara. His periodic motion is two years and 67 days; his daily motion is 27 minutes. He traverses the zodiac by his own motion in about two years. His apogee in the time of Ptolomy was at 25 degrees of Cancer; today it is at 27 degrees of Leo. Mars's greatest northern latitude is at 27 degrees of Leo, and his greatest southern latitude at 27 degrees of Aquarius. The extreme latitude of the epicycle on the northern side at apogee is 1 degree 6 minutes; at perigee 2 degrees 5 minutes. On the southern side at apogee it is 0 degrees 2 minutes; at perigee 7 degrees 30 minutes. The arc of visibility is 11 and a half degrees. When he is at perigee, passing through the extreme parts of Aquarius and opposite the Sun, he shines with an unusually great size and a terrible red glow.

units.la: Magnam autem diversitatem in Marte efficiunt epicycli magnitudo, & velocitas ejus in eccentrico seu deferente, hæc enim velocitas efficit, quod nec in quadrato, nec in trigono, sed multò post fiat retrogradus: magnitudo autem epicycli facit, quòd statim à quadrato motus ejus in singulos dies sensibiliter minuatur, id quod in reliquis duobus non accidit, quæ etiam ratio est, quòd inæquali plane modo nunc in septentrionem, nunc in meridiem feratur. Quin aliquando contingit, ut ratione suæ stationis & retrogradationis commoretur in uno signo sex integris mensibus, propter passiones dictas, ut ann.1533. Mars mense Aug. est ingressus signum geminorum, in quo commoratus est usque ad finem Martii: item anno 44. & 48.
units.tr: Mars produces great variety through the size of its epicycle and the speed of its motion on the eccentric, or deferent. This speed means that it does not turn retrograde at the quadrature or the trine, but much later. The size of the epicycle means that its motion begins to slow noticeably from the quadrature onward, day by day, which does not happen with the other two superior planets. This is also why it moves in a thoroughly irregular way, now northward and now southward. Indeed, it sometimes happens that, because of its station and retrogradation and the irregularities just mentioned, it remains in one sign for six whole months. So in 1533 Mars entered the sign of Gemini in August and stayed there until the end of March; the same happened in 1544 and 1548.

units.la: SOL Planetarum medius, lucidissimus, efficacissimus, lucis fons & autor, calidus & siccus temperatè: ex membris tenet & disponit oculum dextrum, cor, dextrumq; latus: ex morbis Syncopen, tremorem cordis, ophthalmica vitia: ex gemmis sapphyrum, & hiacynthum, ex metallis aurum, ex plantis calidas & siccas moderatè, odorisq; ac saporis boni, acrisq; cum suavitate: ex regionibus Clima 4. & Orientem.
units.tr: The Sun is the middle of the planets, the brightest and most powerful, the fountain and author of light, hot and dry in a temperate degree. Among the parts of the body it rules and governs the right eye, the heart and the right side. Among diseases it governs syncope, palpitation of the heart, and eye disorders. Among gems it governs sapphire and hyacinth, among metals gold, among plants those that are moderately hot and dry, with a good smell and taste, and a sharp taste tempered with sweetness. Among regions it governs the fourth clime and the East.

units.la: Perpetuò fertur sub Ecliptica, quam non exorbitat, eamque percurrit diebus 365. & 5. horis, cum 49. minut. Singulis verò diebus eccentricibus ejus conficit 59. minut. retrocedit enim quotidie contra primum mobile uno fere gradu.
units.tr: It always moves beneath the ecliptic, which it never leaves, and it completes its circuit in 365 days and 5 hours, with 49 minutes. Each day, in its eccentric, it covers 59 minutes; for it retreats every day against the primum mobile by almost one degree.

units.la: Latitudinem habet nullam, quia Eclipticam non egreditur, habet tamen declinationem, id est, distantiam ab æquatore, versus scilicet latera mundi. Epicyclo caret ob motus regularitatem & simplicitatem, in qua tamen regularitate duo ei contingunt, ut alicubi à terra abeat longiùs in sublime, ut cumtenet eccentrici sui apogæum, alibi ad terram accedat propius, ut cum tenet ejusdem eccentrici perigæum: deinde propter eundem eccentricum fit, ut circa locum apogei feratur tardius, circa perigæum velocius, unde diutius commorari deprehenditur in signis æstivis quàm hybernis, quoniam eccentricus in æstivo & septentrionali hemicyclo longius supra centrũ mundi attollitur, quàm hyberno.
units.tr: It has no latitude, since it never leaves the ecliptic, but it does have declination, that is, distance from the equator, namely toward the sides of the world. It has no epicycle, because of the regularity and simplicity of its motion. Yet in this regularity two things happen to it: at one place it recedes farther from the earth on high, namely when it holds the apogee of its eccentric, and at another place it approaches the earth more closely, namely when it holds the perigee of the same eccentric. Further, because of the same eccentric, it moves more slowly near the apogee and more quickly near the perigee, whence it is found to linger longer in the summer signs than in the winter ones, since the eccentric rises higher above the centre of the world in the summer and northern hemicycle than in the winter one.

units.la: Apogæus hodie est in 5. grad. Cancri: tempore Ptolomæi erat in 5. geminorum: perigæus in 5. Capricorni: illic à terris maximè distabat Ptolomæi tempore 605. diametris, hic 561. diametris, tempore nostro apogæum Solis à terra abest 589. diametris tantùm & semisse, quoniam eccentricitas (id est, distantia centri eccentrici à centro mundi) Solis, ut & Martis mutata est, nam apogæum Solis, durante mundo, tandem devenit in Leonem, quoniam apsides ejus moventur tardissimè, qui motus etiam aliquot annorum myriadibus non conficitur per zodiacum: fit autem mutatio horum punctorum non in zodiaco, sed ipso orbe Solis. Itaq; etiam differunt puncta solstitialia ab apogæo & perigæo Solis, illa enim sunt puncta in zodiaco immobilia, hæc verò mobilia.
units.tr: Today the apogee of the Sun is at 5 degrees of Cancer; in Ptolemy's time it was at 5 degrees of Gemini, and the perigee at 5 degrees of Capricorn. In Ptolemy's time it was 605 diameters from the earth at its farthest point, and here 561 diameters. In our time the Sun's apogee is only 589 and a half diameters from the earth, since the eccentricity of the Sun (that is, the distance between the centre of the eccentric and the centre of the world), as also of Mars, has changed. For the apogee of the Sun, while the world endures, will at last arrive in Leo, since its apsides move very slowly; this motion is not completed through the zodiac even in many myriads of years. But the change of these points takes place not in the zodiac but in the Sun's own orbit. Thus the solstitial points also differ from the apogee and perigee of the Sun: the former are fixed points in the zodiac, while the latter are movable.

units.la: Motu primo uno horæ minuto conficit spacium 4552. milliarium, & una hora raptatur per arcum continentem centies decies septies terræ semidiametros: proprio verò motu uno scrupulo horæ percurrit 12. milliaria cum dimidio.
units.tr: By its primary motion it covers a space of 4552 miles in one minute of an hour, and in one hour it is carried through an arc containing 117 times the semidiameter of the earth. By its own motion, however, it traverses 12 and a half miles in one second of an hour.

units.la: Motus, quo omnia signa zodiaci percurrit intra annum, dicitur annuus, & anniversarius, unde annus solaris est, qui continet 12. menses solares. Mensis autem solaris est præcisè 12. pars anni solaris, id est 30. dierum, & 10. horarum, 29. minut. Annus lunaris verò est spacium, quo duodecim integræ lunationes conficiuntur, nam illud temporis spacium, quo Sol & Luna duodecies conjunguntur, est annus lunaris, continens 354. dies, hor. 8. minor igitur anno solari diebus fere 11. Mensis lunaris seu syno-dicus est intervallum temporis inter duo proxima novilunia seu conjunctiones, continetq; dies 29. hor. 12. Motu igitur æ-quali seu medio describit annum solarem, quatuorq; tempo-rum differentias, conjunctionibus vero cum Luna mensem so-larem: motu diurno dierum & noctium metitur incrementa & decrementa, & tandem partes dierum, nempe horas motu eodem.
units.tr: The motion by which the Sun passes through all the signs of the zodiac within a year is called annual, and anniversary, whence the solar year is the one that contains 12 solar months. A solar month is exactly the twelfth part of the solar year, that is, 30 days, 10 hours and 29 minutes. The lunar year, however, is the period in which twelve complete lunations are accomplished; for the period of time in which the Sun and Moon are conjoined twelve times is the lunar year, consisting of 354 days and 8 hours. It is therefore about 11 days shorter than the solar year. The lunar or synodic month is the interval of time between two successive new moons or conjunctions, and it contains 29 days and 12 hours. By its uniform or mean motion, then, the Sun describes the solar year and the differences of the four seasons; by its conjunctions with the Moon, the solar month; by its daily motion it measures the increase and decrease of days and nights, and finally the parts of the day, namely the hours, by the same motion.

units.la: Æqualis seu medius Solis motus est, quo Sol æquales in zodiaco arcus æquali temporis spacio absolvit, progrediens scilicet super centro eccentrici sui, singulis diebus 59. minuta peragrans, & percurrens totum orbem diebus 365. Inæqualis, verus, seu apparens est, quo Sol inæquales in zodiaco arcus æqualibus temporum spaciis, aut contra æquales arcus inæquali temporis spacio perlustrat, hoc est, ex paribus arcubus alterum celerius, alterum tardius, idq; respectu centri zodiaci, seu lineæ etiam visualis, quæ ex oculo intuente Solem excurrit. Nam Sole tenente apogæum, longiores sunt lineæ, quæ ad illum ducuntur, quàm lineæ Solem intuentes in perigæo, unde etiam angu-los & arcus inæquales esse necesse est. Hi motus discernuntur per lineas mobiles, quarum præcipuus est usus, ut per eas zodia-cus & eccentricus in angulos & arcus dividantur, sicut enim constitutis punctis ducuntur lineæ, ita lineis ductis mensuran-tur anguli & arcus. Ejusmodi autem sunt linea medii, & linea veri motus, quæ lineæ in demonstratione veri motus magnum habent usum: in apogæo enim & perigæo nihil differt medius motus ab apparente seu vero, quia linea veri & medii motus coëunt cum linea apogæi & perigæi: progrediente autem stella, lineæ istæ incipiunt disjungi, ac maximè differt medius motus ab apparente & vero circa lineam mediarum longitudinum, seu medii transitus, quæ transit utrinque per centrum terræ ad duo puncta mediae longitudinis, dividitq; lineam apogaei & perigaei ad angulos rectos, quam etiam motu suo imitatur. Sed linea medii motus est linea recta, e centro excentrici ducta ad centrum Solis in suo orbe, in quo motus ponitur aequalis. Veri motus linea e centro terrae per centrum Planetae ad zodiacum usq; protenditur, verumq; & apparentem Solis vel alterius Planetae motum designat: harum certe linearum usus est insignis ad motus Solis accurate investigandos, ac quidem Ptolomaeus sola linea medii motus contentus est, cum de Sole seorsim disputans, aequalem ejus motum determinat.
units.tr: The equal or mean motion of the Sun is that by which the Sun traverses equal arcs of the zodiac in equal spaces of time, advancing, that is, upon the centre of its eccentric, covering 59 minutes each day and completing the whole orbit in 365 days. The unequal, true, or apparent motion is that by which the Sun traverses unequal arcs of the zodiac in equal spaces of time, or conversely equal arcs in unequal spaces of time; that is, of two equal arcs it passes over one more swiftly and the other more slowly. This is reckoned with respect to the centre of the zodiac, or to the visual line which runs out from the eye that beholds the Sun. For when the Sun is at the apogee, the lines drawn to it are longer than the lines which look at the Sun from the perigee; whence it is also necessary that the angles and arcs be unequal. These motions are distinguished by moving lines, whose chief use is to divide the zodiac and the eccentric into angles and arcs; for just as lines are drawn once points are fixed, so angles and arcs are measured once lines are drawn. Of this kind are the line of mean motion and the line of true motion, which lines have great use in demonstrating the true motion. For at the apogee and perigee the mean motion differs in no way from the apparent or true motion, because the lines of true and mean motion coincide with the line of apogee and perigee. But as the star advances, these lines begin to separate, and the mean motion differs most from the apparent and true motion near the line of mean longitudes, or the line of mean transit, which passes on both sides through the centre of the earth to two points of mean longitude, and divides the line of apogee and perigee at right angles; this line also imitates it in its own motion. The line of mean motion, however, is a straight line drawn from the centre of the eccentric to the centre of the Sun in its orbit, in which the motion is posited as equal. The line of true motion extends from the centre of the earth through the centre of the planet to the zodiac, and designates the true and apparent motion of the Sun or of another planet. The use of these lines is indeed notable for investigating the motions of the Sun accurately; Ptolemy, however, was content with the line of mean motion alone, when discussing the Sun separately, and determined its equal motion.

units.la: Venus Planeta est Sole inferior & proximus, omnium, exceptis luminaribus, candidissimus & lucidissimus, temperatae humiditatis: ex membris habet matricem, renes, genitalia, mammillas: ex morbis priapismum, gonorrhoeam, diabeten, luem[?] gallicam: ex gemmis uniones, sapphyrum, carbunculum: ex metallis cuprum, & omnis generis perpolita specula, ex regionibus Clima 5. Austriam, Arabiam, Campaniam, Poloniam majorem.
units.tr: Venus is the planet next below the Sun, and, apart from the luminaries, the whitest and brightest of all, of temperate moisture. Among the parts of the body it governs the womb, the kidneys, the genitals and the breasts. Among diseases it governs priapism, gonorrhoea, diabetes and the French pox. Among gems it governs pearls, sapphire and carbuncle; among metals copper, and every kind of polished mirror. Among regions it governs the fifth clime, Austria, Arabia, Campania and greater Poland.

units.la: Mercurius Planetarum minimus, parum albicans, indif-ferentis est & versatilis naturae, assumit enim naturam illius Planetae vel stellae, cum qua vel jungitur, vel quam radio suo aspicit: ex membris habet linguam, nervos: ex facultatibus cerebri, memoriam, phantasiam, imaginationem: ex morbis significat raucedinem, balbutiem, & omnis generis deliria melancholica: ex lapidibus alectorium: ex metallis mercurium: ex saporibus mixtos: ex regionibus Clima 6. Ægyptum, Græciam, Angliam, Flandriam, Silesiam, &c. Dissimili vero plane modo, & velut motu converso à tribus superioribus circumvolvuntur Venus & Mercurius. Superiores enim celerrimè feruntur in occasu vespertino, inferiores vero tardissimè. Ratio hujus dissi-militudinis est, quia in tali occasu vespertino tres superiores Sóli[?] junguntur, & occidunt occasu heliaco, funtq; tunc etiâ directi, quia in summa epicyclorum suorum existunt auge, inferiores vero in occasu vespertino sunt in opposito augis suorum epicyclorum, quare tardiores, & quamvis ferantur secundum signorum successionem ratione eccentrici, tamen ratione epicycli retrahuntur. Sic tres superiores à terra altissimè absunt, cùm tardissimè moventur, inferiores cùm ocyssimè, hi enim in superiore sui epicycli parte in eandem partem, qua & eccentricus, moventur:igitur extremitas circuli, hoc est, superior pars epicycli accelerat, quia fertur secundum seriem signorum, & ratione eccentrici & epicycli: Mercurius & Venus celerrimè moventur, cùm altissimè absunt à terra ratione epicycli: centrum autem epicycli trium superiorum, cùm est in auge, movetur tardissimè, cumq; accedit propius ad centrum mundi, accelerat motum, æquali enim tempore majus spacium secundum ordinem signorum conficiunt. Unde facile apparet utilitas epicycli, cujus ratione omnia facilimè intelligi & demonstrari possunt.
units.tr: Mercury is the least of the planets, somewhat whitish, of an indifferent and changeable nature; for it takes on the nature of whichever planet or star it is joined with, or whichever it regards with its ray. Among the parts of the body it governs the tongue and the sinews; among the faculties of the brain, memory, fantasy and imagination. Among diseases it signifies hoarseness, stammering, and every kind of melancholic delirium. Among stones it governs the alectorius; among metals quicksilver; among tastes, mixed ones. Among regions it governs the sixth clime, Egypt, Greece, England, Flanders, Silesia, and so on. Venus and Mercury revolve in a quite different manner, and as it were by a reversed motion, from the three superior planets. For the superior planets move most swiftly at their evening setting, while the inferior ones move most slowly. The reason for this dissimilarity is that at such an evening setting the three superior planets are conjoined with the Sun and set at their heliacal setting, and they are then also direct, because they are at the highest point of their epicycles, that is, at their apogees; the inferior ones, however, at their evening setting are opposite the apogees of their epicycles, and therefore move more slowly, and although they are carried in the order of the signs by reason of the eccentric, nevertheless by reason of the epicycle they are pulled back. Thus the three superior planets are at their greatest distance from the earth when they move most slowly, while the inferior ones move most swiftly. For the superior planets move in the upper part of their epicycle in the same direction as the eccentric; so the outer edge of the circle, that is, the upper part of the epicycle, is accelerated, because it is carried in the order of the signs both by the eccentric and by the epicycle. Mercury and Venus move most swiftly when they are at their greatest distance from the earth by reason of the epicycle. But the centre of the epicycle of the three superior planets, when it is at the apogee, moves most slowly, and as it approaches nearer the centre of the world it quickens its motion, for in equal time it covers a greater space in the order of the signs. Hence the usefulness of the epicycle is easily apparent; by its means all things can be most easily understood and demonstrated.

units.la: Hi enim circuli, quia centrum terræ non ambiunt, hanc apparentiarum dissimilitudinem clarè oculis subjiciunt. Porrò Venus candidissimus Solis est comes, alterno meatu vagus, nunc Solem antecedens, nunc subsequens. Sic dicta quasi venusta stella ob luminis claritatem & pulchritudinem. Peculiaris au-tem Veneris & Mercurii ratio est, habent enim certos & præfinitos terminos, quos ultra & citra transfire nequeunt, atque à Phœbo suo discedere longius. Apostaseos[?] tamen atq; digressionis termini à Sole non sunt ubiq; iidem, contingunt namq; majores, cùm epicyclus in perigæo eccentrici versatur, minores cùm in apogæo. Si igitur epicyclus est in apogæo eccentrici Veneris, maxima à Sole elongatio est 44.graduum, Mercurii 16.gr. Si epicyclus est in perigæo eccentrici, Veneris maxima elongatio est 47.gr. Mercurii 28. nam hæc est semidiameter epicycli inzodiaco dimensa, & non potest ultra prædictos terminos à Sole abesse, quia curvatura absidum non habet ibi longitudinem majorem, hoc est, quia diameter epicycli nusquam est major prædicto termino: ut ita tunc stella longissime à Sole abesse intelligatur, cùm est in illo contactus puncto, ubi centrum epicycli est inter Planetam & Solem. Cur autem Veneris & Mercurii elongationes mutentur, ratio est accessus centri epicycli ad centrum mundi. In Mercurio digressio seu elongatio apud septentrionales vix animadvertitur, quod & epicyclus minimus sit, & latitudine in meridiem deviet, nisi cùm est in altero perigæo: habet enim duo perigæa, unum in 9. piscium gradu, alterum in 9. gr. cancri, in his longissime digreditur à Sole, & proxime ad terram accedit, cùm scilicet centrum epicycli est in 9. piscium vel cancri: unum vero habet apogæum, in 7. scorpionis. Eccentricitatem quoq; (id est, distantiam centri eccentrici à centro mundi) habet minimam, unde menses tantùm 4. in epicycli cursu absolvendo consumit, unoq; anno semel atq; iterum omnia loca percurrit.
units.tr: These circles, because they do not encircle the centre of the earth, make this difference of appearances plainly visible to the eyes. Venus, the brightest companion of the Sun, wanders with an alternating course, now ahead of the Sun and now behind it. She is named as if she were a "venusta" (lovely) star, on account of the clarity and beauty of her light. Venus and Mercury have a peculiar feature: they have fixed and determined limits, beyond which they cannot pass on either side, and they cannot move farther away from their Phoebus. The limits of their separation (apostasis) from the Sun are not everywhere the same, for the greater ones occur when the epicycle is in the perigee of the eccentric, the lesser when it is in the apogee. So if the epicycle is in the apogee of Venus's eccentric, her greatest elongation from the Sun is 44 degrees, and Mercury's is 16 degrees. If the epicycle is in the perigee of the eccentric, Venus's greatest elongation is 47 degrees and Mercury's 28 degrees, for this is the semidiameter of the epicycle measured in the zodiac. The planet cannot be farther from the Sun than the aforesaid limits, because the curvature of the apsides has no greater length there; that is, the diameter of the epicycle is nowhere greater than the aforesaid limit. Thus the star is understood to be farthest from the Sun when it is at that point of contact where the centre of the epicycle lies between the planet and the Sun. The reason why the elongations of Venus and Mercury vary is the approach of the centre of the epicycle to the centre of the world. In the case of Mercury, the digression or elongation is hardly noticed by northerners, both because the epicycle is very small and because it deviates in latitude towards the south, except when it is in the other perigee. For it has two perigees, one at 9 degrees of Pisces and the other at 9 degrees of Cancer; in these it departs farthest from the Sun and comes nearest to the earth, namely when the centre of the epicycle is at 9 degrees of Pisces or Cancer. It has one apogee, at 7 degrees of Scorpio. It also has the smallest eccentricity (that is, the distance of the centre of the eccentric from the centre of the world), so it takes only about four months to complete its course in the epicycle, and once and again in each year it runs through all places.

units.la: Venus evagatur extra Eclipticam longissime versus septentrionesad gr. 7. versus meridiem ad gradus 6. Motus ejus diurnus est 36. graduum: periodicus epicycli 583. dierum, & 22. horarum. In eccentrico vero tempus periodicum idem fere cum Sole & Mercurio est, id est, dierum 365. hor. 5. 49. minut. Absis altissima à centro terræ est in 1. gr. cancri, humilima & terræ proxima est in 1. capricorni.
units.tr: Venus wanders outside the ecliptic as far as 7 degrees to the north and 6 degrees to the south. Her daily motion is 36 degrees; the periodic time of the epicycle is 583 days and 22 hours. On the eccentric, however, the periodic time is almost the same as that of the Sun and Mercury, that is, 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes. The highest apse, from the centre of the earth, is at 1 degree of Cancer; the lowest, nearest to the earth, is at 1 degree of Capricorn.

units.la: Ocyssima & altissima existit, cùm attigit metam longissimæ distantiæ, illud videlicet punctum contactus, ubi centrum epicycli est inter Planetam & Solem.
units.tr: She is swiftest and at her highest when she reaches the goal of greatest distance, that is, that point of contact where the centre of the epicycle lies between the planet and the Sun.

units.la: Mercurii motus diurnus est 3. minut. periodicus in epicyclo 115. dierum, 21. horarum: in eccentrico idem cum Venere: apogæum ejus hodie est in 7. scorpii gradu, perigæum in 7. tauri. ri. Maxima ejus latitudo versus feptentr. est 4. gr. versus meri-diem 4.gr. & 33. minut. Maxima autem ejus ut & Veneris elon-gatio fit in perigæo eccentrici: & quantò magis à Sole fecun-dum longitudinem discedunt, tantò magis in latitudinem eva-gantur, quantitate enim semidiametri epicycli à Sole recedunt, quem recessum vocant evagationem latitudinum.
units.tr: The daily motion of Mercury is 3 minutes; the periodic time in the epicycle is 115 days and 21 hours; on the eccentric it is the same as Venus's. Its apogee today is at 7 degrees of Scorpio, its perigee at 7 degrees of Taurus. Its greatest latitude to the north is 4 degrees, to the south 4 degrees and 33 minutes. Its greatest elongation, like that of Venus, occurs in the perigee of the eccentric; and the more they move away from the Sun in longitude, the more they wander in latitude, for they recede from the Sun by the amount of the semidiameter of the epicycle, and this recession they call the wandering of latitudes.

units.la: Denique Venus & Mercurius antecedunt modò Solem, modò sequuntur: antecedunt in epicycli medietate occiden-tali, sequuntur in orientali: disparent verò & junguntur Soli circa apsides epicycli, id est, quando existunt in auge suorum e-picyclorum, discedentes verò ab auge oriuntur ortu vefperti-no, vespere enim post Solis occasum conspiciuntur, digrediun-tur enim à Sole fecundum arcum quantitatis epicycli, donec ad primam stationem pervenerint, ubi iterum ad Solem reciproc-cant, usq; ad augis oppositum-suorum epicyclorum, ubi rursus cum Sole conjunguntur, à qua conjunctione mane ante Solis ortum fulgent, oriunturq; ortu matutino: unde patet, quòd tantùm ratione epicycli à Sole elongentur, curq; neq; ad oppo-fitionem, neq; ad reliquos aspectus digredi à Sole possint, invol-vuntur enim circa Solem, & ad eum reciprocant propter mo-tum ipsorum in epicyclo. Duplices quoq; ortus & occasus in-currunt, priusq; suos epicyclos perambulent, quia eorum fem-per media est cum Sole conjunctio, à Sole enim in orientem & occidentem epicycli motu recedunt: occidunt autem occasu vespertino, quando à statione prima versus augis oppositum-suorum epicyclorum moventur, accedunt enim tam prope ad Solem, ut ipsius radiis obfuscentur & tegantur: deinde verò re-licto Sole in totidem partibus faciunt exortus matutinos, hoc est, digressi iterum à Sole, & emensi arcum visionis rursus con-spiciuntur, ac tum dicuntur oriri ortu matutino. Cùm autem Soli junguntur, vel sunt in apogæo epicycli, vel perigæo: In apogæo, cùm Solem antecedentes radios ingrediuntur: In pe-rigæo, cùm Solem sequentes radios ingrediuntur: itaq; ab ex-ortu matutino, hoc est, post conjunctionem transgressi peri-gæum epicycli, incipiunt latitudinem scandere, inquit Plinius, id est, latitudo ipsorum augetur.
units.tr: Finally, Venus and Mercury sometimes precede the Sun and sometimes follow it: they precede it in the western half of the epicycle and follow it in the eastern. They disappear and are joined to the Sun near the apses of the epicycle, that is, when they are at the apogee of their epicycles; but, departing from the apogee, they rise with an evening rising, for they are seen in the evening after sunset, since they withdraw from the Sun along an arc equal to the size of the epicycle, until they arrive at the first station, where they return again towards the Sun, as far as the opposition of the apogee of their epicycles, where they are again joined with the Sun. From this conjunction they shine in the morning before sunrise and rise with a morning rising. Hence it is clear that they are elongated from the Sun only by reason of the epicycle, and since they cannot move away from the Sun to opposition or to the other aspects, they are enveloped about the Sun and return to it because of their motion in the epicycle. They also undergo double risings and settings before they have traversed their epicycles, because the conjunction with the Sun is always in the middle of their course: for they move away from the Sun to east and west by the motion of the epicycle. They set with an evening setting when they move from the first station towards the opposition of the apogee of their epicycles, for they draw so near the Sun that they are dimmed and hidden by its rays. Then, leaving the Sun, they make morning risings in the same number of parts; that is, having separated again from the Sun and traversed the arc of visibility, they are seen again, and then they are said to rise with a morning rising. When they are joined to the Sun, they are either at the apogee or at the perigee of the epicycle: at the apogee when they enter the rays preceding the Sun; at the perigee when they enter the rays following the Sun. So from the morning rising, that is, after conjunction, when they have passed the perigee of the epicycle, they begin to climb in latitude, as Pliny says; that is, their latitude increases.

units.la: Luna Planetarum infimus, terræ proximus, temperaturæ humidæ & frigidæ, menses dispensans, noctesq; collustrans. Ex membris habet oculum sinistrū, vesicam, intestina, cerebrum, stomachum, epar: ex morbis epilepsian, & dictorum membrorum infirmitates: ex metallis argentum: ex lapidibus crystal-lum: ex regionibus Clima 7. Hollandiam, Selandiam, Daniam: ex plantis saporis salsi, mediocrisq; inter bonum & malum.
units.tr: The Moon is the lowest of the planets, nearest the earth, of a moist and cold temperament, dividing the months and lighting the nights. Among the parts of the body she rules the left eye, the bladder, the intestines, the brain, the stomach, the liver; among diseases, epilepsy and the infirmities of the aforesaid parts; among metals, silver; among stones, crystal; among regions, the seventh clime: Holland, Zealand, Denmark; among plants, those of salty taste, midway between good and bad.

units.la: Ad iter Solis perpetuò dirigitur, ab eo enim in totum mutua luce, fulget, ut inquit Plinius, totaq; inæquali lumine a-spicitur: quin ex adverso demum plena, reliquis diebus ex se terris ostendit, quantum à Sole ipsa concipit: in coitu quidem non cernitur, quoniam haustum lumen illo regerit, unde acce-pit. Plin. l. 2. c. 9. Ob hanc causam Babylonii & Ægyptii Lunam Solis uxorem faciebant. Et Aristoteles Lunam propter Solis societatem minorem Solem nominat, lib. 5. de generat. anim. c. 10. Et quidem si ad cursum Lunæ respiciamus, animad verte-mus, eam quovis mense præstare id, quod Sol toto anno agit, & in eodem mense modò esse quandam brumæ, modò quandam solstitii similitudinem.
units.tr: The Moon is constantly directed to the course of the Sun, for she shines wholly by borrowed light from him, as Pliny says, and is seen with unequal light throughout her whole course. Indeed, when she is full, opposite the Sun, she shows the earth from her own surface how much light she receives from the Sun; but at conjunction she is not seen, because she gives back the light she has drawn from him, from whom she received it. Pliny, book 2, chapter 9. For this reason the Babylonians and Egyptians made the Moon the wife of the Sun. And Aristotle, because of her association with the Sun, calls the Moon the lesser Sun, book 5 On the Generation of Animals, chapter 10. And indeed, if we look at the course of the Moon, we shall observe that in each month she performs what the Sun does in the whole year, and that within the same month she is sometimes like a winter solstice and sometimes like a summer solstice.

units.la: Totum zodiacum perlustrat motu proprio ab occasu in-ortum 27. diebus, 7. horis, & 15. min. Motus autem hic proprius Lunæ, quia fit super duobus centris, duplex est, unus æqualis seu medius, alter verus & inæqualis. Hoc super centro ecliptiæ seu mundi æqualiter movetur, & regulariter juxta ordinem si-gnorum singulis in zodiaco diebus conficiens 13. gradus, illo su-per centro eccentrici fertur inæqualiter, aliasq; zodiaci partes celerius, alias autem percurrit tardius, & hoc motu velocior Luna in eccentrico est, si summam tenet absidem, tardior circa imam. Singulis quoq; mensibus Luna bis est in apogæo, id est, in eccentrici sui summo fastigio, & bis in perigeo, id est, ima eccen-trici parte, illud contingit in omni conjunctione & oppositio-ne, hoc verò in quadraturis, cùm scilicet apparet orbe dimidia-to, tam crescens quàm decrescens. Maxima ejus latitudo, id est, recessus à via Solis seu ecliptica, vel in septentriones, vel in me-ridiem est 5. graduum. Præcipuè autem hic consideranda est & cognoscenda anomalia seu inæqualitas motus lunaris, quæ fit vel secundum longitudinem ab ortu in occasum, vel contra, aut secundum latitudinem ab polo ad polum, id est, austro in meridiem, & contra: discessus hic Lunæ ab ecliptica versus bo-ream vel austrum, est præcisè 5. graduum. Latitudinis hujus li-mites dicuntur, caput & cauda draconis, suntque nihil aliud quàm eccentrici & ecliptice intersectiones, quas Luna attin-gens, vel à meridie in septentrionem ascendit, ut fit in limite bo-reali, qui caput draconis dicitur, vel à septentrione in meridiem descendit, quod fit in limite meridionali, qui dicitur cauda dra-conis: intersectiones enim illæ Solis & Lunæ, draconis quo-dammodo referunt imaginem, qui ventre amplo & oblongo, capiteq; acutiori, caudà paulatim attenuata, pingitur, unde Lu-na à meridie per nodum, velut portam quandam ingrediens la-tidinem septentrionalem, caput transfire dicitur, caudam verò permeare, cùm septentrionalem latitudinem relinquens, in-meridionale latus à nobis recedit. Orbis autem deferens caput & caudam draconis reliquos omnes Lunæ orbes ambit, estque mundo cōcentricus, & latitudinis æqualis: hic ecliptican duo-bus in locis oppositis intersecat, quæ intersectiones dicuntur nodi: unde Luna bis tantùm attingit ecliptican, cùm scilicet incurrit in nodos, & nullam habet latitudinem. Porrò notanda hic veniunt, quae Lunae accidunt respectu Solis, ut sunt conjunctio, oppositio, apparitio & defectus. Conjunctio, ut & oppositio duplex est, media una, altera vera. Media, cum lineae medii motus in utroq; luminari, aut concurrunt, aut per hemicyclum distant, illic apogaeum eccentrici, centrum epicycli Lunae, & Sol in eodem zodiaci loco concurrunt, hic, id est, in oppositione media, centrum epicycli Lunae & apogaeum eccentrici opponuntur medio Solis loco in zodiaco, unde quovis mense synodice bis ad summam apsidem sui eccentrici devehitur, scilicet in novilunio & plenilunio: nam in quadraturis seu dimidiationibus, cum scilicet est dimidiata, est in perigaeo eccentrici, tunc enim centrum epicycli occupat perigaeum eccentrici, opponiturq; eccentrici apogaeo, medius vero Solis locus in zodiaco versatur in medio loco inter centrum epicycli, & apogaeum eccentrici lunaris: eadem Luna, si corniculata apparet, & utrinq; gibbosa, versatur in longitudinibus mediis eccentrici, nam bis quolibet mense apparet corniculata & gibbosa.
units.tr: The Moon traverses the whole zodiac by her own motion from west to east in 27 days, 7 hours and 15 minutes. This proper motion of the Moon, since it takes place around two centres, is twofold: one is equal or mean, the other true and unequal. The first moves uniformly about the centre of the ecliptic or of the world, and regularly, following the order of the signs, completing 13 degrees in the zodiac each day; the second is carried unequally about the centre of the eccentric, and passes some parts of the zodiac more quickly and others more slowly. By this motion the Moon is swifter on the eccentric if she holds the highest apse, and slower near the lowest. Likewise, each month the Moon is twice in the apogee, that is, at the highest summit of her eccentric, and twice in the perigee, that is, the lowest part of the eccentric. The former happens at every conjunction and opposition, the latter at the quadratures, when she appears half-lit, both waxing and waning. Her greatest latitude, that is, her recession from the path of the Sun or the ecliptic, either to the north or to the south, is 5 degrees. But the anomaly or inequality of the lunar motion is especially to be considered and understood here, which occurs either in longitude, from east to west or the reverse, or in latitude, from pole to pole, that is, from south to north and the reverse. This departure of the Moon from the ecliptic towards the north or the south is precisely 5 degrees. The limits of this latitude are called the head and tail of the Dragon, and they are nothing other than the intersections of the eccentric and the ecliptic, which the Moon touches when she ascends in latitude from south to north, as happens at the northern limit, which is called the head of the Dragon, or when she descends from north to south, which happens at the southern limit, called the tail of the Dragon. For these intersections of the Sun and Moon somehow represent the image of a dragon, which is painted with a broad and elongated belly, a sharper head, and a tail gradually tapering; hence the Moon, entering from the south through the node as through a certain gate, is said to pass the head, the northern latitude, while, leaving the northern latitude and passing the tail, she withdraws from us on the southern side. The deferent orb, which carries the head and tail of the Dragon, encircles all the other orbs of the Moon, is concentric with the world, and is of equal latitude; it cuts the ecliptic at two opposite places, and these intersections are called nodes. Hence the Moon touches the ecliptic only twice, namely when she falls upon the nodes, and then she has no latitude. Next, the things which happen to the Moon with respect to the Sun must be noted here, such as conjunction, opposition, appearance and eclipse. Conjunction, like opposition, is twofold: one mean, the other true. In the mean conjunction, when the lines of mean motion in each luminary either coincide or lie a half-circle apart, there the apogee of the eccentric, the centre of the lunar epicycle and the Sun meet at the same place in the zodiac; in the mean opposition, that is, here the centre of the lunar epicycle and the apogee of the eccentric are set opposite the mean place of the Sun in the zodiac. Hence in every month, by synodic reckoning, she is carried twice to the highest apse of her eccentric, namely at new moon and full moon. At the quadratures, or half-moons, when she is dichotomized, she is in the perigee of the eccentric; for then the centre of the epicycle occupies the perigee of the eccentric and is opposite the apogee of the eccentric, while the mean place of the Sun lies in the zodiac midway between the centre of the epicycle and the apogee of the lunar eccentric. The same Moon, when she appears crescent and gibbous on either side, is in the mean longitudes of the eccentric, for twice in any month she appears crescent and gibbous.

units.la: Vera conjunctio est, cum lineae veri motus in utroque luminari aut conjunguntur, aut opponuntur, seu per hemicyclum distant. Triginta autem fere dierum intervallum intercedit ab una conjunctione ad aliam, quod intervallum est tempus mensis synodici. Etsi enim motu proprio 27. tantum dies, & 13. horas Luna conficit, donec ad idem zodiaci punctum, unde est digressa, redeat, tamen, ubi ad Solem appropinquaverit, rursus occultatur, & quia Sol integrum fere interea signum est emensus, dum Luna, peragrato zodiaco, ad idem punctum redit, in quo prius Soli fuerat juncta, ideo reliquis diebus, nempe biduo fere Solem consequitur, donec rursus cum eo conjungatur. Unde mensis est tempus, quo Luna 12. signa emensa, vel redit ad punctũ suum, vel ad Solem. Est igitur verus vel apparens. Verus est periodicus, vel synodicus: Apparens est mensis illuminatio-nis. nis.Periodicus,quo Luna redit ad idem zodiaci punctum,unde est digressa: dierum est 27. & 7.hor. 43. minut. Hic enim nume-rus emergit, si 360. gradus, id est, integrum circulum distribuas per motum longitudinis Lunæ, videlicet per 13.gradus,10. min. Synodicus mensis est tempus inter duo proxima novilunia, quo scilicet Luna redit ad locum Solis in zodiaco, unde prius discesserat,& hic dierum est 29.horarum 12. & 44.min.Horum mensium 12. constituunt annum lunarem, tempus videlicet, quo Sol & Luna duodecies conjunguntur, nam in intercalari Sol & Luna tredecies conjunguntur: minor autem annus lu-naris solari est diebus fere 11. qui dies, quibus annus lunaris su-peratur ab anno solari, dicuntur epactæ, id est, insertitii seu ad-ditii. Mensis apparitionis seu illuminationis est tempus à pri-mo conspectu Lunæ nascentis ad [illegible, ~7 letters], id est, ad momentum iterum evanescentis numeratum, estq; 28. fere dierum, non ta-men perpetuò, interdum enim nova luna conspicitur ipso no-vilunii die, interdum secundo, interdum quarto, ut plurimum tamen tertio à coitu die, idq; ob sequentes rationes: primo ob inæqualem Lunæ motum. Si enim motu est velox, citius post conjunctionem prodit, quàm si cursu est tarda. Primo enim die pene signi medietatem peragrans, & ocyus à Sole excurrens (quod fit in ima parte epicycli) citius & velocius à radiis solari-bus se liberat, nobisq; suum lumen ostentat, quàm si motu lentiori sese à Solis vicinia elonget. Altera causa sumitur à latitudine Lunæ: si enim post congressum à Sole in maximam latitudinem septentrionalem fuerit subvecta, fiet parallelus Lunæ solari septentrionalior. Itaq; tardius descendet: tardus autem de-scensus post occasum Solis, quia majus temporis spacium à no-ctis principio effluxisse indicat, causa est citioris apparitionis. Tertia ratio sumitur ab habitudine obliquitatis zodiaci ad ho-rizontem. Si enim Solis & Lunæ conjunctio fuerit in signis tarde seu recte descendentibus, Luna à Sole digressa citius apparebit, quàm si extiterit in signis obliquè seu velociter descendentibus. Quod si igitur tres hæ causæ simul concurrerint, tum uno & eodem die mane ante exortum Solis novissima Luna, & vesperi post illius occasum renascens, conspici poterit. Si prædictarum causarum duæ concurrant, secundo post conjunctionem die apparebit: sin unica tantùm, tertio: si verò conjunctio fiat in hemicyclo zodiaci descendente, Luna cursu tarda in meridionalem latitudinem exorbitans, quarto demum die in conspectum prorumpet.
units.tr: True conjunction occurs when the lines of true motion of the two luminaries either coincide or are opposite, that is, lie half a circle apart. About thirty days pass from one conjunction to the next, and this interval is the time of the synodic month. For although by its own motion the Moon completes only 27 days and 13 hours before it returns to the same point of the zodiac from which it set out, it is hidden again as soon as it draws near the Sun. Since the Sun has meanwhile traversed almost an entire sign, the Moon, having gone round the zodiac, returns to the point where it had earlier been joined to the Sun, and so for the remaining days, almost two, it follows the Sun until they are conjoined again. The month is therefore the time in which the Moon, having passed through the twelve signs, returns either to its own point or to the Sun. It is accordingly either true or apparent. The true month is periodic or synodic; the apparent month is the month of illumination. The periodic month is the time in which the Moon returns to the same point of the zodiac from which it departed, and it lasts 27 days, 7 hours and 43 minutes. This number emerges if you divide 360 degrees, that is, the whole circle, by the Moon's motion in longitude, namely 13 degrees and 10 minutes. The synodic month is the time between two successive new moons, in which the Moon returns to the place of the Sun in the zodiac from which it had previously withdrawn; this lasts 29 days, 12 hours and 44 minutes. Twelve of these months make up the lunar year, that is, the time in which the Sun and Moon are conjoined twelve times; in an intercalary year they are conjoined thirteen times. The lunar year is shorter than the solar year by about 11 days, and these days, by which the lunar year falls short of the solar year, are called epacts, that is, inserted or added days. The month of appearance or illumination is the time from the first sighting of the new Moon to [illegible], that is, to the moment when it is counted as disappearing again. It is about 28 days, though not always: sometimes the new moon is seen on the very day of conjunction, sometimes on the second day, sometimes on the fourth, but most often on the third day after conjunction. This happens for the following reasons. First, because of the unequal motion of the Moon. If it is swift in its motion, it appears sooner after conjunction than if its course is slow. On the first day, traversing almost half a sign and moving away from the Sun more quickly (which happens in the lower part of the epicycle), it frees itself sooner and more rapidly from the solar rays and shows its light to us, than it would if it moved more slowly and so withdrew from the Sun's neighbourhood. The second cause is taken from the Moon's latitude. If after conjunction with the Sun it has been carried to its greatest northern latitude, it will lie further north, parallel to the Sun, and so it will descend more slowly. A slow descent after sunset indicates that a greater span of time has passed since the beginning of night, and this is the cause of an earlier appearance. The third reason is taken from the relation of the obliquity of the zodiac to the horizon. If the conjunction of Sun and Moon occurs in signs that descend slowly or straight, the Moon, once separated from the Sun, will appear sooner than if the conjunction were in signs that descend obliquely or swiftly. If these three causes concur, then on one and the same day the last Moon may be seen in the morning before sunrise, and the newly reborn Moon in the evening after sunset. If two of these causes concur, it will appear on the second day after conjunction; if only one, on the third day. But if the conjunction takes place in the descending half of the zodiac, the Moon, slow in its course and wandering into southern latitude, finally breaks into view on the fourth day.

units.la: Cæterum varias radiorum Solis Luna sentit differentias, non uno eodemq; modo à Sole illuminata: prout enim ad ipsum accedit vel recedit, ita diversas illuminationum vices sustinet. Radii enim, qui incidunt in Lunam inflexè, hebetiores sunt, minusq; efficaces, non enim illustrare possunt totam Lunam, propter cœli convexitatem, sicut illi qui rectè in eam incidunt, ut qui in Lunam ex diametro oppositam cadunt, implentq; eam lumine, & undiquaq; plenam efficiunt. Semper autem Lunæ dimidius globus, qui scilicet Solem respicit, illuminatur, altera medietas, quæ à Sole est aversa, nobis verò obversa, manet obscura, quod ostendit novilunium, cùm tanta vis radii solaris non fit, ut is totum Lunæ corpus transfire possit, est enim id solidum, nec totum diaphanum. Sed noster oculus semper minus medietate illuminata de corpore Lunæ intuetur, non enim tota medietas illuminata in oculum nostrum incurrit, ideoq; ab eo non potest apprehendi. Tantam enim radius visivus illuminati orbis Lunæ partem apprehendit, quantam radio incidenti contingere per tumorem globi Lunæ licet. Unde in plenilunio non tota, sed medietas fere tota ejus apparet, id est, semper illa corporis lunaris superficies, quæ Soli obversa radium illius ex adverso recipit, illuminatur. Tantum enim nobis semper de Luna in plenilunio videtur, quantum basis pyramidis visualis de illa medietate abscindit, seu, quantum basis pyramidis illuminatio-nis habet commune cum basi pyramidis visualis.
units.tr: Moreover, the Moon receives various differences of the Sun's rays and is not illuminated in one and the same way. For according as it approaches or recedes from the Sun, so it undergoes different changes of illumination. The rays that strike the Moon obliquely are duller and less effective, since on account of the convexity of the sky they cannot light up the whole Moon. Rays that strike it directly, such as those falling on the Moon from the opposite point of the diameter, fill it with light and make it entirely full. The half of the lunar globe that faces the Sun is always illuminated; the other half, turned away from the Sun but towards us, remains dark. This is why the new moon appears: the force of the solar ray is not strong enough to pass through the whole body of the Moon, for that body is solid and not wholly transparent. Our eye, however, always sees less than half of the Moon's body illuminated, for the whole illuminated half does not enter our eye and so cannot be apprehended by it. The visual ray takes in only as much of the illuminated orb of the Moon as the incident ray is allowed to touch, given the swelling of the lunar globe. Hence at full moon not the whole but almost all of the half is visible; that is, that surface of the lunar body which faces the Sun and receives its ray head-on is always the part that is illuminated. As much of the Moon is seen by us at full moon as the base of the visual pyramid cuts off from that half; or, put differently, as much as the base of the pyramid of illumination has in common with the base of the visual pyramid.

units.la: Quæritur igitur causa diversarum figurarum & apparentiarum Lunæ, quòd videlicet aliquando falcata & μηνοειδὴς[?], in-terdum dimidiata, & διχότομος, aliquando ἀμφίκυρτος, id est, utrinq; gibbosa, & tandem πανσέληνος, id est, plena conspicitur. Causa hujus diversitatis apparentiarum est radius visivus oculi in Lunam incidens, qui semper tantam partem illuminati orbis lu-naris complectitur, quantam radius incidentiæ propter tumo-rem globi Lunæ potest contingere. Unde linea incidentiæ, hoc est, quæ determinat partem illuminatam Lunæ visam, à parte ejusdem Lunæ illuminata non visa, aliàs circumscribit lumen Lunæ linea incurva & arcuali, aliàs verò linea recta, ut cùm in quadraturis cernitur dichotomos: lumen enim in Luna semper à circulari linea terminatur versus Solem inclinantem, propter globi convexitatem, atque propter angulum acutum, quem intersectio axium constituit in illo arcu, qui ad Solem & ad nos vergit: sed quia sphæra procul conspecta videtur esse plana, & maximè illa parte, qua nobis est obversa, etiam hæc linea non semper arcualis à nobis judicatur, ut cùm Luna est in quadraturis, vel prope, cùm scilicet falcata esse definit, atq; jam facta est διχότομος. In hac enim habitudine nos hanc lineam arcualem separantem illuminatam partem ab opaca, judicamus esse lineam rectam, non enim magis ad superiorem, quàm inferiorem partem inclinat: æquidistat enim hæc linea ex omni parte lineæ perpendiculari ex visus centro eductæ, id quod in aliis habitudinibus sui circuli nusquam accidit, ut cùm est sal- cata, hæc linea oblique incidit, oculus enim tantùm extrema globi illuminati conspicit, quæ ex inferiori loco illuminatæ partis nobis obversa sunt. Præterea axis illuminationis incidens in-
units.tr: The question, then, is what causes the different shapes and appearances of the Moon: why it is sometimes seen falcate and crescent-shaped [μηνοειδὴς], sometimes half-lit and dichotomous [διχότομος], sometimes gibbous on both sides [ἀμφίκυρτος], that is, swollen on both sides, and finally full [πανσέληνος]. The cause of this variety of appearances is the visual ray of the eye falling upon the Moon, which always embraces as much of the illuminated orb of the Moon as the incident ray can touch on account of the swelling of the lunar globe. Hence the line of incidence, that is, the line that determines the illuminated part of the Moon that is seen as distinct from the illuminated part that is not seen, sometimes bounds the moonlight with a curved, arched line, and sometimes with a straight line, as when the half-moon is seen at the quadratures. For the light on the Moon is always bounded by a circular line on the side that inclines towards the Sun, on account of the convexity of the globe, and on account of the acute angle that the intersection of the axes forms in the arc that faces the Sun and us. But because a sphere seen from afar appears flat, especially the part turned towards us, this line too is not always judged by us to be arched. This happens when the Moon is at the quadratures, or near them, when it ceases to be falcate and has become dichotomous. In this aspect we judge the arched line that separates the illuminated part from the dark part to be straight, for it does not incline more towards the upper than the lower part. This line runs parallel on every side to the perpendicular drawn from the centre of vision, which never happens in the Moon's other aspects. When it is falcate, for instance, the line falls obliquely, for the eye sees only the extreme edges of the illuminated globe, which face us from the lower position of the illuminated part. Moreover, the axis of illumination falling upon the centre of the Moon forms a right angle, and so the intersecting line also seems to be straight.

units.la: Apparitionum Lunæ varia-rum causa vera, ex vero princi-pium oriuntur. centrum Lunæ, angulum rectum constituit, unde & linea intersecans recta esse videtur. Quando vero distantia Lunæ à Sole quadrantem excessit, tum Luna tumida & utrinq; gibbosa apparet: angulus enim interfectionis est obtusus, id est, prius axis illuminationis orbem Lunæ secat, quàm ad ejus perveniat centrum. Sed in oppositione, cùm visus noster est quasi medius inter duo luminaria, tum Luna cernitur pleno orbe, quia medie-tas illustrata eadem & visui nostro, & Soli simul obversa est, & tota visionis pyramis incidit in totam pyramidem illuminationis, ita ut nulla fiat communis sectio. Et pari ratione postea decrescit. Propter hanc autem permutationē seu apparitionum varietatem in 12. Luna dividitur partes, quæ dicuntur digiti, suntq; Lunæ 12. partes, æquales integræ diametri corporis lunaris, ut digitus sit unica seu duodecima pars corporis Lunæ. Nam Astronomi diametrum corporis Lunæ, quia apparet trium palmorum ferè, quorum singuli 4. constant digitis, in 12. æquales portiones, quas digitos appellant, dividunt. Cùm igitur propter diversas causas luminaria irregulariter moveantur super centro mundi in propriis orbibus, & etiam propter diversitatem eorum, qui ex superficie terræ Lunam intuentur, necesse est ex hac dissimili habitudine maximam illuminationis existe-re varietatem. Illuminationis enim Lunæ, ut dictum est, quoniam causa est radius visivus in globum Lunæ illuminatum incidens, sequitur propter diversam harum linearum habitudinem, contingentium & multipliciter incidentium variari lumen, & ex consequenti aliquando plus, aliquando minus de illuminata & visibili parte globi conspici. Magis autem particu-lares causæ illuminationis sunt eccentricitas Lunæ, quæ eam & propinquiorem & remotiorem ad centrum terræ, & etiam visus reddit: deinde diversus situs centri visus in superficie terræ, ut Orientales & Occidentales, qui Amphiscii sunt, eandem partem Lunæ, & in eodem cœlo illuminatâ diversimodè contuentur, aliis enim major, aliis minor pars Lunæ illuminatæ conspicitur. Huc accedit diversitas motuum orbium Lunæ, ut deferentiû centrum epicycli, qui defert corpus Lunæ, & deferentis caput & caudam draconis: deniq; eccentricitas Solis, & latitudo ipsius Lunæ, quæ singula Lunæ apparitiones mutant. Ipsæ autem Lunæ permutationes seu apparitiones his nominibus exprimuntur. Secundo aut tertio à coitu die dicitur falcata, seu in cornua curvata: 7. & 21. die est dimidiata, illic crescens, hic decrescens: 11. & octavo est ἀμφίχωλος, id est, sinuata in orbem: 14. verò & 15. πανσέληνος [?], id est, plena: postea eodem ordine iterum decrescit, donec ad conjunctionem pervenerit, quam interlunium & novilunium, Plinius & Virgilius Silentia Lunæ appellant. Licet autem statim post conjunctionem Luna non cernatur, tamen quoties à Sole 15. gradibus discedit, digitum unum de medietate illuminata ad nos convertit. Pontanus has Lunæ vicissitudines describit sequentibus versibus:
units.tr: The true cause of the variety of the Moon's appearances arises from a true principle. When, however, the Moon's distance from the Sun exceeds a quadrant, the Moon appears swollen and gibbous on both sides: the angle of intersection is obtuse, that is, the axis of illumination cuts the orb of the Moon before it reaches the centre. But at opposition, when our sight lies as it were midway between the two luminaries, the Moon is seen with a full orb, because the illuminated half is turned at once to our sight and to the Sun, and the whole visual pyramid falls within the whole pyramid of illumination, so that no common section arises. By the same reasoning it afterwards wanes. On account of this alternation or variety of appearances, the Moon's diameter is divided into 12 parts, which are called digits. The Moon's 12 parts are equal parts of the whole diameter of the lunar body, so that a digit is one twelfth part of the body of the Moon. For astronomers divide the diameter of the lunar body, which appears to be nearly three palms and each palm of which contains four digits, into 12 equal portions, which they call digits. Since the luminaries move irregularly about the centre of the world in their own orbs for various causes, and since the observers who look at the Moon from the surface of the earth also differ, the greatest variety of illumination must necessarily arise from this dissimilar arrangement. For the Moon's illumination, as has been said, is caused by the visual ray falling on the illuminated globe of the Moon, and so, because these lines are variously arranged, touching and falling in many ways, the light varies. Consequently, at one time more and at another less of the illuminated and visible part of the globe is seen. The more particular causes of illumination are the eccentricity of the Moon, which makes it both nearer to and farther from the centre of the earth and thereby also affects our sight; then the differing position of the observer's centre of sight on the earth's surface, as with the Easterners and Westerners, who are Amphiscii and who look at the same illuminated part of the Moon in the same heaven in different ways, for to some a greater and to others a smaller part of the illuminated Moon is visible. To this is added the diversity of the motions of the Moon's orbs, namely the centre of the epicycle that carries the body of the Moon, and the head and tail of the dragon, which carry the deferent; finally, the eccentricity of the Sun and the latitude of the Moon itself, each of which alters the Moon's appearances. The alterations or appearances of the Moon itself are expressed by these names. On the second or third day after conjunction it is called falcata, or curved into horns; on the seventh and twenty-first day it is dimidiated, growing on the one day and waning on the other; on the eleventh and eighth day it is amphichôlos [ἀμφίχωλος], that is, curved into a circle; on the fourteenth and fifteenth day it is full [πανσέληνος]; afterwards it wanes again in the same order until it reaches conjunction, which Pliny and Virgil call the interlunium or silence of the Moon. Although the Moon is not seen immediately after conjunction, nevertheless, whenever it withdraws 15 degrees from the Sun, it turns one digit of its illuminated half towards us. Pontanus describes these vicissitudes of the Moon in the following verses:

units.la: Quantumcunq; ab Apollinis igne recedit, Hoc magis ipsa suum fundit mortalibus ignem. Cornibus auratis primùm, mox fronte refulget Jam media, medium cœli dimensa volumen. Atq; hinc obliquos vultus, turgentiaq; ora Nocte refert, tandemq; vago digressa meatu Exurgit Solem contra, plenoq; coruscam Orbe comam, & fulvo totum caput explicat auro.
units.tr: However far she withdraws from Apollo's fire, the more she pours her own fire on mortals. First she shines with golden horns, then soon her brow gleams at mid-course, having measured the middle of the heavenly circuit. From there she shows, by night, her sidelong face and swollen cheeks; and at last, departing on her wandering path, she rises opposite the Sun, unfolds her bright hair with a full orb, and spreads her whole head in tawny gold.

units.la: Restat ultimum Lunę pathos ratione Solis ei contingens, videlicet Eclipsis, quæ est privatio luminis solaris in Luna plena Soli diametraliter oppositâ, ita, ut tria corpora, Sol, Luna, & terra sint in una recta linea, quod fit in nodis vel propè, id est, intra terminos Eclipticos, qui sunt distantiæ ab utraq; intersectio-ne viæ Solis & Lunæ tantæ, quantis luminare contactum umbrae vitare potest : hi in Luna sunt 15.grad.In Sole septentriona-les 20.gr.40.min. meridionales vero 11.gr. 22.min. Semperigi-tur Eclipsis Lunae fit circa oppositionem diametralem, ergo etiam umbra terrae, quae vera est causa efficiens, pertingit ad Lu-nam, in quacunq; coeli parte illa extiterit. Si enim ipsa est in O-riente supra horizontem, Sol erit in occasu sub horizonte, vel e contra, ergo necesse est Lunam incurrere in umbram terrae, ubicunq; tandem illa fuerit. Unde facilis ratio reddi potest, cur non singulis mensibus fiant Eclipses Lunae, cùm tamen quovis mense Soli opponatur, quoniam Sol & Luna non opponuntur secundum diametralem seu rectam, unde etiam umbra terrae non pertingit ad Lunam, sed alio procidit, seu quia Luna Soli non opponitur secundum absidum commissuras. Nusquam enim Luna diametraliter Soli potest opponi, nisi in nodis, quamvis etiam fieri Lunae Eclipsis potest, cùm Luna ultra vel citra nodos fuerit tanto intervallo, quanta est semidiameter Lunae visibilis conjuncta cum semidiametro umbrae, id est, spa-cio fere 65.min.Semidiameter enim Lunae apparens est 18. min. umbrę vero 46.min.quę junċta efficiunt 65.nam diameter um-brae est fere duplus ad diametrum Lunae.Igitur intra hos termi-nos consistens Luna in oppositione pati potest luminis defe-ctum : at si latitudo Lunae fuerit major 65. min. aut praecise tot minutorû, tum luminis obscuratio nulla fit, sed diameter um-brae tantùm stringit semidiametrum terrae. Ex quo apparet, ra-tiones Eclipsium mortales animos subducere in coelum, ac ve-lut inde contemplantibus trium maximarum naturae partium, ut loquitur Plinius, magnitudinem detegere, hoc est, trium-maximorum ac illustrissimorum corporum, Solis, Lunae, ac ter-rae magnitudinem patefacere, & verissimum est, nulla certiore ratione magnitudines horum corporum deprehendi posse, quàm ex Eclipsibus. Unde reliquorum coelestium corporum, quæ nullas Eclipsium vices sustinent, magnitudines nulla certa ratione constare, neque posse aliquam exactam rationem iniri aut haberi, quæ ipsorum magnitudines patefaciat, fatendum est. Cæterum in confesso est omnibus, Lunam aliquando totam obscurari, aliquando secundum corporis sui partem: illud, cum præcise est in nodis, & latitudine prorsus caret, tunc enim transit per mediam umbram, in qua tantisper delitescit, donec ex al-tera rursus parte emergat. Ingreditur autem umbram ea sem-per parte, quæ spectat ortum, emergitq; ea parte, quæ tendit in-occasum: umbra vero ad motum Solis primum magis, quam motum Solis proprium videtur moveri, unde umbræ motus celerior est, quam motus Solis. Partialiter autem obscuratur Luna, cum latitudo ejus aut minor est semidiametro umbræ, & major semidiametro Lunæ, aut eadem latitudo semidiametrum umbræ exæquat, aut latitudo Lunæ major est quam semidiameter umbræ: priori modo plus dimidio corporis luna-ris obscuratur, secundo dimidia, tertio minor pars de corpore lunari obtenebratur. Cur autem cæteræ stellæ non ita deficiant, causa est, quoniam propria luce lucent: & licet Venus Mercu-riusq; maxime lucem quandam suam à Sole accipiant, nunquam tamen ei diametraliter, ut Luna, opponuntur, tum umbra etiam terræ illo pertingere nequit, multo minus ad stellas fixas protendi. Quæstiones præterea hic occurrunt illustres, quæ excutiendæ sunt, 1. quando Eclipses in eodem zodiaci puncto iterum contingant? 2. quantum sit intervallum inter duas Eclipses? 3. an Sol uno mense bis possit occultari? 4. an utroq; luminari constitutio supra horizontem, alterum deficere possit? Ad 1. Eclipses non possunt iterum in eodem zo-diaci puncto accidere, id est, redire in suos orbes, nisi confectis annis 18. & 6. mensibus, tanto enim tempore circulus deferens nodos conficit suam revolutionem, atque iterum redit ad illud punctum, in quo antea Eclipsis facta est. Cùm enim, ut dictum est, Eclipses fiant in nodis, vel terminis eclipticis, qui non procul à nodis recedunt, nodi autem ad eadem puncta non redeant, nisi post tantum temporis, sequitur nec eclipses in iisdem punctis accidere posse, nisi confecto prædicto temporis spacio, & quidem (NB.) progrediendo ad signa præcedentia, non conse-quentia, motus enim nodorum fit contra signorum ordinem, non secundum, ut si eclipsis fuit in tauro, post annum unum atque alterum non iterum fiet in tauro, sed ariete, vel piscibus, propter nodorum in hanc partem motum, quotidie enim ultra motum diurnum moventur versus occidentem 3. fere minutis.
units.tr: There remains the last affection of the Moon, which arises from her relation to the Sun, namely the eclipse. This is the privation of solar light in the full Moon, which is diametrically opposed to the Sun, so that the three bodies, Sun, Moon and Earth, lie in one straight line. This happens at the nodes or near them, that is, within the ecliptic limits, which are distances from the intersection of the path of the Sun and of the Moon, as great as the luminary can be in contact with the shadow. These limits are 15 degrees for the Moon; for the Sun, 20 degrees 40 minutes to the north and 11 degrees 22 minutes to the south. An eclipse of the Moon therefore always occurs near the diametrical opposition, and so the shadow of the Earth, which is the true efficient cause, reaches the Moon wherever in the heavens she may be. For if she is in the east above the horizon, the Sun will be in the west below the horizon, or the reverse; so the Moon must run into the Earth's shadow, wherever she then is.
