Hence an easy reason can be given why eclipses of the Moon do not occur every month, although she is opposed to the Sun every month: the Sun and Moon are not opposed along a diameter or straight line, so the Earth's shadow does not reach the Moon but falls elsewhere; or because the Moon is not opposed to the Sun at the points where the apsides meet. For the Moon can never be diametrically opposed to the Sun except at the nodes, although a lunar eclipse can also happen when the Moon is beyond or short of the nodes by an interval equal to the apparent semidiameter of the Moon added to the semidiameter of the shadow, that is, about 65 minutes. For the apparent semidiameter of the Moon is 18 minutes, and that of the shadow 46 minutes, which together make 65; the diameter of the shadow is about twice the diameter of the Moon. So, if the Moon lies within these limits at opposition, she can suffer a loss of light; but if her latitude is greater than 65 minutes, or exactly that many minutes, no darkening occurs, and the diameter of the shadow only grazes the semidiameter of the Earth. From this it is evident that the reasons of eclipses lead mortal minds up into heaven, and, as Pliny says, from there, as if contemplating, they reveal the greatness of the three greatest parts of nature, that is, they disclose the magnitude of the three greatest and most illustrious bodies, the Sun, the Moon and the Earth. And it is most true that the magnitudes of these bodies cannot be ascertained by any more certain reasoning than from eclipses. Hence it must be admitted that the magnitudes of the remaining heavenly bodies, which undergo no such eclipses, cannot be established by any sure reasoning, nor can any exact method be devised or held which would reveal their magnitudes. Moreover, everyone agrees that the Moon is sometimes wholly obscured and sometimes only in part of her body. The former happens when she is exactly at the nodes and has no latitude at all; for then she passes through the middle of the shadow, in which she lies hidden for a while, until she emerges again on the other side. She always enters the shadow on the side facing the east, and emerges on the side tending to the west. The shadow, however, seems to move at first more with the motion of the Sun than with its own motion, so that the motion of the shadow is faster than the motion of the Sun. The Moon is partially obscured when her latitude is either less than the semidiameter of the shadow and greater than the semidiameter of the Moon, or the same latitude equals the semidiameter of the shadow, or the latitude of the Moon is greater than the semidiameter of the shadow. In the first case more than half of the lunar body is obscured, in the second half, and in the third a smaller part of the lunar body is darkened. As for why the other stars do not suffer such eclipses, the cause is that they shine with their own light; and although Venus and Mercury receive from the Sun a certain light of their own, they are never diametrically opposed to it as the Moon is, so the shadow of the Earth cannot reach them, much less extend to the fixed stars. Besides, there arise here noteworthy questions which must be examined: (1) When do eclipses recur at the same point of the zodiac? (2) What is the interval between two eclipses? (3) Can the Sun be eclipsed twice in one month? (4) Can one luminary be eclipsed while the other is above the horizon? To the first: eclipses cannot recur at the same point of the zodiac, that is, return to their former orbits, unless 18 years and 6 months have passed; for in that time the circle carrying the nodes completes its revolution and returns to the point at which an eclipse had occurred before. For since, as has been said, eclipses happen at the nodes or at the ecliptic limits, which do not lie far from the nodes, and the nodes do not return to the same points except after that length of time, it follows that eclipses cannot occur at the same points except after the said span of time has elapsed. And indeed (NB.) they advance towards the preceding signs, not the following ones, for the motion of the nodes is against the order of the signs, not with it. So if an eclipse occurred in Taurus, after a year or two it will not happen again in Taurus but in Aries or Pisces, because of the motion of the nodes in this direction; for they move daily towards the west, beyond the daily motion, by about 3 minutes.

units.la: Ad 2. & 3. De periodicatione & tempore inter duas Eclipses, inquit Plinius l.2.c.2.nat.hist.[?] non esse statos defectus, neque etiam menstruos, id est, neque singulis mensibus recurrere, neque alias æquale tempus existere inter duas eclipses solares vel lunares supra terram apparentes, propter obliquitatem Zodiaci & Lunæ multivagos flexus, hoc est, propter inæqualitatem motus Solis & Lunæ: non enim propter latitudinem Lunæ singulis mensibus fieri possunt, quæ diametralem, id est, centralem conjunctionem vel oppositionem probibet. Plinius ait quinq; mensium spacio posse Lunam lumine deficere, ut si Sol fertur à libra, & Luna in alteram zodiaci medietatem secundum seriem signorum, potest fieri prior Eclipsis in ariete, posterior verò in virgine, idq; spacio quinq; mensium: Solem autem, ait idem spacio septem mensium bis posse eclipsari, ut, cùm fertur per boreales signiferi partes, ubi ejus motus est tardior, fieri potest, ut deficiat in piscibus, & postea rursus in libra, idque spacio septem mensium: quin eundem in 30. diebus bis supra terram occultari idem autor est, ut, cùm fertur per punctum tropicum, potest priori loco deficere, cùm accedit ad hoc punctum, altero verò cùm digreditur, atq; ita unam Eclipsin videbunt climata australiora, alteram borealiora: quæ tamen Pliniana hac egent explicatione Regiomontani, si Luna diversitatem aspectus in latitudine non habet, impossibile est, ut Sol bis eclipsetur in 7. mensibus, scilicet in prima harum conjunctionum, & extrema. Item nō est possibile, ut Sol bis eclipsetur uno mense, nisi diver-sitas aspectus Lunæ ad Solem sit major 1. gradu, 27.min. & in utraq; conjunctione differentia diversitatum aspectus in latitudine in eandem partem sit major 1.gr. 27.min. Sed non est locus in terra, ubi hoc fiat. Si enim in uno mense bis debet eclipsari Sol, necesse est, ut diversitas aspectus in utraq; conjunctione sit in partes contrarias, & aggregatum earum sit uno gr. majus, & 27.min. Sub æquinoctiali autem maxima diversitas aspectus in latitudine major non est 25.minut. in quamcunq; partem. Neq; in aliquo 7. climatum versus Septentriones procedendo diversitas aspectus in latitudine major est 1.gr. Quare fieri etiam non potest, ut uni plagæ terræ Sol bis in uno mense eclipsetur: quamvis nihil prohibet, homines unius habitabilis plagæ eclipsin Solis videre, & in sequente conjunctione alterius plagæ homines quoque habere eclipsin, quòd ambæ diversitates aspectus eis contingentes in partes contrarias simul possunt esse majores 1. gr.27.min. ut si una plaga esset ad meridiem ab æquatore, & ad Septentrionem alia.
units.tr: As to the second and third questions, concerning the periodicity and the time between two eclipses: Pliny (Nat. Hist. 2.2?) says that the failures are neither fixed nor monthly, that is, they do not recur every month, nor is there any equal interval between two solar or lunar eclipses visible above the earth, on account of the obliquity of the zodiac and the many-wandering windings of the Moon, that is, on account of the unequal motion of the Sun and Moon. For they cannot occur every month because of the Moon's latitude, which prevents a diametrical, that is, central, conjunction or opposition. Pliny says that within a span of five months the Moon can be eclipsed; for example, if the Sun is carried from Libra and the Moon moves through the other half of the zodiac in the order of the signs, the first eclipse may occur in Aries and the later one in Virgo, within a span of five months. He also says that the Sun can be eclipsed twice within a span of seven months: when it is carried through the northern parts of the zodiac, where its motion is slower, it may fail in Pisces and afterwards again in Libra, within seven months. Moreover, the same author says that the Sun can be hidden twice above the earth within 30 days: when it is carried through the tropical point, it may fail at one place as it approaches this point and at another as it departs; thus the more southern climes will see one eclipse, and the more northern the other. Yet these Pliny statements need the explanation of Regiomontanus: if the Moon has no difference of aspect in latitude, it is impossible for the Sun to be eclipsed twice in seven months, namely at the first and the last of these conjunctions. Likewise it is not possible for the Sun to be eclipsed twice in one month, unless the difference of the Moon's aspect to the Sun is greater than 1 degree 27 minutes, and in both conjunctions the difference of aspect in latitude lies in the same direction and is greater than 1 degree 27 minutes. But there is no place on earth where this happens. For if the Sun must be eclipsed twice in one month, it is necessary that the difference of aspect in each conjunction lie in opposite directions, and that their sum be more than one degree and 27 minutes. Under the equinoctial line, however, the greatest difference of aspect in latitude is not more than 25 minutes in either direction. Nor, proceeding from any of the seven climes towards the north, is the difference of aspect in latitude greater than 1 degree. Therefore it is also impossible for the Sun to be eclipsed twice in one month for one region of the earth. Yet nothing prevents the people of one inhabited region from seeing a solar eclipse, and in the following conjunction the people of another region from also having an eclipse, since the two differences of aspect affecting them, lying in opposite directions, can together be greater than 1 degree 27 minutes, as would be the case if one region lay south of the equator and another to the north.

units.la: Ad 4.Hæc quæstio videtur in universum eclipsium causas tollere, videlicet qui fiat, quòd in occasu Luna potest deficere utroq; sidere supra terram conspicuo, cùm dictum sit, Eclipsin omnem Lunæ fieri in diametrali oppositione: in nulla autem oppositione utrumq; sidus existit supra terram: ubi responde-tur, posse fieri eclipsin Lunæ utroq; sidere in ipso horizonte existente, ita tamen, ut alterum statim descendat, alterumq; protinus supra horizontē elevetur: præterea rotunditas terræ prohibet utrumq; luminare contueri per rectam lineam diametralem, illa enim per centrum, non per superficiem terrae educitur, ergo cum eclipses tantum in visibili oppositione, & non in vera fiant, nihil prohibet, quo minus utrumq; luminare in terminis ecliptics supra horizontem aliquantulum conspiciatur. Cleomedes huius apparentiae aliam affert causam, cum inquit, multas & varias in aere affectiones vim agnatam consistendi habere, unde impossibile non fuerit, cum jam Sol occiderit, subq; fi-nitore fuerit, visionem nobis incidere, tanquam necdum occi-derit, aut a nube crassiore existente in occasu, & luce perfusa a radiis solaribus, Solemq; nobis remittente visionis imaginem, potest porro effusus ab oculis radius perfringi, nactus madidum & humentiorem aerem, Solemq; assequi jam sub finitore occul-tum. Haec Cleomedes.
units.tr: To the fourth point: This question seems to remove the causes of eclipses in general, namely how it can happen that the Moon may be eclipsed at setting while both luminaries are visible above the earth, since it has been said that every eclipse of the Moon occurs at diametrical opposition, and in no opposition do both luminaries stand above the earth. The answer is that a lunar eclipse can happen with both luminaries on the horizon itself, provided that one sets at once while the other rises immediately above the horizon. Moreover, the roundness of the earth prevents us from seeing both luminaries along a straight diametrical line, since that line is drawn through the centre and not through the surface of the earth. Therefore, since eclipses occur only at apparent opposition and not at true opposition, nothing prevents both luminaries from being seen a little above the horizon, on the ecliptic. Cleomedes gives another cause of this appearance, when he says that the air has many and varied conditions with an inherent power of retaining light, so that it is not impossible for the sight to reach us when the Sun has already set and is below the horizon, as if it had not yet set, either because a thicker cloud lies in the west and, suffused with light from the solar rays, sends back to us the image of the Sun; or because the ray poured out from the eyes can be refracted, meeting moist and more humid air, and so reach the Sun already hidden below the horizon. Thus Cleomedes.

units.la: Hactenus praecipuorum coeli luminum, naturas, vires, & motus exploravimus, nunc perquirendae etiam propriae quas-dam Planetarum affectiones & passiones sunt, quae iis contingunt vel ratione eccentrici & epicycli, & hac ratione omnis Planeta, Sole & Luna exceptis, potest esse directus, retrogradus, stationarius, auctus, tardus, vel cursu mediocris: vel ob varium inter se positum, & motum, atq; huc pertinent aspectus & applicationes: vel collati ad Solem, & tunc fiunt aucti vel minuti lumine, extra radios, seu in suo lumine, vel sub radiis, seu combusti, matutini vel vespertini, &c. vel secundum longitudinem latitudinemve, & tunc sunt vel ascendentes, vel descendentes, humiles vel alti, ultra vel citra eclipticam. Ex quibus apparet, 4. esse praecipua passionum genera, quae Planetis contingunt.
units.tr: Thus far we have explored the natures, powers and motions of the principal heavenly lights. Now we must also inquire into certain proper affections and passions of the planets, which befall them either by reason of the eccentric and epicycle. By this reason every planet, except the Sun and Moon, can be direct, retrograde, stationary, swift, slow, or of medium speed. Or they arise from their varied positions and motions relative to one another, and to this belong aspects and applications. Or they arise from their relation to the Sun, and then they become increased or diminished in light: outside the rays, or in their own light; or under the rays, that is, burnt; or matutine or vespertine, and so on. Or they arise according to longitude or latitude, and then they are ascending or descending, low or high, north or south of the ecliptic. From these things it appears that there are four principal kinds of passions that befall the planets.

units.la: Directus Planeta dicitur, cum incedit secundum signorum seriem & ordinem, id est, cum motus ejus ad sequentem diem crescit. Retrogradus contra, & tunc Planeta incedit contra signorum ordinem, ut cum ex tauro redit in arietem, hoc est, ab ortu in occasum. Epicyclus enim secundum signorum ordinem nem progrediens, motum Planetæ regularem & proprium in eccentrico remoratur & impedit.
units.tr: A planet is called direct when it advances according to the order and sequence of the signs, that is, when its motion increases from day to day. Retrograde is the opposite: then the planet advances against the order of the signs, as when it returns from Taurus into Aries, that is, from east to west. For the epicycle, moving forward according to the order of the signs, delays and hinders the planet's regular and proper motion on the eccentric.

units.la: Stationarius, cùm apparet quasi immotus, id est, cùm linea veri motus sub una hærens zodiaci parte, neq; ad orientem, neq; ad occidentem moveri videtur. Puncta, in quibus id accidit, dicuntur stationes. Estq; prima vel secunda. Prima seu matutina est, cùm Planeta post mediam conjunctionem, quæ fit in apogæo cum Sole, distat ab eodem in latere epicycli orientali quadrato vel triquetro, ut accidit tribus superioribus, nam Venus ad quadratum vel trigonum à Sole non discedit, Mercurius verò celerius stationes suas superat, quàm ut observari possint, at Luna propter motus velocitatem summam stationalis non fit. In principio autem hujus stationis primæ Planeta semper fit retrogradus. Secunda seu vespertina statio est, cùm post oppositionem in latere occidentali epicycli distat à Sole Planeta per triquetrum, quod contingit tribus superioribus tantùm. In hujus principio Planeta incipit fieri directus, estq; in epicyclo ascendens.
units.tr: A planet is stationary when it appears as if motionless, that is, when the line of its true motion, resting under one part of the zodiac, seems to move neither eastward nor westward. The points at which this happens are called stations, and there is a first and a second station. The first, or matutine, station occurs when, after the middle conjunction, which takes place with the Sun at apogee, the planet is distant from the Sun by a square or trine on the eastern side of the epicycle, as happens to the three superior planets; for Venus does not depart from a square or trine to the Sun, and Mercury passes through its stations too quickly to be observed, while the Moon, because of its very great speed, is never stationary. At the beginning of this first station the planet is always retrograde. The second, or vespertine, station occurs when, after opposition, the planet is distant from the Sun by a trine on the western side of the epicycle, which happens only to the three superior planets. At the beginning of this station the planet begins to become direct, and on the epicycle it is ascending.

units.la: Auctus cursu seu velox Planeta est, cùm motus ejus verus, secundum ordinem signorum major seu velocior est motu medio: tardus, cùm motus ejus verus est serior medio: mediocris, cùm motus verus secundum signorum seriem medio æquatur.
units.tr: A planet is swift in course, or fast, when its true motion, according to the order of the signs, is greater or faster than its mean motion; slow, when its true motion is slower than the mean; of medium speed, when its true motion according to the sequence of the signs is equal to the mean.

units.la: Aspectus certa Planetarum irradiatio est in signiferi locis, quâ mutuò se vel juvant, vel impediunt. Longâ enim experientia observatum est, Planetas secundum diversas radiorum vibrationes & commixtiones diversos ciere effectus, non tantùm in genituris hominum, sed aliis etiam rebus sublunaribus. Sunt autem conjunctio, sextilis, quadratus, trigonus & oppositus.
units.tr: An aspect is a certain irradiation of the planets in the places of the zodiac, by which they either help or hinder one another. For by long experience it has been observed that the planets, according to the diverse vibrations and mixtures of their rays, produce diverse effects, not only in the nativities of men but also in other sublunary things. The aspects are conjunction, sextile, square, trine and opposition.

units.la: Conjunctio est aspectus, cùm duo plúresve Planetæ in uno signo conjunguntur, ut hoc anno 1611. mense Majo, Mars & Jupiter in cancro, quæ, quia conjunctio magna est, magna etiam porportendet. Ubi tamen notandum, si Luna vel alius Planeta sit in extremis signi alicujus gradibus, & alter in sequentis signi principio, veram conjunctionem esse dicendam, quoniam extremi signi gradus, ut 28.29. 30. cum sequentibus tribus primis cohærent. Porrò conjunctio est vel longitudinis, vel latitudinis.*
units.tr: Conjunction is an aspect when two or more planets are joined in one sign, as in the month of May 1611 Mars and Jupiter were in Cancer; and because this is a great conjunction, it portends great things also. Here, however, it should be noted that if the Moon or another planet is at the extreme degrees of one sign, and the other at the beginning of the following sign, it must be called a true conjunction, since the last degrees of a sign, such as 28, 29 and 30, cohere with the first three of the following sign. Moreover, conjunction is either of longitude or of latitude.

units.la: Longitudinis est duplex, seu fit duobus modis, vel in uno signo, vel in aspectu. Initium conjunctionis in uno signo est, cum fuerint inter Planetas 12. gradus, quantoq; magis alter alteri in gradibus & minutis appropinquat, tantò erit illorum conjunctio fortior, perfectissima autem & fortissima est, quæ fit in uno gradu, ut cum Luna jungitur Jovi in 26.gr. cancri. Cum autem in diversis signis fuerint, pauciq; sint inter eos gradus, licèt proprie conjunctio non fit, nec dici possit, ut ea, quæ fit in eodem signo, tamen nihilominus virtutem alter alteri suam per radios communicat. Conjunctio per aspectum est, cum Planetæ sunt in signis, in quibus aspiciunt se configuratione vel triangula, vel quadrangula, vel sextangula, vel oppositā, quæ conjunctio rectè dicitur per corradiationem seu aspectum.
units.tr: Conjunction of longitude is twofold, or occurs in two ways: either in one sign, or by aspect. The beginning of conjunction in one sign is when the planets are within twelve degrees of each other, and the closer one approaches the other in degrees and minutes, the stronger their conjunction will be. The most perfect and strongest is that which occurs within one degree, as when the Moon is joined to Jupiter at 26 degrees of Cancer. But when they are in different signs, and there are few degrees between them, although strictly speaking it is not a conjunction, nor can it be called one as that which occurs in the same sign is, nevertheless each communicates its power to the other by rays. Conjunction by aspect is when the planets are in signs in which they regard one another by a triangular, square, sextile or opposite configuration; this conjunction is rightly called by corradiation or aspect.

units.la: Triangularis aspectus est, cum Planetæ à se invicem distant tertia circuli parte, id est, gradibus 120. estq; aspectus perfectè bonus, quia fit in signis ejudem naturæ & complexionis, ut cum Jupiter aspicit ex cancro Lunam in piscibus.
units.tr: A triangular aspect is when the planets are distant from one another by a third part of the circle, that is, by 120 degrees; it is a wholly good aspect, because it occurs in signs of the same nature and complexion, as when Jupiter, from Cancer, aspects the Moon in Pisces.

units.la: Quadratus, cum Planetæ à se invicem distant quarta zodiaci parte, id est, gradibus 90. est autem semper malus, quia fit in signis, vel una qualitate dissidentibus, & tunc est malus mediocriter, vel utraq;, & tunc extremè malus, ut cum Luna exacte intuetur Jovem in cancro, qui aspectus insigniter malus est, quoniam fit in signis utraq; qualitate luctantibus atque dissidentibus, aries enim signum est calidum & siccum, cancer verò frigidum & humidum. Cum verò Luna ex piscibus aspicit Jovem in geminis, aspectus est mediocriter malus, quia gemini & pisces una qualitate, videlicet humiditate conveniunt, frigiditate vero & caliditate discordant.
units.tr: A square is when the planets are distant from one another by a fourth part of the zodiac, that is, by 90 degrees. It is always bad, because it occurs in signs that disagree in one quality, and then it is moderately bad, or in both qualities, and then it is extremely bad; as when the Moon exactly regards Jupiter in Cancer, which aspect is notably bad, because it occurs in signs struggling and at odds in both qualities: for Aries is a hot and dry sign, while Cancer is cold and moist. But when the Moon, from Pisces, regards Jupiter in Gemini, the aspect is moderately bad, because Gemini and Pisces agree in one quality, namely moistness, but disagree in cold and heat.

units.la: Sextilis radiatura est, cùm Planetæ à fe invicem distant fe-xta circuli parte, id est, gradibus sexaginta: eftq; aspectus hic semper mediocriter bonus, non quidem ratione signorum, fit enim in signis altera qualitate sibi inimicis, sed ratione portio-nis ipsius circuli. Sextili igitur fe irradiant, Luna in tauro, & Ju-piter in cancro, Mars in leone, & Luna in geminis, Sol in cancro, & Luna in virgine.
units.tr: A sextile radiation is when the planets are distant from one another by a sixth part of the circle, that is, by sixty degrees. This aspect is always moderately good, not indeed by reason of the signs, for it occurs in signs with one quality hostile to the other, but by reason of the portion of the circle itself. Thus they irradiate one another by sextile: the Moon in Taurus and Jupiter in Cancer; Mars in Leo and the Moon in Gemini; the Sun in Cancer and the Moon in Virgo.

units.la: Oppositus aspectus seu diametralis est, cùm stellæ invicem distant medietate circuli, hoc est, sex signis, id est, gradibus 180. eftq; hic quoq; perpetuo malus, quia Planetæ ex oppositis coeli locis & signis feferiunt: talis constitutio hoc anno est, cùm Lu-na fertur in virgine, tunc enim habet oppositum Saturnum in- piscibus, cùm in capricorno Jovem in cancro, cùm in aquario Martem in leone, idq; Junio tantùm usq; in 20. Julii, tunc enim Mars ingreditur virginis astrum, incurritq; in oppositum Saturni.
units.tr: The opposite aspect, or diametrical, is when the stars are distant from one another by half the circle, that is, by six signs, or 180 degrees; this too is always bad, because the planets strike one another from opposite places and signs in the heavens. Such a configuration happens this year: when the Moon is in Virgo, then it has Saturn opposite in Pisces; when in Capricorn, Jupiter in Cancer; when in Aquarius, Mars in Leo; and this only from June until 20 July, for then Mars enters the sign of Virgo and runs into the opposition of Saturn.

units.la: Ex his aspectibus quidam dicuntur partiles, quidam platici seu imperfecti. Illi sunt fortiores, hi imbecilliores.
units.tr: These aspects are some partile and some platic, or imperfect. The partile ones are stronger, the platic ones weaker.

units.la: Partiles, cùm Planeta ad Planetam radium projicit intra medietatem fui orbis. Est autem medietas orbis Saturni 10. Jo-vis 9. Martis 7. Veneris 8. Mercurii 7. Lunæ 12. Solis vero 15. gra-duum. Partilis igitur aspectus est, cùm Sol in cancri 12. gradu, aspicit Lunam triquetro existentem in 18. gradu piscium vel scorpionis. Sed partilifsimus & fortissimus etiam est, fi fit in gra-dibus iisdem, ut fi Luna pariter 12. piscium gradum teneret.
units.tr: An aspect is partile when one planet projects its ray to another within half of its own orb. The half-orbs are: Saturn 10 degrees, Jupiter 9, Mars 7, Venus 8, Mercury 7, the Moon 12, and the Sun 15. So the aspect is partile when the Sun is at 12 degrees of Cancer and sees the Moon, in trine, at 18 degrees of Pisces or Scorpio. It is most partile and strongest of all if it falls within the same degrees, for example if the Moon also stood at 12 degrees of Pisces.

units.la: Platicus aspectus est, qui fit extra medietatem orbis Plane-tarum, ut fi ex 12. gradu cancri Sol aspiceret Lunam in 29. gra-du scorpionis, vel Luna in 19. gradu piscium, Jovem in 3. gr. can-cri: atq; hic eo est debilior, quo major Planetarum in gradibus distandistantia. Non autem hic omittenda est divisio aspectus in dextrum & sinistrum. Ille enim fit in signa antecedentia, & contra seriem signorum, hic vero in consequentia, & secundum seriem ordinemq; signorum. Certum namq; est, quemlibet Planetam in coelo 7. diffundere radios, & quemvis locum 7. radiis illustrari: tres enim radios jaculatur sursum, seu in dextrum, hoc est, ad eas partes, à quibus jam recessit, totidemq; deorsum & in sinistrum, hoc est, ad partes illas, ad quas recto jam tramite accedit: 7. radius tendit in partem oppositam. Sic Sol oriens cum 1. gradu arietis jaculatur radios dextros, trigonos, quadratos & sextiles in signa antecedentia, sinistros vero in consequentia, diametrali autem oppositione intuetur ipsum occasum.
units.tr: An aspect is platic when it falls outside the half-orb of the planets, as when the Sun at 12 degrees of Cancer sees the Moon at 29 degrees of Scorpio, or the Moon at 19 degrees of Pisces sees Jupiter at 3 degrees of Cancer. It is weaker the greater the distance between the planets in degrees. Nor should the division of aspects into right and left be passed over here. The one falls on the signs that precede, moving against the order of the signs; the other falls on those that follow, in the order and sequence of the signs. For it is certain that every planet in the heavens sends out seven rays, and illuminates every place with seven rays: it shoots three rays upward, or to the right, that is, towards the parts it has already left, and as many downward and to the left, that is, towards those parts it is already approaching by its direct course; the seventh ray is aimed at the opposite part. Thus the rising Sun, at 1 degree of Aries, shoots its right-hand rays, trine, square and sextile, into the preceding signs, and its left-hand rays into the following signs, while by diametrical opposition it looks upon its setting.

units.la: Cur vero nec plures nec pauciores sint aspectus, ratio hæc est, quòd duodenarius numerus tantùm potest distribui in 2. 3. 4. & 6. nec recipit plures divisiones æquales, quæ integra signa comprehendant: item, circulo, cujus ambitus in 12. æqualia segmenta distinguitur, non possunt inscribi plura schemata rectilinea & æquilatera, præter trigonum, quadratum & sextilem, sic, ut integris horum lateribus integra non mutilata segmenta respondeant. Aspectus autem tamdiu durat, quamdiu distant radii Planetarum per unius signi quantitatem: item quamdiu Planetæ se aspicientes continent radios intra orbium suorum medietatem, tamdiu etiam durat aspectus. Robur omnium aspectuum quod attinet, sciendum, conjunctione esse omnium efficacissimâ, quia in ea Planetæ vires suas corporaliter habent conjunctas. Vis enim unita fortior semper dispersâ. Secundum locum habet oppositus, tertium trigonus, quartum quadratus, quintum sextilis. Partiles quoq; platicis semper efficaciores, & dextros sinistris experientia docuit.
units.tr: The reason why there are neither more nor fewer aspects is this: the number twelve can be divided only into 2, 3, 4 and 6 equal parts that each comprise whole signs, and it admits no more equal divisions of this kind. Likewise, into a circle whose circumference is divided into twelve equal segments, no more rectilinear and equilateral figures can be inscribed than the triangle, the square and the sextile, so that whole sides of these correspond to whole, undivided segments. An aspect lasts as long as the rays of the planets are distant by the extent of one sign; likewise, it lasts as long as the planets that see each other keep their rays within half of their orbs. As for the strength of all the aspects, it should be known that conjunction is the most powerful of all, because in it the planets have their powers bodily joined together; for a united power is always stronger than a dispersed one. Opposition has the second place, trine the third, square the fourth, and sextile the fifth. Experience has also taught that partile aspects are always more effective than platic ones, and right-hand aspects than left-hand ones.

units.la: Aspectibus quoque affinis est applicatio, cùm scilicet Planeta levior (id est, qui pauciores habet gradus) ad ponderosiorem[?] appropinquat, sive corporaliter, sive per aspectum, sive fit sextilis, quadratus, trigonus vel oppositus: (nisi distantia fuerit ultra orbium mediocritatem.) Levis Planeta ponderosiori (id est, qui plures obtinet gradus) vim donat applicando, ponderosus autem virtutem recipit: & hinc oritur dignitas Planetae, quae receptio virtutis dicitur, cum scilicet Planeta debilior, ab alio, qui in domo vel exaltatione sua est, ideoque potentior, accipit vi-res, ut, si Mars & Luna jungerentur in ariete, tunc Luna recipe-ret virtutem Martis, qui in essentiali sua dignitate est, videlicet domicilio: eadem in signo eodem juncta Soli recipit vires sola-res, quia Sol in ariete exaltatur, ideoque Luna fortior, unde Luna ita constituta fit solaris. Quod si vero Planeta levis jungitur ponderosiori, hic vero adhuc alteri, tunc ponderosus naturam levis transfert ad eum, cui jungitur, & dicitur haec applicatio translatio virtutis. Huic est annexa virtutis commissio, cum sci-licet Planeta quispiam est in essentiali aliqua sua dignitate, ut domicilio, exaltatione vel triplicitate, eiq; alius jungitur, tunc qui in essentiali dignitate est, committit virtutem suam ei, cui jun-gitur. Item, cum Planeta existens in dignitate sua, aspicit alium, tunc committit ei virtutem suam: si vero uterq; sit in essentiali sua dignitate, tunc alter alteri virtutem suam communicat. Ex-empli gratia, si Mercurius est in virgine cum Sole, committit Soli dispositionem & naturam suam, in virgine enim Mercu-rius habet domicilium & exaltationem, & est constitutus in es-sentialibus dignitatibus. Idem aspiciens Lunam in cancro vel tauro, mittit ad Lunam virtutem suam, & Luna vicissim suam ad Mercurium, quia uterq; in essentialibus suis dignitatibus est, in cancro enim Luna habet suum domicilium, in tauro vero exaltationem. Exemplum translationis virtutis est: sit Mercu-rius in 4. arietis gradu junctus Jovi, in tertio gradu signi ejus-dem, Luna vero teneat 12. gradum, hic Mercurius à Jove recedens, transportat natura Jovis ad Lunam, cui Mercurius quo-tidie fit propior, Luna vero accipit per Mercurium virtutem Jovis. Sit item Venus in 3. gr. arietis, Jupiter in 5. Luna in 7. hic Jupiter naturam Veneris transfert in Lunam, Luna vero per Jovem Veneris virtutem recipit. Idemq; judicium fit & de aliis.
units.tr: Closely related to aspects is application, when a lighter planet (that is, one with fewer degrees) approaches a heavier one, whether bodily, or by aspect, whether sextile, square, trine or opposition (unless the distance is beyond the mean of the orbs). The lighter planet, by applying itself, gives power to the heavier one (that is, the one with more degrees), while the heavier one receives virtue. From this arises the dignity of a planet, which is called reception of virtue, when a weaker planet receives strength from another that is in its own domicile or exaltation and therefore more powerful. For example, if Mars and the Moon were joined in Aries, the Moon would receive the virtue of Mars, who is in his essential dignity, namely his domicile. If the Moon is joined in the same sign to the Sun, it receives solar powers, because the Sun is exalted in Aries; so the Moon, being stronger, is made solar in that position. But if a lighter planet is joined to a heavier one, and this one in turn to another, then the heavier transfers the nature of the lighter to that to which it is joined; this application is called transference of virtue. Connected with this is commission of virtue: when a planet is in some essential dignity, such as domicile, exaltation or triplicity, and another is joined to it, then the one that is in essential dignity commits its virtue to the one to which it is joined. Likewise, when a planet standing in its own dignity sees another, it commits its virtue to it; and if both are in their essential dignities, then each communicates its virtue to the other. For example, if Mercury is in Virgo with the Sun, it commits to the Sun its disposition and nature, for Mercury has its domicile and exaltation in Virgo and is placed in its essential dignities there. If Mercury, in the same way, sees the Moon in Cancer or Taurus, it sends its virtue to the Moon, and the Moon in turn sends its own to Mercury, since both are in their essential dignities: the Moon has its domicile in Cancer and its exaltation in Taurus. An example of transference of virtue: let Mercury be joined to Jupiter at 4 degrees of Aries, Jupiter at the third degree of the same sign, and the Moon hold 12 degrees. Here Mercury, withdrawing from Jupiter, carries the nature of Jupiter over to the Moon, to which Mercury comes nearer every day, and the Moon receives the virtue of Jupiter through Mercury. Again, let Venus be at 3 degrees of Aries, Jupiter at 5, and the Moon at 7. Here Jupiter transfers the nature of Venus to the Moon, and the Moon receives the virtue of Venus through Jupiter. The same judgement is made of the other planets.

units.la: Porro auctus lumine Planeta dicitur, cum post conjunctionem cum Sole, Sol ab ipso, vel ipse a Sole eo usq; recedit, ut sensibiliter iterum apparere incipiat mundo, Sole scilicet fulgorem ejus non impediente: hac ratione Luna augetur lumine a novilunio usq; in plenilunium: & tunc Planeta est in suo lumi-ne. Colligere autem lumen Planeta dicitur, cum duo vel plures ei junguntur, ut si Mercurius esset in tauro junctus Lunae & Veneri, ita ut ei applicent, Mercurius vero fit ponderosior, Mercurius diceretur colligere illorum lumina.
units.tr: Further, a planet is said to be increased in light when, after conjunction with the Sun, the Sun withdraws from it, or it from the Sun, so far that it begins again to appear visibly to the world, the Sun's brightness no longer hindering it. In this way the Moon is increased in light from the new moon to the full moon, and then the planet is in its light. A planet is said to gather light when two or more are joined to it, applying to it; for example, if Mercury were in Taurus joined to the Moon and Venus, so that they apply to it, and Mercury were the heavier, Mercury would be said to gather their lights.

units.la: Minutus lumine Planeta dicitur, cum ipse ad Solem, vel Sol ad eum properat, & talis est Luna ab oppositione seu plenilunio usq; ad coitum, seu novilunium.
units.tr: A planet is said to be diminished in light when it hastens towards the Sun, or the Sun towards it; and the Moon is such from opposition, or full moon, until conjunction, or new moon.

units.la: Combustus Planeta est, cum a Sole distat minus sui orbis seu corporis medietate, si enim plus, liber a combustione dicitur: ut ita combustio recte agnosci possit per orbis Planetae medietatem.
units.tr: A planet is combust when it is distant from the Sun by less than half of its own orb or body; for if it is more, it is said to be free from combustion. Thus combustion can be rightly recognised by the half-orb of the planet.

units.la: Sub radiis vero latitare adhuc seu oppressus dicitur post orbis sui medietatem ante vel post usq; in 16. gradum. Exemplis haec declaranda sunt, saepe enim contingit, ut Planeta quispiam sit liber a combustione, qui tamen sub radiis adhuc latitat, ut sit Mercurius in 14. gradu virginis, Sol in 9. gr. signi ejusdem, hic Mercurius dicitur combustus, quia distantia ejus a Sole est intra medietatem orbis sui, videlicet 5. graduum: idem vero in 17. virginis gradu non amplius erit combustus, quia distantia est 8. graduum, id est, ultra medietatem orbis Mercurii, medietas enim orbis Mercurii ante vel post praecise est 7. gr. & nihilo tamen minus adhuc sub radiis Solis latet, quoniam, ut Planeta sit extra radios, requiritur, ut à Sole distet ad minimum 16. gradi-bus. Hæc divinaturo ex astris accuratissimè observanda sunt, ad prædictionibus suis conciliandam laudem.
units.tr: A planet is said to lie hidden, or oppressed, under the rays when it is within half of its own orb, before or after, up to the 16th degree. These things must be explained by examples, for it often happens that a planet is free from combustion and yet still lies hidden under the rays. Thus if Mercury is at 14 degrees of Virgo and the Sun at 9 degrees of the same sign, Mercury is said to be combust, because its distance from the Sun is within half of its orb, namely 5 degrees. But at 17 degrees of Virgo it will no longer be combust, because the distance is 8 degrees, that is, beyond the half-orb of Mercury, which before or after is exactly 7 degrees; yet even so it still lies hidden under the Sun's rays, since for a planet to be outside the rays it is required that it be distant from the Sun by at least 16 degrees. These things must be most carefully observed by one who would make predictions from the stars, so as to win praise for his forecasts.

units.la: Matutinus Planeta est, cùm manè paulò ante Solis ortum incipit apparere: Vespertinus, cùm vesperi paulò post occasum Solis. Nam ortu matutino heliaco oritur Planeta, cùm manè ante Solis ortum, ejusdem radiis antea occultatus, iterum prodit in conspectum nostrum: hoc ortu oriri possunt omnes Planetæ, excepta Luna, quia Sol eam celeritate adæquare non potest, multò minus post se relinquere. Occasu matutino heliaco occidit Planeta, cùm ad Solem tam propè accedit, ut, licèt prius ante Solis ortum in Orientis cardine conspicuus, tandem tamè radiis Solis quasi abreptus evanescat. Hoc casu occidit Luna senescens, id est, antelucès postremis horis noctis, festinans ad Solis coitū, seq; tandem omninò sub radiis illius condens. Venus similiter & Mercurius in occidetali epicycli medietate propter suum ad Solem accessum, hoc occasu occidunt. Hac autè occasus specie superiores, Saturnus, Jupiter & Mars occidere nequeunt, quia tam veloces non sunt, ut, cùm matutino tempore se conspiciendos exhibeant, Solem assequantur & occultentur.
units.tr: A planet is "morning" when it begins to appear early in the morning, shortly before sunrise, and "evening" when it appears in the evening, shortly after sunset. A planet makes its morning heliacal rising when, having been hidden earlier by the Sun's rays, it reappears to our sight early in the morning before sunrise. All planets can rise in this way except the Moon, because the Sun cannot match her speed, much less leave her behind. A planet makes its morning heliacal setting when it comes so close to the Sun that, although it was previously visible before sunrise in the eastern quarter of the sky, it finally vanishes as if snatched away by the Sun's rays. In this way the waning Moon sets, that is, in the last hours of the night before dawn, hastening towards conjunction with the Sun and at last hiding herself completely under its rays. Venus and Mercury likewise set in this way in the western half of their epicycle, because of their approach to the Sun. The superior planets, Saturn, Jupiter and Mars, cannot set in this manner, because they are not swift enough: when they show themselves to be seen in the morning, they cannot overtake the Sun and be hidden.

units.la: Ortu vespertino heliaco oritur Planeta, cùm Solis radios vesperi egrediens, mox post Solis occasum in angulo occidentali se profert: atq; sic oritur Luna, cùm ex radiis Solis tempore novilunii elucidata, mox post occasum per tenuia cornua se promit. Similiter Venus & Mercurius, cùm in orientali epicycli medietate à conjunctione cum Sole aliquantulum digressi sunt. Itaq; hoc occasu superiores nō oriūtur, ratio est ipsorū tarditas.
units.tr: A planet makes its evening heliacal rising when, emerging from the Sun's rays in the evening, it soon after sunset appears in the western quarter of the sky. The Moon rises in this way when, illuminated by the Sun's rays at new moon, she soon after sunset shows herself with thin horns. Venus and Mercury rise likewise when they have moved a little away from conjunction with the Sun in the eastern half of their epicycle. Therefore the superior planets do not rise in this way; the reason is their slowness.

units.la: Occasu heliaco vespertino occidit Planeta, cùm sic ad Solem accedit, vel ad eum, ut, prius vesperi conspicuus, jam radiis Solis occultetur: & sic possunt occidere omnes: superiores quidem, cùm in apogæo epicycli sui Soli conjunguntur, & duo inferiores, Mercurius & Venus, cùm post ortum vespertinum ad imum epicycli delabuntur: Luna excipitur, quæ radios Solis, cùm vesperi conspicitur, celerrimè fugit, unde Sol radiis eam suis assequi non potest.
units.tr: A planet makes its evening heliacal setting when it approaches the Sun, or comes so near to it, that, previously visible in the evening, it is now hidden by the Sun's rays. In this way all planets can set: the superior planets indeed when they are conjoined with the Sun at the apogee of their epicycle, and the two inferior planets, Mercury and Venus, when after their evening rising they sink to the bottom of their epicycle. The Moon is an exception, since when she is seen in the evening she flees the Sun's rays very swiftly, so that the Sun cannot overtake her with its rays.

units.la: Altitudo est motus Planetæ, cùm ab imo sui orbis loco, aut à centro terræ fertur in locum altissimum. Humilitas, cùm defertur ad locum terræ proximum, & sui orbis infimum: illic Planeta dicitur elatus, hic depressus. Verum majoris momenti est huc apponere dignitatem Planetæ, quam accipit, si supra omnes alios in natalitio themate est elatus seu elevatus. Id verò, ut rectè secundum artis principia cognoscatur, consideranda diligenter sequentia sunt, quæ magnam & lucem afferent, & usum, ad Astrologicum judicium dextrè informandum.
units.tr: Altitude is the motion of a planet when it is carried from the lowest point of its orbit, or from the centre of the earth, to its highest place. Lowness is when it is carried to the place nearest the earth and the lowest point of its orbit. There the planet is said to be raised up, here depressed. But it is of greater importance to set out here the dignity which a planet acquires if it is raised or elevated above all others in the nativity chart. In order to know this correctly according to the principles of the art, the following points must be carefully considered, which will bring great light and use for forming the astrological judgment rightly.

units.la: Elevatus seu elatus supra alios Planeta dicitur:
units.tr: A planet is said to be elevated or raised above the others when:

units.la: 1. Qui minus distat ab auge seu apogæo eccentrici sui, is tunc elevatur supra eum, qui magis distat ab auge sua.
units.tr: 1. the one that is less distant from the apogee or upper point of its eccentric is then elevated above the one that is more distant from its apogee.

units.la: 2. Planeta existens supra terram, elevatur supra eum, qui est infra terram: ut si Luna sola esset supra terram, infra verò reliqui omnes, Luna diceretur elevata supra Planetas omnes.
units.tr: 2. A planet existing above the earth is elevated above one that is below the earth: so that if the Moon alone were above the earth and all the rest below it, the Moon would be said to be elevated above all the planets.

units.la: 3. Cùm Planeta distat ab alio per 10. aut 11. signa, juxta signorum ordinem, tunc qui est in 10. aut 11. signo ab altero, dicitur elevatus supra alterum.
units.tr: 3. When one planet is distant from another by 10 or 11 signs, in the order of the signs, then the one that is in the 10th or 11th sign from the other is said to be elevated above it.

units.la: 4. Is qui in culmine coeli est, vel prope, vel ab oriente in medium coeli tendens, dicitur elevatus supra eum, qui in 11. domo est, & in 11. supra eum, qui in 12. est, medium enim coeli elevatur supra 11. & 11. supra 12. & hæc supra ascendens.
units.tr: 4. The one that is at or near the top of the heaven, or moving from the east towards the middle of heaven, is said to be elevated above the one that is in the 11th house, and the one in the 11th above the one in the 12th; for the midheaven is elevated above the 11th, and the 11th above the 12th, and these above the ascendant.

units.la: 5. Planeta in angulo elevatur supra eum, qui ab angulo seu cardine recedit.
units.tr: 5. A planet in an angle is elevated above one that is receding from an angle or cardinal point.

units.la: 6. Si omnes sunt supra terram, quod tamen raro contingit, tunc qui medio coeli est proximus, supra reliquos omnes est elevatus.
units.tr: 6. If all are above the earth, which however rarely happens, then the one nearest to midheaven is elevated above all the rest.

units.la: 7. Si omnes sunt infra terram, quod æquè rarū est, tunc qui ascendenti est proximus, elevatus supra alios est omnes.
units.tr: 7. If all are below the earth, which is equally rare, then the one nearest to the ascendant is elevated above all the others.

units.la: 8. Sed maximè elevatio Planetæ etiam consideranda est secundum latitudinem zodiaci: si enim duo conjunguntur, tunc is qui habuerit latitudinem Septentrionalem (id est, distantiam ab ecliptica septentriones versus) elevatur supra eum, qui habet latitudinem meridionalem, id est, distantiam ab ecliptica versus meridiem.
units.tr: 8. But the elevation of a planet is to be considered above all according to its latitude in the zodiac: for if two are conjoined, then the one that has northern latitude (that is, distance from the ecliptic towards the north) is elevated above the one that has southern latitude, that is, distance from the ecliptic towards the south.

units.la: 9. Quod si ambo habuerint latitudinem septentriona-lem, ille, qui habet maiorem, elevatur supra eum, qui habet minorem: ubi notandum venit, Saturnum, Jovem & Martem, in-ea parte eccentrici, quâ apogæum est, vergere in septentriones, quâ perigæum, in meridiem.
units.tr: 9. But if both have northern latitude, the one that has the greater is elevated above the one that has the lesser. Here it must be noted that Saturn, Jupiter and Mars, in that part of the eccentric where the apogee is, incline towards the north, and where the perigee is, towards the south.

units.la: 10. Duo verò Planetæ juncti, si ambo haberent latitudinem meridionalem, tunc ille, qui habuerit minorem, elevatur supra eum qui habet majorem.
units.tr: 10. If two conjoined planets both have southern latitude, then the one that has the lesser is elevated above the one that has the greater.

units.la: 11. Si unus fuerit in Ecliptica, alter verò ultra, & tertius citra eclipticam, tunc septentrionalis elevari diceretur supra eum, qui in Ecliptica est, & hic supra eum vicissim, qui meridionalis est.
units.tr: 11. If one is in the ecliptic, another beyond it, and a third on this side of the ecliptic, then the northern planet is said to be elevated above the one that is in the ecliptic, and this one in turn above the southern planet.

units.la: 12. Quod si verò contigerit, ut duo Planetæ sint in me-dietate zodiaci ascendente vel descendente, habeantq; eandem longitudinem, quicunq; tunc eorum in longitudine majorem habuerit declinationem (id est, distantiam ab æquatore) in se-ptentrionem, is elevatur supra alterum.
units.tr: 12. But if it happens that two planets are in the half of the zodiac that is ascending or descending, and have the same longitude, then whichever of them has the greater declination in longitude (that is, distance from the equator) to the north is elevated above the other.

units.la: 13. Quod si ambo latitudinem habuerint meridionalem, quicunque ex iis minorem habuerit declinationem meridionalem, is supra alterum elevari rectè dicetur.
units.tr: 13. If both have southern latitude, whichever of them has the lesser southern declination is rightly said to be elevated above the other.

units.la: Cæterùm Planeta decurrens in medietate zodiaci ascen-dente, ut à capricorno usq; in cancrum, dicitur ascendens in-septentrionem, à cancro verò ad capricornum, dicitur descen-dens in meridiem.
units.tr: Moreover, a planet moving through the ascending half of the zodiac, from Capricorn to Cancer, is said to be ascending towards the north; but from Cancer to Capricorn, it is said to be descending towards the south.

units.la: Inter passiones deniq; seu affectiones Planetarum considerandus quoque est motus in longitudinem vel latitudinem. Motus Planetæ in longitudinem est, quo per zodiaci longitudinem e signo scilicet in signum fertur, donec eam fuerit emensus. Motus latitudinis est, quo Planeta Eclipticam egressus, modo in austrum, modo in septentriones evagatur. Excipitur Sol, quia planum eccentrici sub eclipticæ plano sempermanet: unde, etsi Soli latitudo, id est, distantia ab ecliptica non convenit, tamen accidit ei declinatio, id est, distantia ab æquatore versus alterutrum mundi polum. Hincigitur & latitudo & declinatio septentrionalis vel meridionalis intelligitur.
units.tr: Finally, among the passions or affections of the planets, the motion in longitude or latitude must also be considered. The motion of a planet in longitude is that by which it is carried along the length of the zodiac, that is, from sign to sign, until it has traversed it. The motion of latitude is that by which a planet, leaving the ecliptic, wanders now to the south and now to the north. The Sun is an exception, because the plane of its eccentric always remains beneath the plane of the ecliptic; hence, although the Sun has no latitude, that is, distance from the ecliptic, it nevertheless has declination, that is, distance from the equator towards one or other pole of the world. Hence both latitude and declination are understood as northern or southern.

units.la: Exploratis Planetarum affectionibus præcipuis, concitato nunc cursu properandum est ad distinctionem cœli in 12. do-micilia, seu duodenas sectiones partésve æquales, & quatuor quadrantes, plurimum enim interest scire, in quo cœli spacio quilibet Planeta volutetur, an scilicet cardinibus inhæreat, an vero extra cardines feratur. Longâ enim & indubitata experientia deprehensum est, Planetas in aliis atque aliis cœli locis, alios atq; alios effectus produxisse, & etiamnunc excitare atque producere. Hoc cum animadverterent antiqui Astronomi, stellas scilicet errantes in circulo obliquo, quem postea à 12. imaginibus zodiacum appellarunt, varias & insignes ciere mutatio-nes ac vicissitudines in corporibus sublunaribus, pro diversis scilicet concursibus ac configurationibus partim inter se, partim etiam cum stellis octavi orbis, divina quadam ingenii vi observatis primo solstitiorum & æquinoctiorum punctis, circulum ipsum in 4. partes per duos coluros distribuerunt, iisq; 4. anni tempora artificiose distinxerunt: postea eundem in duodenas partes æquales, propter duodenas Lunæ & Solis syno-dos in annuo spacio subdiviserunt, circulis magnis utrinq; per polos zodiaci ductis, singulorum signorum initia & fines discreverunt, verūnt, singulis signis tricenos annumerantes gradus, diligen-ter observantes, quæ, quibus in partibus, cujus qualitatis aut naturæ effent sidera. Diversos autem stellarum effectus in aliis atq; aliis cœli partibus deprehendentes, viam præmonstrante experientiâ, fenfuq; prælucente, fecundum 12. fignifera signa, duodecim quoq; cœli loca, quæ domicilia dicuntur & mansio-nes, quia in harum qualibet Planetæ quolibet die per tempus aliquod commorantur, constituerunt, ut ita in confesso fit, 12. domiciliorum cœli constitutionē à signifero primùm esse sum-tam. Sic enim Pontanus l.2.c.1. de rebus cœl. Fit autem, inquit, cùm signa 12. signiferum constituant, ut 12. quoq; cœli domici-lia seu loca constituendæ sint. Omnem igitur cœli orbiculatio-nem ab horofcopo progressi, eodem regredientes in 12. loca partiemur, quod autem inter medii cœli apicem, gradumque horofcopantem spacii interjacet, quadram, quadraturamque appellabimus, unde & ipse signifer in 4. quartas fuit diftribuen-dus. Circulus enim transiens per capitis nostri Zenith, seu verti-cale punctum, & per polos zodiaci, singulis momentis diftin-guit 4. cœli quadrantes. Alii horizonte & meridiano dispescunt in 4. æquales quadrantes totum cœlum, & postea ad hos affu-muntalios 4. circulos, perq; communem eorundem circulo-rum interfectionem transeuntes, cœlum totum in 12. partes æ-quales, quæ domicilia dicuntur, dispescunt, idq; huncin finem, ut sciri quovis tempore possit, stellæ, in quibus cœli locis hæ-reant & morentur, alios enim effectus stellas promere ex hoc, aliosq; ex illo loco cœli deprehensum est.
units.tr: Having examined the principal affections of the planets, we must now hasten at full speed to the division of the heaven into 12 houses, or twelve equal sections or parts, and four quadrants. For it matters greatly to know in what space of the heaven each planet moves: whether it keeps to the angles, or is carried outside the angles. For by long and undoubted experience it has been found that the planets, in different places of the heaven, have produced and still produce different effects. When the ancient astronomers noticed this, namely that the wandering stars in the oblique circle, which they later called the zodiac from its twelve figures, stir up various and notable changes and vicissitudes in sublunary bodies, according to their different conjunctions and configurations, partly among themselves and partly also with the stars of the eighth sphere, they first observed the points of the solstices and equinoxes by a certain divine power of mind, and divided that circle into four parts by two colures, and thereby marked the four seasons of the year artfully. Afterwards they subdivided it into twelve equal parts, on account of the twelve lunar and solar synodic months in the year, drawing great circles on both sides through the poles of the zodiac, and determined the beginnings and ends of the individual signs, assigning thirty degrees to each sign, carefully observing which stars were in which parts and of what quality or nature they were. Discovering the various effects of the stars in different parts of the heaven, experience showing the way and sense giving light, they constituted, according to the twelve signs of the zodiac, also twelve places of the heaven, which are called houses and mansions, because in each of these a planet dwells for some time on any day. So, as is commonly agreed, the constitution of the twelve houses of the heaven was first taken from the zodiac. For so Pontanus, book 2, chapter 1, On Celestial Matters: "It happens," he says, "that since the twelve signs constitute the zodiac, the twelve houses or places of the heaven must also be constituted." Therefore, proceeding from the horoscope through the whole circuit of the heaven and returning again, we shall divide it into twelve places; and the space lying between the summit of midheaven and the rising degree we shall call a quadrant, or quadrature, whence the zodiac itself was to be divided into four quarters. For the circle passing through the zenith of our head, or the vertical point, and through the poles of the zodiac, at each moment divides the four quadrants of the heaven. Others divide the whole heaven by the horizon and meridian into four equal quadrants, and afterwards, taking other four circles to these, passing through their common intersection, divide the whole heaven into twelve equal parts, which are called houses; and they do this for this purpose, so that at any time one can know in which places of the heaven the stars are fixed and dwell, for it has been found that stars produce different effects from this place of the heaven and from that.

units.la: Suntigitur domicilia, totius cœli partes duodecimæ: quod-libet autem continet præcisè 30. zodiaci gradus, qui cuspidem domus antecedunt partim, & partim sequuntur, nisi cùm in-ipsa cuspide est primus signi gradus, alias decima extenditur uf-que ad 11. & undecima ufq; ad 12. scilicet per 30. gradus æquatoris. Horum domiciliorum quædam sunt nobiliora & digniora, plusq; potentiæ obtinent, ut 1. 10. 7. & quartum, in his enim Planetæ constituti magnarum sunt virium: dicuntur aliâs cardinalia, quia occupant cœli cardines seu angulos, ut cardo orientis, culmen seu medium cœli, cardo occidentis, & imum cœli, seu angulus terræ. Dignitate his proximè succedunt ea, quæ dicuntur succedentia, ut 2. 11. 8. & 5. Postremum locum obtinent, quæ cadentia dicuntur, quoniam cadunt ab angulis, ut 3. 12. 9. & 6. Ex his omnibus quædam dicuntur infortunata, & abjecta cœli loca, ut sexta, quæ morborum domus, 8. quæ mortis, & 12. quæ carceris & inimicitiarum locus est.
units.tr: The houses, then, are the twelve parts of the whole heaven. Each contains exactly 30 degrees of the zodiac, which partly precede and partly follow the cusp of the house, unless the first degree of a sign lies on the cusp itself. Otherwise the tenth house extends up to the eleventh and the eleventh up to the twelfth, namely through 30 degrees of the equator. Some of these houses are nobler and more worthy and have greater power, such as the 1st, 10th, 7th and 4th, since planets placed in them have great strength. They are otherwise called cardinal, because they occupy the cardines or angles of heaven: the cardo of the East, the midheaven or culmination, the cardo of the West, and the lower heaven, or angle of the earth. Next in dignity come those called succeedent, such as the 2nd, 11th, 8th and 5th. The last place is held by those called cadent, since they fall away from the angles, such as the 3rd, 12th, 9th and 6th. Of all these, some are called unlucky and abject places of heaven: the sixth, the house of sicknesses, the eighth, the house of death, and the twelfth, the place of prison and enmities.

units.la: Prima domus cœli vocatur ascendens, horoscopus (<bl>der[?] auffsteigende ort des Himmels</bl> / tempore horæ natalis) cardo orientis: suâ natura est felix ac fausta (scilicet per se, nam per accidens, ut præsentiâ Saturni vel Martis, potest reddi infausta) phlegmatica, Orientalis, fœminina: ex membris habet caput, oculos, faciem: sumitur ex ea judicium de vita longa vel brevi, temperamento & complexione corporis, ingenio, moribus, & propria nati cujusvis industria. Derisores hujus scientiæ explorent, quid habeant in suo ascendente seu horoscopo: quisquis enim invenerit ibidem Saturnum & Martem cum Mercurio, retrogrado in scorpione, ariete, vel tauro, Luna per sextilem aut trigonum non respiciente, is nulla arte, nulla doctrina, nulla assuefactione, nulla educatione, & nullo, nisi ad Deum fusis precibus, medio, ad ingenii morumq; placiditatem, concinnitatem, & mansuetudinem potest reduci, quantumvis parentes talibus fuerint præditi moribus. Sic multi sunt animi motus impetusque, qui temperamento seu materiæ ex toto assignari non possunt, ut furor Empedoclis, Neronis sævitia, Sophoclis delirium, amentia Luculli, Archimedis melancholia, Sardanapali effœminatio, superbia Thersitis, fraus Sinonis, placiditas, momorumque concinnitas in Lælio, ira Herculis, Bellerophontis mœstitia, Penelopes pudor, Catilinæ crudelitas, & mores posteri: & certè in multis aliis, cumprimis verò Regibus quibusdam & Principibus, generosi quidam, heroici & admirandi deprehenduntur animi impetus ac motus, qui nec temperamento, nec assuefactioni, nec educationi possunt accepti referri, sed ad divinius, quàm sunt elementa & temperamenta, principium sunt referendi.
units.tr: The first house of heaven is called the ascendant, or horoscope (German gloss: the rising point of heaven at the hour of birth), the cardo of the East. By its nature it is lucky and fortunate (that is, in itself; by accident, through the presence of Saturn or Mars, for instance, it can be made unfortunate). It is phlegmatic, Oriental and feminine. Among the body's members it governs the head, eyes and face. From it is taken judgment about a long or short life, the temperament and complexion of the body, intellect, morals, and the individual industry of the one born. Let the mockers of this science examine what they have in their ascendant or horoscope. For whoever finds there Saturn and Mars with Mercury retrograde in Scorpio, Aries or Taurus, with the Moon not aspecting by sextile or trine, can by no art, no teaching, no habituation, no education, and no means except prayers poured out to God, be brought back to a placid, harmonious and gentle disposition of mind and character, however much his parents were endowed with such morals. Thus there are many movements and impulses of the mind which cannot be wholly assigned to temperament or matter: the fury of Empedocles, the savagery of Nero, the madness of Sophocles, the insanity of Lucullus, the melancholy of Archimedes, the effeminacy of Sardanapalus, the pride of Thersites, the treachery of Sinon, the placidity and harmony of character in Laelius, the anger of Hercules, the sadness of Bellerophon, the modesty of Penelope, the cruelty of Catiline, and other such characters. Certainly in many others, especially in certain kings and princes, generous, heroic and admirable impulses and movements of mind are found which cannot be attributed to temperament, habituation or education, but must be referred to a principle more divine than the elements and temperaments.

units.la: Cæterùm in domorum cœlestium constitutione quæritur, cur ab horoscopo potiùs quàm alio cardine, incoaverint numerationem domorum? R.[?] pulcrè & erudite hoc explicat Pont.lib.2.c.2. Cœli pars, inquit, ascendens genituræ tempore, quæ horoscopus Græcè dicitur, primam nati ætatem indicat, culmen, id est, medium cœli ætatem nati ejusdem mediam, occasus ultimam, imum mortem, vitæque ipsius exitum, quiq; post mortem futuri sunt honores aut opprobria. Rectè quidem & appositè hæc omnia. Etenim si cœli stellarumq; motus, orbiculatioq; sunt causa omnium, quæ in mundo sublunari, tum generando, tum corrumpendo fiunt, & est aliquod, ut certè est vitæ principium, quemadmodum homo in lucem & vitam venire dicitur, quo tempore ex utero matris prodit, sic cœli pars ipsa, quæ supra horizontem & terras nunc exit, comitaturque motu atq; adventu suo prodeuntis hominis ex utero motum, videtur primæ hujus commotionis, primæq; ætatis jus judiciumq; penes se merito assumere, quæ vero ei opponitur occidens cœli pars, obitus atq; corruptionis: unde etiam Astrologi omnes maximi faciunt, magnamque vim tribuunt vero ascendentis gradui.
units.tr: But in the constitution of the celestial houses it is asked why the numbering of the houses began from the horoscope rather than from another cardo. I answer that Pont. (book 2, chapter 2) explains this beautifully and learnedly. The part of heaven rising at the time of birth, which is called horoscope in Greek, he says, indicates the first age of the one born; the culmination, that is the midheaven, indicates his middle age; the setting, his last age; the lower heaven, his death and the end of life itself, and the honours or disgraces that will follow after death. All of this is rightly and aptly said. For if the motions and orbits of the heavens and stars are the cause of all that happens in the sublunary world, in generation and in corruption alike, and there is some beginning, as there certainly is for life (just as a man is said to come into light and life at the moment he issues from his mother's womb), then that part of heaven which now rises above the horizon and the earth, accompanying by its motion and arrival the movement of the man coming forth from the womb, seems rightly to claim for itself the right and judgment over this first commotion and first age. The part of heaven opposed to it, the setting, claims the right over death and corruption. Hence all the greatest astrologers also set great store by this, and attribute great power to the degree of the ascendant.

units.la: Diligentissimè enim verum nativitatis tempus inquirendum, priusq; judicium ex astrorum positu instituatur. Ac primo ex Ptolomæo discant artis contemtores, vim cœli tempore ortus seu nativitatis non in momento aliquo diffundi, sed suc-cessivè, quoniam sunt plura initia, quæ temporibus non exiguis differunt. Primum tempus est, cùm fœtus convertitur capite ad inferiora, & se quasi ad exituram præparant. Secundum, cùm aperit os uteri, caputq; exerit, & tunc incipit respirare, & inter utrumque intercedit quandoq; spacium aliquot horarum, & quandoq; etiam dierum, utin[?] iis, qui difficulter pariunt. Ter-tium, cùm totus prodiit ex utero matris. Inter hæc tempora præcipuum est exitus & capitis, & totius, seu totum interval-lum inter exitum capitis & totius infantis, ita ut verum nativi-tatis tempus sit illud, quod comprehenditur inter ascendens na-turale, & finem. Ascendens naturale est, quod semper sumitur à principio respirationis, principium enim nascendi est, cùm incipit infans respirare: medium, cùm ita respirat, ut jam possit per se vivere: finis, cùm jam tantum aëris attraxit, ut arteriæ umbilici sponte sua respirare & moveri cessent, ut ita principiu[?] na-tivitatis, medium & finis sumatur à principali operatione, videlicet respiratione. Licet vero toto ortus sui tempore infans vim acquirat ab astris, præcipuè tamen medium nativitatis tempus exactè investigandum est, gradusq; ascendentis juxta illud in-quirendus. Cùm enim infans jam prodiit, & respirat perfectè, post scilicet abruptionem cotyledonum, infantisq; mundationem, verum & exactum nativitatis tempus, quod scilicet fit in-star hominis originis, dici non potest. Itaq; temporis annotatio ad medium nativitatis principium est dirigenda, & diligentissi-mè ab obstetricibus, aliisq; enixurę astantibus, auxiliumq; præ-bentibus, scíscitandum, partúsne fuerit facilis, nec ne, id est, an longum fuerit intervallum inter tempus, quo primùm capite, & inter tempus, quo totus prodiit: hoc enim cognito, prudens Astrologus verum ascendens facile secundum artis regulas & præcepta inventurus est, id est, tale ascendens, quod partui fit conconforme. Semper enim vera nativitas praecedit illam, quam obstetrices partuiq; assistentes patri gratulabundae annunciant, vera autem nativitas seu genesis est, dum foetus est medius extra, & medius in utero materno, & hoc est principale initium hominis, quod quidem initium plura alia subsequuntur, quae actu in infante antea non erant, ut respiratio per nares & palatum, pulmones, & asperam arteriam, assumtio nutrimenti per os, quae dum in utero adhuc detineretur, natura administrabat per venas & arterias umbilicales: adde ridere, plorare (tametsi quidam plorasse in utero materno crediti sunt pro ostento) lo-qui, uti sensibus exterioribus ac interioribus, ambulare, tussire, sternutare, singultire, titillationem sentire, formare vocem, ex-altare, deprimere, & id genus alia. Unde nativitates Ptolomaeo agunt non tanquam signa, sed solum tanquam causae, in quo multi sunt decepti. Ut autem possit haberi verum ascendens, ad praenoscenda ea, quae nato ex figura & dispositione coeli eventura sunt, veteres varias commenti sunt regulas & modos, quos inter certior est, qui fit ex directionibus notabilis cujus-dam effectus. Dato igitur tempore alicujus nativitatis factae, primum constituenda & erigenda est ejusdem temporis dati, figura coelestis, cum inscriptione omnium Planetarum. Deinde studiose explorandi anni & dies, quibus tali nato adversi quid in corpore acciderit: quibus perceptis, quaero in Ephemeridi-bus, an tali die, quo adversitas illa accidit, ex infortunis aliqua, ut Saturnus vel Mars, feriat gradum ascendentis erectae figurae, vel transitu corporali, vel malo radio: quod si haec ita evene-rint, dico gradum talis infortunae esse verum ascendens nativitatis: Saturnus quidem transitu corporali, vel quadrato oppo-sito suo [?] causatur secundum sui naturam melancholicas tam corporis, quam mentis passiones, Mars vero transiens super ascendens genituræ excitat iracundiam, vulnera, & Martiales infirinfirmitates. Examinandus autem est dominus ascendentis, quando feratur per loca infortunatarum stellarum, vel quando radios malos & infaustos incurrat. Quoniam autem corporis accidentia quædam sunt, quæ non per transitus super ascen-dens, sed per profectiones, vel per directiones significatorum ad promissores contingunt, alia via incedendum est: ac in iis quidem, quæ fiunt per profectiones annuas, diligenter videndum, an annua profectio ascendentis genituræ propositæ, pos-sit pertingere ad corpus vel radios malignos alicujus infortu-næ: & si hoc evenerit, numerandi sunt dies intermedii inter diem nativitatis, & diem accidentis: hi dies postea extendendi per sex, id est, ducendi in sex, & fient sextæ dierum: has sextas dierum divido per 73. (nam 73. sextæ dierum faciunt in annuis profectionum unum gradum) & proveniens numerus ostendet gradus & remanentia minuta: hos gradus & minuta sub-traho à loco promissoris seu significatoris accidentis, & remanebit verus gradus & minutum ascendentis genituræ propositæ: ut sit aliquis natus anno 1477. 16. die Jan. à meridie hor. 11. in latitudine 50. graduum: anno autem completo 58. 1. Jan. ceci-dit de alto ferè funestè, cujus casus causa fuit Saturnus retro-gradus in Leone, & decima domo. Per hunc notabilem casum, qui ita ex radice nativitatis processit, examinandus venit gradus ascendentis genituræ propositæ: reperitur autem annua ascendentis profectio tali anno devoluta ad cancrum, & antequam compleretur annus, pertinget profectio prædicta ad signum Leonis, in quo erat Saturnus in radice nativitatis: jam ergo numerandi dies sunt primò intermedii à die nativitatis in diem Januarii primum, annum scilicet casus, & reperiuntur dies 349. qui per senarium aucti faciunt 2094. sextas scilicet dierum. Hi dividendi per 73. sextas, & emergunt gr. 28. 50. min. qui sub-ducendi à loco promissoris accidentis in propositæ genituræ, scilicet à signis 4. gradibus 20. minutis 32. loci Saturni, & in resi-duo erunt 21. gr. 42. minuta, veri ascendentis gradus, scilicet fi-gni librae. Pro rectificatione vero seu verificatione nativitatis propositae per directionem ascendentis ad infortunas vel ra-dios earum malignos sic procedendum: quaerenda prius ascen-sio obliqua promissoris accidentis pro regionis latitudine est, & ab ea subtrahendi gradus & minuta, qui debentur annis completis a nativitate, usq; ad annum & dies accidentis (nam quilibet annus valet unum gradum, & dies 6. minutum unum in directionibus) & id quod remansit, erit ascensio obliqua a-scendentis veri. Eam ascensionem obliquam quaere in tabula ascensionum obliquarum ejusdem regionis, & invenies verum gradum ascendentis praedictae nativitatis: ut, anno ætatis com-pleto 40. is, cujus genituram nunc rectificandam proposui, sca-bie multum infectus fuit, ulceribus ac apostematibus, aliisque melancholicis affectibus, quod erat notabile accidens de signi-ficatis Saturni. Circa idem tempus passiones etiam febriles ex-pertus est. Examinata directione, gradus ascendentis nativitatis ipsius ad infortunas eodem anno accidentium, repertum est, circa illos dies directionem ascendentis applicuisse ad quadra-turam Saturni, quae erat in 20. gr. 32. min. Scorpii. Hujus ascen-sio obliqua est 250. gr. 46. min. Ab hac subtrahendi propter 40. annos, & 192. dies, gradus 40. minuta 32. & remanebunt 210. gr. 14. min. ascensio scilicet obliqua veri ascendentis, quae ostende-bat 21. gradus, & 40. fere minuta librae, verum nativitatis ascen-dens, eodemq; modo cum aliis etiam promissoribus & signifi-catoribus procedendum est, diligenterq; notandi sunt vario-rum accidentium ac eventuum genera, ex progressionibus sive directionibus ad praecipua in themate seu figura loca, ut ascen-dens, medium coeli, tum etiam ad Solem & Lunam. Quando enim ascendenti per progressionem occurrit Saturnus, ejus qua-dratus, dratus, vel oppositus, portendit is occursus nato frigidos & siccos morbos, melancholicasq; perturbationes. Estq; hic occursus senibus semper fere funestus. Impedit praeterea omnem in consiliis successum, involvitq; natum curis gravioribus, eumq; animi doloribus quasi opprimit. Sed advertendum diligenter hoc est, quod, si ascendenti vel Lunae Saturnus, vel radii ipsius infausti occurrant in signis naturae igneae, ut leone, sagittario, & ariete, minitetur tunc discrasian, frigidiq; & calidi pugnam, quae corpus est infestatura. At si in signis terreis occurserit, ut tauro, virgine, vel capricorno, vitiosa & melancholica apostemata: in signis aeriis, ut geminis, libra & Aquario, excitat flatus corpori noxios, & quandoq; venenatos: in aqueis denique, ut cancro, piscibus & scorpione, phlegmatica vitia progenerat. Interdum deformat nati corpus cicatricibus, aliisq; vitiis, quibus membrum functionem suam amittit, ut in contractionibus, idque efficit in iis partibus corporis, quas ejus signi natura respicit, in quo infaustus iste contingit occursus.
units.tr: For the true time of birth must be inquired into most diligently before any judgement is made from the position of the stars. And first let the despisers of the art learn from Ptolemy that the power of the heavens at the time of birth or nativity is not poured out in a single moment, but successively, since there are several beginnings, which differ from one another by no small intervals of time. The first time is when the foetus turns its head downward and prepares itself, as it were, for leaving. The second is when it opens the mouth of the womb, puts its head out, and then begins to breathe; between these two there sometimes intervenes a space of some hours, and sometimes even of days, as in those who give birth with difficulty. The third is when it has come forth entirely from its mother's womb. Among these times the most important is the emergence of the head, and the whole interval between the emergence of the head and that of the whole infant, so that the true time of birth is that which is comprehended between the natural ascendant and the end. The natural ascendant is that which is always taken from the beginning of respiration, for the beginning of birth is when the infant begins to breathe; the middle is when it breathes in such a way that it can now live on its own; the end is when it has drawn in so much air that the umbilical arteries spontaneously cease to respire and move. Thus the beginning, middle and end of birth are taken from the principal operation, namely respiration. Although, indeed, the infant acquires power from the stars during the whole time of its coming forth, nevertheless the middle time of birth above all must be investigated exactly, and the degree of the ascendant must be sought according to it. For when the infant has now come forth and breathes perfectly, that is, after the separation of the cotyledons and the cleansing of the infant, the true and exact time of birth, which is of course like the origin of a man, can no longer be stated. Therefore the noting of the time is to be directed to the middle beginning of birth, and it must be asked most diligently of the midwives and of the others who stand by the childbirth and give help, whether the delivery was easy or not, that is, whether the interval between the time when the head first emerged and the time when the whole infant came forth was long. For once this is known, the prudent astrologer will easily find the true ascendant according to the rules and precepts of the art, that is, such an ascendant as agrees with the delivery. For the true nativity always precedes that which the midwives and those assisting at the delivery joyfully announce to the father; the true nativity or genesis, however, is when the foetus is half outside and half still in the maternal womb, and this is the principal beginning of the man. Many other things follow this beginning, which in the infant previously did not exist in act: respiration through the nostrils and palate, the lungs and the windpipe, the taking in of nourishment by the mouth, which while it was still detained in the womb nature supplied through the veins and umbilical arteries; add laughing, weeping (although some have been believed to have wept in the maternal womb, as a portent), speaking, the use of the outer and inner senses, walking, coughing, sneezing, hiccupping, feeling tickling, forming the voice, raising up, lowering, and other things of this kind. Hence Ptolemy holds that nativities act not merely as signs but only as causes, in which matter many are deceived. Now, so that the true ascendant may be had, for foreknowing those things which are going to befall the one born from the configuration and disposition of the heavens, the ancients devised various rules and methods, among which the more certain is that which is made from the directions of some notable effect. Therefore, given the time of some birth that has taken place, first the celestial figure of that given time must be set up and erected, with all the planets inscribed.
