Causæ enim potentiores magis movent quàm debiles. Causæ universales sunt potentiores causis propriis. Igitur causæ universales magis movent. Minor probatur, quoniam causæ majorum effectuum potentiores sunt causis effectuum minorum, ergò cùm effectus universales, ut cùm pe-rit una gens tota, & uno prælio multa millia interficiuntur, majores sint effectibus singularibus, ut cùm occidit unus homo, manifestum est propositum. Itaq; quantò effectus sunt univer-saliores, ut si tota Germania affligitur, tantò etiam sunt potentiores & efficaciores causæ, quantò verò debiliores, ut cùm una urbs, vel certæ regionis tractus seu pars fulmine tangitur, eò sunt debiliores. Sic universalis effectus est, quòd non tantùm hic Marpurgi hoc anno arbores florum ubertate luxuriârint, & paulò tamen post continuatis æstibus torrefactæ, ceu quodam uredinis carbone exustæ sint, sed in Hassia tota, imò & extra Hassiam, quoniam scilicet dependet ab universali constitutione à constanti stellarum certarum influxu, & dispositione aëri impressa, id quod serenitatis dierum & noctium præteritarū nunc fere per mensem continuatio demonstrat. Cæterùm universales prædictiones quantitate effectus distinguuntur, unde duæ oriuntur species, magna & levis. Magnam appellat Ptolom. l.2. de judiciis astrorum, c.1. text. 4. quæ omninò præter naturam est, ut inundatio, bellum, pestis, sudor anglicus: Levem, quæ secundum quidem naturam est, sed quantitas immutata, ut immodicæ nives, grandines, pluviæ, æstus, annonæ caritas. Atq; hos effectus vocat Ptolomæus majores, & magis universales, quæ à potentioribus magisq; universalibus causis imprimuntur, quarum etiam scientia prior est minus universalibus. Ut si esset constellatio, quæ Marpurgo significet maximam felicitatem, & sitalia quæ toti Hassiæ bellum indicet exitiale, quomodo quis possit ex constellatione, quæ spectat Marpurgum, divinare felicitatem, quam totius regionis calamitas esset perversura? Hic certè majora, magisq; universalia sunt præferenda specialioribus, cum hac tamen cautela, quòd causarum universalium quædam sint potentes, quædam debiles. Potentes cum potentioribus, & debiles cum debilioribus debent conferri, semper enim generales sunt propriis efficaciores & generalio-res minus generalibus. Sed & hoc diligenter hic notandum venit, quòd debilis universalis non potest vincere validam propriam, ut si constellatio universalis faciat aërem benignum, serenum & salubrem, qualem nunc per integrum feré mensem-sumus experti, aliquis verò ex propria nativitate debeat graviter ægrotare, nō evadet ille quidem à gravi morbo ex toto propter generalem constitutionem, sed minus graviter ægrotabit: similiter si constitutio universalis pestiferos denunciet morbos, non tamen validissima sit, aliquis verò ex nativitate & revolutione debeat optimè valere, omninò non ægrotabit: sin autem universalis impressio sit validissima, licèt ex nativitate quis ægrotare non debuerit, ægrotare tamen potest, propter constitutionem universalem quæ particulari est potentior. Sic, sit futura pesa pestis hoc anno Francofurti multos interfectura, quidam-vero hic Marpurgi ex morbo laterali decumbens, eodem anno moriturus est ob constitutionem propriam, dico quòd facilius sit illum posse evadere à morte, qui decumbit Marpurgi, quàm efficere, ne pestis multos occidat Francofurti, quia comparatio constellationis universalis ad incertam multitudinem, est comparatio ad proprium effectum, sicut geneseos propriæ ad eum, cujus est genesis. Unde pestem Francofurti plures occisurum-verius est, quàm alterum ex morbo laterali moriturum, quia causa, ut dictum, universalis comparata ad proprium effectum, potentior est quàm propria ad illum, qui laborat pleuritide. Quod si verò comparatio instituatur utriusq; constitutionis ad eundem hominem, qui laterum morbo decumbit, tunc sic oportet distinguere: Vel enim genitura ejus est valdè conjuncta cum universali constitutione, & tunc potentior est universalis & certior, vel parum conjuncta, & tunc propria prævalet universali. Ideoq; ille, qui ægrotat tempore pestis, & moritur, habuit conjunctam constitutionem propriam cum universali, sin autem evadit, parum fuit conjuncta, aut omninò repugnavit propria nativitas. Atque hæc causa est, cur pestis tempore quidam etiam procul fugientes, & absentes moriantur, quia scilicet habent dispositionem propriam conjunctam cum universali, vel etiam universali planè non repugnantem: sic qui evasit è navi, quæ submersa in mari est, aut è prælio, in quo plurimi interficiuntur ( his enim duobus argumentis legitur Lutherus sæpiùs exagitasse Phil.Melanchthonem[?], ut etiam aliquando in-hunc sarcasmum proruperit: Dn. Philippe, hanc mihi nucem-frange, persuasum enim sibi habebat, Prognosticum Astrologicum planè illis prosterni) habuit constitutionem repugnantem submersioni, quamvis illa evasio non fuerit sine periculo, ideoqueistud habet aliquid annexum cum scientia fati. An enimqui submerguntur in navi, aut in prælio interficiuntur, habeant hoc ex genitura sua, an vero tribuendus casus sit horæ discessus vel ingressus in navim, vel etiam tempori constructionis navis, quæstio est multorum animos suspendens, item, an si in navi sit unus, vel etiam plures, quibus propria constitutio & nativitas denunciet eo tempore, quo navim conscendunt, ventisq; se committunt, suffocationem in aquis, an, inquam, unius hujus, vel etiam trium causa tota navis cum multis aliis, quibus nullum aquæ periculu ex propria constitutione metuendum fuit, sit peritura? Cui quæstioni ex Astrologicis principiis sic occurrendum est, licet genituræ hominum, quid cuiq; eventuru sit, plerumq; decernant, tamen in constitutione universali, & magna, ut in navi submergenda, civitate destruenda, exercitum profligando, necessario etiam ii intereunt, qui cum universali constitutione nihil habent commune, qui autem evadunt, dominum & præsidem genituræ vel habent potentiorem Domino universalis constitutionis, vel præses genituræ est etiam dominus ipsius constitutionis universalis, maxime si fuerit benefi-cus: si enim maleficus extiterit, servabitur quidem, sed paulo tamen post calamitosam experietur hypostrophen. Sic, qui exit e patria sua peste afflicta, evadit periculum, nisi habeat genituram conjunctam constitutioni, quæ respicit patriam, ut ita futuris eventibus quis maxime etiam subjiciatur secundum naturam & dispositionem loci, in quo habitat. Est enim omni scientia dignum hoc, quod omnis homo, ubicunq; natus fit, illius loci habeat connexam constitutionem, quoniam stellæ verticales, & altitudo poli sunt eædem illi, & loco, in quo natus est, & similiter dominus trianguli dominatur illi. Verum universa-les causæ singulis hominibus, ut Socrati, Platoni, applicari non possunt, generales enim constitutiones impetus suos effundunt in multitudinem incertam, quod manifestum ex ipsis eventibus est, nam in quibuscunque calamitatibus publicis videmus multos omnino interire, paucos vero affici, sed non interire, ut in peste aegrotare, in civitatum direptionibus spoliari, capi, vel vulnerari, plures etiam evadere omnino illaesos, ac si nihil mali civitas esset perpessa, aliquos etiam melius se habere ex propriae civitatis calamitate, veluti ditari, observari, honorari, magistratum inire: unde illorum genesi constat constellationem convenire, his vero non. Ut igitur contingat effectus, necesse est, ut propria genesis concordet cum civitate, in qua degit ille, cujus est genesis. Non enim afficiuntur homines a generalibus constitutionibus, nisi afficiatur civitas: unde quilibet fere potest ejusmodi generalia infortunia evitare mutando regionem & civitatem, nisi fit connexus mutuus per ascendens, & infortuniorum significatores ac promissores. Hic igitur inprimis etiam fixarum stellarum vires ad regiones sunt traducendae. Sicut enim cuique regioni suum est signum, & suus Planeta, qui signo praeest, ita fixae non ex dominio signi, siquidem non dominantur signis, sed ex loco adjunguntur: ut, oculus tauri tempore Ptolomaei erat in tauro, & ita afficiebat Cyprum, & maritima loca Asiae minoris, nunc afficit Hircanos, Armenios & Aegyptios, quia hodie est in Geminos ingressus. Eodem modo cor scorpii olim existens in scorpio afficiebat Syriam, Mauros, & Cappadocas, nunc vero Hispaniam, Galliam, Celticam, & in ea Lutetiam, Nortmannos, & Brittannos Galliae, recessit enim hodie in sagittarium, qui, quoniam Jovis domicilium est, malignitatem ejus aliqua ex parte videtur correxisse, ut ita mirum videri non debeat, cur hodie longe alii stellarum fixarum vires, quam olim, deprehendantur. Atq; hinc patescit, universales constitutiones non sufficere ad divinandum de singulis hominibus, quia non semper conveniunt cum loco, in quo habitat homo ille, tum etiam, quod quandoq; adeo sunt potentes, ut plane evertant propriam illius constitutionem, seu principium genethliacum, idq; disponant secundum naturam dispositionis universalis. Particularis igitur & propria constitutio, quam scilicet quis ex nativitate est consecutus, universalis magnitudine oppressa vel interrupta, alios quandoq; sortitur eventus, quam ipsa genitura decrevit. Cæterum non ignorandum hic universalem constitutionem regionum non solum ad privatos, sed etiam ad Reges pertinere & magnates. Nam Scotiæ Reges fere omnes ferro pereunt, adeò, ut ex centum quinque vix 5. morbo perierint. Imò ex Jacobi nomine omnes violentam mortis sortem sunt experti. Nam Jac. 1. à familiaribus conjuratis in cubiculo trucidatus est. 2. diffracti ænei tormenti ictu ad castellum quod oppugnabat, interemtus. 3. à filio ad Sterlingum justa acie victus & interfectus. 4. In bello Gallico à Surejo, Britanniæ duce, cum magna clade occisus. 5. à Maria Regina veneno sublatus est, teste Buchan. 6. est adhuc in vivis, quem Deus Ecclesiæ & Reipubl. clementer conservet. Anglorum Reges fere omnes seditionibus agitantur. Gallorum autem ab utrisq; fuerunt immunes, & constitutionem generalem habent faventiorem ac mitiorem, plerumq; tamen in bellis capiuntur, & iterum salvi dimittuntur. Unde Franciscus I. Rex Gallorum, non obiit in prælio anno 1525. cum captus fuit à Cæsarianis, inq; Hispaniam deductus, nec seditione fuit exturbatus à duce Borbonio, nec mortuus in carcere Hispanico, nam in his omnibus regnum, & constitutio universalis servavit Regem, non Rex regnum. Johannes quoq; Vallesius, Galliæ Rex, captus & dimissus est. In duobus tamen Henricis propria genesis & constitutio parum fuit conjuncta cum universali constellatione, unde etiam propria prævaluit universali, juxta præc. supra traditum, nam uterq; in propria genitura mortis significatores habuit violen-tos, & calamitosi exitus prænuncios. Suecorum Reges ut pluri-mùm mùm universali constitutione turbulentantur. Danorum vero mitiori fato fere semper usi sunt, nisi quòd Christiernus in car-cere obiit. Memorabile est, quod etiam refert Joh. à Wower in Panegyrico suo scripto ad Dan. Regem Christianum IV. Daniæ Reges intrepido semper animo & pectore per maria inerrasse, animiq; magnitudine in mari persæpe ostedifse[?], ipsosq; gubernaculis assedisse, fluitantia vela collegisse, summum navis fasti-gium conscendisse (quod hisce meis oculis fecisse vidi Christia-num IV. adhuc in vivis, & quidem tam expedita velocitate, ut qui astarent omnes ad stuporem usq; admirarentur) ut ita ma-ria quasi ipsos venerentur, ferìq; fluctus imperio eorum se sub-jicere videantur, ita quidem, ut vix hominum memoria audi-tum sit, unum animam mari commendasse. Est in memoria proximorum annorum, Christianum IV. cùm remotas regni sui partes inviseret, cymba ex more per mare vagatum esse, & sollicitante aura longiùs provectum, mox verò contentioso fluctu convulsa maria inhorruisse, nubesq; coelo obductas in-ternitetem[?] diem suppressisse. Cumq; jam spumantes undarum vertices obnoxiam navis partem hucilluc converterent, quò cursum flecteret gubernator, ignorabat, omnesq; jam timen-da mortis imagine comites nautæq; sanguinem & calorem amiserant, ecce intrepida mente validaq; manu Rex periclitan-tibus succurrit, & spiritum metu submotū omnibus reddidit, reluctantesq; ventos obliquata velificatione domat, fluctusq; obvia molitione & conatu frangit, magnanimam in hoc peri-culo talem vocem emittens, non præbituram fortunam hoc casus ludibrium, ut Reges animam fluctibus deberent, quæ certè vox intrepidi pectoris fuit nuncia, & digna, quæ annalium mo-nimentis consignetur. Hactenus de universali Astrologiæ par-te, quæ spectat, gentes, regna, regiones, & urbes: sequitur par-ticularis, quæ singulorum hominum fata ac eventus ex genitura inquirit, quid scilicet quoad vitam, vitæq; accidentia, ut tem-peramenta, ingenia, morbos, dignitates, itinera, amicitias, ini-micitias, & mortem, mortisq; genus, ex astrorum positu sit e-venturum. In qua quidem divinandi parte hoc primo atten-dendum, non referenda ad sidera esse omnes omnium homi-num actiones & eventus, nec ex astris omnia prædici posse nec debere (ut Ægyptii & Hebræi falsò somniabant, unde etiam to-ties in sacris literis eorum divinationes superstitiosæ damnatæ, propterea quòd artis principiis perversè utebantur, ad impo-sturas scilicet & superstitiones, unde ipsa etiam ars merito à Pro-phetis tanquam sortilega, & malè utentium vanitatibus con-spurcata, damnabatur) sed eos tantum, quorum causæ & signa in astris conspiciuntur, nam horum consideratio divinorum o-perum est aspectio & contemplatio. Itaq; pius & verus Astro-logus non evagatur extra & ultra cœlos. Non affirmanda sunt ea, quæ à potestate astrorum oriri non possunt, nec miscendæ sortes, & ejusmodi genera divinationum, quæ Ptolomæus vo-cat ἀναλογιστικά[?]. Galenus, præter Hippocr. autor gravissimus, ani-mantium corpora affici à luminibus cœli affirmat, magnamq; vim omnium Planetarum esse in temperamentis & miscendis & turbandis, & quidem graviter reprehendit eos, qui dissen-tiunt, ait enim manifestam experientiam hanc vim siderum te-stari, & Sophisticum esse eam negare, cum certò constet, multa judicari posse, & judicata esse ex positu astrorum de valetudine corporum, ingeniorum diversitate & natura, multisq; in vita casibus & eventibus, quarum rerum consideratio plurimum conducit prudentibus, in officio constitutis, & ad Reipubl. gu-bernacula sedentibus. Magni, inquam, interest scire, quo quis loco seu parte cœli tempore genituræ seu exitus è claustro ma-terno habuerit, Saturnum, Jovem, Martem, Lunam vel Solem, plurimum enim id conducit ad vitæ actiones, animiq; motus moderandos atque temperandos. Mars in angulo occidentis cum Luna quoties fuit multis calamitosus? Saturnus in eodem loco, quoties fuit multis funestus? si vellem per geniturarum variarum exempla procedere, dies me deficeret. Si multi scirent locum Saturni vel Martis tempore geniturarum suarum, vehe-mentiores animi impetus saepe refrenarent, mentemq; eorum domaret respectus honesti. Sapientis igitur est aspicere natu-ram suam, major tamen sapientia est adjungere Rectorem Deum, ut, si quid mali aut astrorum positus, aut inclinatio na-turae minitetur, sciamus Deum posse & velle, piis tamen preci-bus exoratum, moderari eventus ac mitigare. Vere igitur dixit Ptolomaeus, sapientem animam adjuvare coelestem operatio-nem, non secus ac optimus agricola arando, expurgandoq; ad-juvat naturam. Hoc latissimè, Auditores, patet in cura valetu-dinis, in deligendo vitæ genere, in suscipiendis negotiis vel con-venientibus, vel abhorrentibus a natura & ingenio. Si Curionis aut Antonii parentes satis intellexissent naturam & ingenium filiorum, flectere singulari arte fera & inquieta ingenia ad mo-derationem potuissent. Philippum Macedonem legimus Re-gem imprimis callidum, cum animadvertisset in filio Alexan-dro non sane pravam, sed tamen asperiorem & impatientem imperii naturam esse, videretq; cum non pati domitorem aspe-rum, coepit consilium, doctrina & Philosophia flectendi eum ad suavitatem & comitatem, qua etiam ratione adeo excoluit illam naturam, ut in ipso victoriarum cursu vix quisquam fue-rit unquam humanior, ut ita videre prosit, quo quisq; inclinet, quoq; quemquam ducat natura, ut disciplina idonea ad virtu-tem flectatur, & a vitiis abducatur. Non certè contemnendæ sunt conversionum, revolutionum, progressionumq; annua-rum, nec non conjunctionum magnarum indicationes & si-gnificationes, experientiæ testimonio confirmatæ ac stabilitæ, tum etiam rationibus à priori collectis, quæ duo, λόγῳ[?] & περὶ[?] omnium artium sunt κεφάλαια[?]. Ac licet Prognosticum Genethliacum apodixes non habet à priori ita illustres, firmas, explicatas-que, & è causis extructas, non tamen destituitur altero ἀποδείξεων[?] genere, τὸ δὲ ἐκ[?] ex effectis texto, quo utimur, cùm illis destituimur, aut nō abundamus. Id, si quis negaverit, & tollet τὴν[?] omnem, fereq;omnem Physicam abolebit. Et certè manent certæ notitiæ, notitiarumq; certitudo, manet evidentia & firmitas demonstrationum, videlicet tali vel tali positu cœlestes causas, eàsdem semper idoneo subjecto, in quod vires intendunt, ἀνα-μεῖς[?] inferre, effectusq; ciere mirificos in naturis sublunaribus notitiæ, quæ cùm sint experientia duce, & ratione magistra acquisitæ ac exploratæ, demonstrationum vim acceperunt.
units.tr: Puffed up with this conviction, they advance against astrology with wagons full of arguments, so that one might wonder how anyone can muster such weapons against the art, which nonetheless remains standing and unshaken, and is not weakened in the least. For it has never feared them, and it has never given up anything of its truth. So much so that you would rightly call it like a palm tree, which rises higher the more weight is laid upon it. They ought rather to consider that one should not lightly depart from the judgements of the most learned and wise of men, who, having come to know the usefulness and practice of this art, judged it worth handing down to posterity as useful for life. It is arrogance, combined with great folly, to hunt for a trophy of glory by attacking and harassing arts that have been accepted on the authority and judgement of learned and prudent men, and fortified by the examples and testimonies of reasoned experience of undoubted reliability. Therefore, since these slanderers, like dogs that always return to their vomit, are free to come back, and since I see that their calumnies can easily be cut away and rooted out, I have thought it useful and very necessary to stop the mouths of ... [the obscure word], to free the minds of many from error, and to restore to this divine art its former honour and glory. But what, and of what kind, is astrology? It is the art of divining and judging, from the motion, position and rays of the stars, the events in the sublunary world that are to come. It has (by the agreement of the more famous authors) two parts: the universal and the particular. For the effects of the heavenly bodies, as related to the subjects they act upon, are considered in two ways: namely, as they extend over wide tracts of air and land and affect the things below the moon, or as they are impressed on the bodies of individual men. The universal part reveals the fates of whole peoples, regions and cities; the special or particular part reveals the fates of individual men, and is called genethliacal from the birth-charts (genitures), and its exact knowledge cannot be had unless one has knowledge of the universal, because universal things are moved by their causes with greater force and efficacy. For more powerful causes move more than weak ones. Universal causes are more powerful than their own particular causes. Therefore universal causes move more. The minor premise is proved as follows: the causes of greater effects are more powerful than the causes of lesser effects. Since universal effects, such as when a whole nation perishes, or many thousands are killed in one battle, are greater than individual effects, such as when one man dies, the proposition is clear. Hence the more universal the effect, for example if the whole of Germany is afflicted, the more powerful and efficacious are its causes; and the weaker the causes, the more limited the effect, as when one city, or one part or tract of a certain region, is struck by lightning. So it is a universal effect that not only here at Marburg this year the trees grew lush with abundant blossom and then, after the heat had continued for some time, were scorched as if burnt by a coal of mildew, but that the same happened over the whole of Hesse, and even beyond Hesse, because it depends on the universal constitution, on the constant influx of certain stars, and on the disposition impressed on the air. This is shown by the continuation of the fair days and nights of the past weeks, which has now lasted nearly a month. Moreover, universal predictions are distinguished by the quantity of the effect, whence arise two kinds, great and small. Ptolemy, in the second book of his Judgements of the Stars, chapter one, text four, calls great those effects that are wholly against nature, such as a flood, war, plague, or the English sweating sickness. Small are those that are indeed according to nature, but unusual in amount, such as excessive snows, hail, rains, heat, or dearth of grain. Ptolemy calls these effects greater and more universal, and they are impressed by more powerful and more universal causes, and knowledge of them comes earlier than knowledge of less universal things. Suppose there were a constellation that signified the greatest happiness for Marburg, and yet another that announced a deadly war for all of Hesse: how could anyone divine, from the constellation that regards Marburg, a happiness that the calamity of the whole region would overturn? Here, certainly, the greater and more universal things are to be preferred to the more particular, with this caution, however: some universal causes are powerful and some weak. Powerful causes must be compared with more powerful ones, and weak with weaker ones, for the general causes are always more efficacious than the particular, and the more general more efficacious than the less general. But here it must also be carefully noted that a weak universal cause cannot overcome a strong particular one. For example, if a universal constellation makes the air mild, clear and healthy, as we have now experienced for almost a whole month, yet someone, by his own birth-chart, ought to fall seriously ill, he will indeed not escape a grave sickness altogether, because of the general constitution, but he will be ill less severely. Likewise, if the universal constitution foretells pestilential diseases, but is not very strong, and someone by his birth and revolution ought to enjoy the best of health, he will not be ill at all. But if the universal impression is very strong, then even though by his birth he ought not to fall ill, he can still fall ill, on account of the universal constitution, which is more powerful than the particular. Thus: suppose a plague is to come this year at Frankfurt and kill many, while someone here at Marburg, lying ill with pleurisy, is to die in the same year because of his own constitution. I say that it is easier for the man who lies sick at Marburg to escape death than to prevent the plague from killing many at Frankfurt. For the comparison of a universal constellation with an uncertain multitude is a comparison with a proper effect, just as the birth-chart of an individual is compared with the person whose chart it is. Hence it is more true that the plague will kill many at Frankfurt than that another man will die of pleurisy, because the universal cause, as said, when compared with its proper effect, is more powerful than the particular cause is with the man who suffers from pleurisy. But if the comparison is made between both constitutions and the same man who is lying sick of a disease of the side, then the distinction must be made as follows: either his birth-chart is closely connected with the universal constitution, and then the universal is more powerful and more certain; or it is only weakly connected, and then the particular prevails over the universal. Therefore the man who falls ill at the time of the plague and dies had a particular constitution closely connected with the universal; but if he survives, it was only weakly connected, or his own nativity was entirely opposed to it. And this is the reason why, at the time of plague, some people die even when they flee far away and are absent, namely because they have a personal disposition connected with the universal, or one not at all opposed to the universal. So too with the man who escaped from a ship that sank at sea, or from a battle in which very many are killed. (It is on these two arguments that Luther is said to have often harassed Philip Melanchthon, so that he once burst out with this sarcasm: "Master Philip, crack this nut for me," for he was persuaded that the astrological prognostic was utterly overthrown by these examples.) This man had a constitution that resisted drowning, although that escape was not without danger; and so this has something attached to knowledge of fate. For it is doubtful whether those who sink in a ship, or are killed in battle, have this from their birth-chart, or whether the event should be assigned to the chance of the hour of departure or embarkation on the ship, or even to the time when the ship was built. This question keeps the minds of many in suspense. Likewise: if there is one person, or even several, on a ship whose own constitution and birth indicate, at the time they go aboard and trust themselves to the winds, that they will be suffocated in the waters, then will the whole ship, with many others for whom no danger from the water was to be feared by their own constitution, perish because of this one person, or three? To this question, from astrological principles, the answer must be given as follows. Although the birth-charts of men mostly determine what will happen to each, nevertheless in a universal and great constitution, as when a ship is to sink, a city to be destroyed, or an army to be routed, those also necessarily perish who have nothing in common with the universal constitution; but those who escape have as the lord and guardian of their birth-chart either a lord more powerful than the lord of the universal constitution, or the guardian of their chart is also the lord of that universal constitution itself, especially if he is a benefic. For if he is a malefic, the man will indeed be saved, but after a little while he will experience a calamitous reversal. So too, the man who leaves his fatherland afflicted by plague escapes the danger, unless he has a birth-chart connected with the constellation that governs his fatherland. For thus a man is most subject to future events according to the nature and disposition of the place in which he lives. For it is worthy of all knowledge that every man, wherever he is born, has the constitution of that place connected with him, since the vertical stars and the altitude of the pole are the same for him and for the place where he was born, and similarly the lord of the triangle rules over him. But universal causes cannot be applied to individual men, such as Socrates or Plato, for general constitutions pour out their force upon an uncertain multitude. This is clear from the events themselves: for in any public calamities we see that many perish altogether, while a few are affected but do not perish: they fall ill in a plague, are robbed, captured or wounded in the sacking of cities, while many others escape entirely unharmed, as if the city had suffered no evil; some even fare better from the calamity of their own city, as by growing rich, being noticed, honoured, or entering public office. Hence it is clear that the constellation agrees with the birth-charts of the former, but not of the latter. So, for an effect to come about, it is necessary that one's own birth-chart agree with the city in which the man whose chart it is lives. For men are not affected by general constitutions unless the city is affected. Hence almost anyone can avoid such general misfortunes by changing region and city, unless there is a mutual connection through the ascendant and the significators and promisers of misfortunes. Here, therefore, above all the powers of the fixed stars must also be transferred to regions. For just as every region has its own sign and its own planet that presides over the sign, so the fixed stars act not by lordship over the sign (since they do not rule the signs), but by the place they occupy. Thus the Eye of the Bull, in Ptolemy's time, was in Taurus and affected Cyprus and the seacoasts of Asia Minor; now it affects the Hyrcanians, Armenians and Egyptians, because today it has entered Gemini. In the same way the Heart of the Scorpion, once in Scorpio, affected Syria, the Moors and the Cappadocians, but now affects Spain, Gaul, Celtica, and within it Lutetia, the Normans and the Britons of Gaul; for today it has withdrawn into Sagittarius, which, because it is the house of Jupiter, seems to have partly corrected the malignity of the star. So it ought not to seem surprising why today quite different powers of the fixed stars are found than formerly. And from this it is evident that universal constitutions are not sufficient for divining about individual men, both because they do not always agree with the place where that man lives, and also because sometimes they are so powerful that they utterly overturn his own constitution, or his birth-principle, and arrange it according to the nature of the universal disposition. Therefore the particular and personal constitution, which a man has obtained from his birth, when it is overwhelmed or interrupted by the magnitude of the universal, sometimes receives other outcomes than the birth-chart itself had decreed. Yet it must not be overlooked here that the universal constitution of regions pertains not only to private persons but also to kings and nobles. For almost all the kings of Scotland perish by the sword, so that of one hundred and five scarcely five died of disease. Indeed, all those of the name James have experienced a violent fate. For James I was slaughtered in his bedchamber by conspirators who were his own courtiers. Second, he was killed by the blow of a burst bronze cannon, before the castle he was besieging. Third, he was defeated and killed by his son at Stirling in a proper battle line. Fourth, in the French war he was slain with great slaughter by Surrey, the duke of Britain. Fifth, he was carried off by poison given by Queen Mary, as Buchanan testifies. Sixth, he is still alive, whom God mercifully preserve for the Church and the commonwealth. Almost all the kings of England are harassed by sedition. The kings of France, however, were free from both, and have a more favourable and milder general constitution. Nevertheless they were often taken captive in wars, and then released unharmed. Hence Francis I, king of the French, did not die in battle in the year 1525, when he was captured by the Imperialists and led into Spain; nor was he driven from his kingdom by sedition under the duke of Bourbon, nor did he die in a Spanish prison. For in all these things the kingdom and the universal constitution preserved the king; the king did not preserve the kingdom. John of Valois, also king of France, was captured and released. But in the two Henries, their own birth-chart and constitution were only weakly connected with the universal constellation, and therefore their own prevailed over the universal, according to the rule set out above; for each of them had violent significators of death in his own nativity, and forewarnings of a calamitous end. The kings of Sweden are for the most part disturbed by the universal constitution. The kings of Denmark, however, have had an almost always milder fate, except that Christian (II) died in prison. It is worth remembering what John à Wower also relates in his panegyric written to King Christian IV of Denmark: the Danish kings have always wandered over the seas with a fearless spirit and courage, have often shown their greatness of mind at sea, have sat at the helm themselves, gathered the floating sails, and climbed to the very top of the ship's mast (which I saw Christian IV do with my own eyes, while he is still alive, and indeed with such quick agility that all who stood by were amazed to the point of astonishment), so that the seas seem as it were to revere them, and the waves seem to submit to their command. So much so that scarcely within human memory has it been heard that anyone entrusted his life to the sea. Within the memory of recent years, when Christian IV was visiting the distant parts of his kingdom, it is recorded that the boat drifted over the sea as usual, and, driven by a favouring breeze, was carried rather far out; but soon the sea, stirred up by contrary waves, bristled, and clouds covering the sky hid the day in eternal darkness. And when the foaming crests of the waves were turning the exposed part of the ship this way and that, the helmsman did not know which way to steer; and all his companions and sailors, already overcome by the image of dreaded death, had lost their blood and warmth. Then, with a fearless mind and a strong hand, the king came to the aid of those in peril, restored courage to all whose fear had been removed, and tamed the resisting winds by slanting the sails, and broke the waves by a hostile effort and struggle, uttering in this danger a magnanimous word: that fortune would not offer this chance as a plaything, so that kings should give up their lives to the waves. Certainly that word was a messenger of a fearless heart, and worthy to be recorded in the monuments of the annals. So far concerning the universal part of astrology, which regards nations, kingdoms, regions and cities. There follows the particular part, which inquires into the fates and events of individual men from their birth-chart, namely what will come about from the position of the stars concerning life and the accidents of life, such as temperaments, talents, diseases, dignities, journeys, friendships, enmities, death, and the kind of death. In this part of divination, the first thing to be noted is this: not all the actions and events of all men are to be referred to the stars, nor can and ought all things to be predicted from the stars (as the Egyptians and Hebrews falsely dreamed; whence in the sacred letters their superstitious divinations are so often condemned, because they misused the principles of the art, namely for impostures and superstitions; and so the art itself was rightly condemned by the Prophets as sorcery, and defiled by the vanities of those who misused it). Rather, only those are to be referred to the stars whose causes and signs are seen in the stars; for the consideration of these is the observation and contemplation of divine works. Thus the pious and true astrologer does not wander outside and beyond the heavens. What cannot arise from the power of the stars must not be affirmed, nor should lots be mixed in, nor divinations of that kind which Ptolemy calls analogistic [ἀναλογιστικά]. Galen, besides Hippocrates, a most weighty authority, affirms that the bodies of animals are affected by the lights of heaven, and that all the planets have great power in mixing, tempering and disturbing the temperaments; and indeed he sharply rebukes those who dissent. For he says that clear experience bears witness to this power of the stars, and that it is sophistical to deny it, since it is certain that many things can be judged, and have been judged, from the position of the stars concerning the health of bodies, the diversity and nature of talents, and many chances and events in life. The consideration of these things is of great use to prudent men who hold office and sit at the helm of the commonwealth. It is of great importance, I say, to know in what place or part of the heavens, at the time of one's birth or one's exit from the maternal womb, one had Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Moon or the Sun; for this contributes greatly to moderating and tempering the actions of life and the motions of the mind. How often has Mars in the western angle with the Moon been calamitous for many? How often has Saturn in the same place been deadly for many? If I wished to proceed through examples of various birth-charts, the day would fail me. If many knew the place of Saturn or Mars at the time of their birth, they would often restrain the more violent impulses of their minds, and regard for what is honourable would tame them. It is therefore the mark of a wise man to look to his own nature; but greater wisdom is to join God, the ruler, so that if the position of the stars or the inclination of nature threatens any evil, we may know that God can and will moderate and mitigate the events, if he is entreated by pious prayers. Rightly therefore did Ptolemy say that a wise soul helps the heavenly operation, just as the best farmer helps nature by ploughing and clearing. This, listeners, is evident most widely in the care of health, in choosing a way of life, and in undertaking business that agrees or disagrees with one's nature and talent. If the parents of Curio or Antony had understood sufficiently the nature and talent of their sons, they could have bent wild and restless talents to moderation by a singular art. We read that Philip of Macedon was a king especially shrewd: when he noticed that in his son Alexander the nature was not wicked indeed, but rather harsh and impatient of rule, and saw that he would not tolerate a harsh tamer, he began to plan how to bend him to gentleness and courtesy by teaching and philosophy. By this method he so cultivated that nature that, in the very course of his victories, there was hardly anyone more humane. So it is useful to see toward what each man inclines, and to what nature leads him, so that suitable instruction may be bent toward virtue and drawn away from vices. Certainly the indications and significations of conversions, revolutions and annual progressions, as well as of great conjunctions, confirmed and established by the testimony of experience, are not to be despised, nor are the reasons gathered a priori; these two are the principal headings [κεφάλαια] of all the arts, the one by reasoning [λόγῳ] and the other concerning [περὶ]. And although the genethliacal prognostic does not have demonstrations a priori so clear, firm and explained, and built from causes, it is not for that reason deprived of the other kind of demonstration, the one from effects [ἐκ τῶν ἔργων], which we use in the text when we lack or do not abound in the former. If anyone denies this, he will remove all [τὴν] and will well-nigh abolish all of physics. And certainly there remain certain notions, the certainty of those notions, and the evidence and firmness of demonstrations: namely that such and such a position of the celestial causes always brings forth the same effects in a suitable subject upon which their powers are directed, and that the notions of marvellous effects are stirred up in sublunary natures. These notions, since they have been acquired and tested with experience as guide and reason as teacher, have received the force of demonstrations.

units.la: 1. Sic notum est ac certum, Martis cum Venere congres-sus naturas salaces, inq; Venerem gignere proclives.
units.tr: 1. It is known and certain that the nature of Mars joined with Venus is lustful, and that it is inclined to produce lust in Venus.

units.la: 2. Certum est ac notum, Lunam in cancro & tertia domo, Saturnum in libra & sexta domo, immoderatam frigiditatem, humidamq; intemperiem in cerebro operari, ratione Lunæ, pectus angustum ac debile ob qualitates easdem, immoderatam pituitam ob calorem naturalem debilem, unde spirandi difficultas, & tandem tabes corporisq; extenuatio succedunt: sic ergo ex cancri & Saturni immoderata frigiditate & humiditate, secundo ex ipsius Lunæ natura in cancro, tertio ex robore Saturni in libra, & quarto ex sexta domo, quæ morbos significat, deniq; ratione primarum qualitatum in tabis cognitionem devenitur: quas progressiones annotari diligenter oportet, ut artis hujus calumniatores videant esse φυσικὸν[?] ἐ[?] ... ἀστρολογ-ικὸν[?] καὶ τέχνην[?] ἀληθέστατον[?].
units.tr: 2. It is certain and known that the Moon in Cancer and the third house, and Saturn in Libra and the sixth house, produce an immoderate coldness and a moist disorder in the brain. By reason of the Moon, the chest becomes narrow and weak because of the same qualities, and an excess of phlegm arises from weak natural heat, whence comes difficulty in breathing and at last consumption and wasting of the body. Thus, from the immoderate cold and moisture of Cancer and Saturn, secondly from the nature of the Moon itself in Cancer, thirdly from the strength of Saturn in Libra, and fourthly from the sixth house, which signifies sickness, and finally from the primary qualities, knowledge of consumption is reached. These steps ought to be carefully noted, so that the slanderers of this art may see that it is physical [φυσικὸν], astrological [ἀστρολογικὸν] and the most true [ἀληθέστατον] art [τέχνην].

units.la: 3. Certum est ac notum, tria facere ad hyemis temperiem, Martem in cancro & leone, Saturnum in aquario, & Jovem cum Sole, nam Saturnus, cùm plurimum abest, frigus augere nequit, Mars vero est parvus quidam Sol, denique Jupiter cum Sole calorem illius maxime fovet.
units.tr: 3. It is certain and known that three things contribute to the mildness of winter: Mars in Cancer and Leo, Saturn in Aquarius, and Jupiter with the Sun. For Saturn, when it is very far away, cannot increase the cold; Mars is in a sense a little Sun; and finally Jupiter with the Sun greatly fosters the Sun's heat.

units.la: 4. Sic notum est hyemem sævam, & æstatem temperatam, contrariis de causis accidere, ut si Sol, Mars, Jupiter absint in aquario, & Saturnus sit in cancro vel leone.
units.tr: 4. Thus it is known that a harsh winter and a temperate summer arise from contrary causes, namely if the Sun, Mars and Jupiter are absent in Aquarius, and Saturn is in Cancer or Leo.

units.la: 5. Sic, quantò fidus [?] est majus, ac motus velocior, eò etiam fideris [?] opera sunt manifestiora, ut opera Solis manifestissima sunt, postea Lunæ, inde Veneris, postea Mercurii, ut enim Mercurius celerior est, ita Venus robustior ob magnitudinem, inde Saturnus, & post Jupiter, eaq; omnia in comparatione ad Solem, Mars vero habet obscuriora opera, quia serius Soli jungitur, atq; etiam ipso Jove minor est.
units.tr: 5. Likewise, the greater a star is and the swifter its motion, the more evident are the effects of that star. Thus the works of the Sun are most evident, after them those of the Moon, then those of Venus, then those of Mercury. For as Mercury is swifter, so Venus is stronger because of its size; then Saturn, and after it Jupiter. All these are compared with the Sun. Mars, however, has less obvious works, because it joins the Sun later and is also smaller than Jupiter itself.

units.la: 6. Planetæ in opposito vel quadrato Solis, si fuerint in ipsis punctis, ita se habent: in primo stationis primæ puncto tanto sunt calidiores, quanto humidiores, in secundo, tanto calidiores, quanto ficciores [?].
units.tr: 6. Planets in opposition or square to the Sun, if they are exactly at these points, are disposed thus: at the first point of the first station they are as much hotter as they are moister; at the second, they are hotter in proportion as they are drier.

units.la: 7. Cor cœli validius est omnibus, postea ascendens, sed in vita & affectibus animi, corporisq; dispositionibus, ascendens est validius, postea domus 7.4.11.9.2.5.
units.tr: 7. The heart of heaven [medium caeli] is more powerful than all the others, then the ascendant; but in life, in the affections of the mind, and in the dispositions of the body, the ascendant is more powerful, then the seventh, fourth, eleventh, ninth, second and fifth houses.

units.la: 8. Jupiter præstat temperamentum, quoniam virtutes, moresq; boni, & naturæ robur consistunt circa temperantiam, iccirco Jupiter significabit hæc omnia, simulq; divitias & honores, talia enim ex moderatis proveniunt actionibus, nunquam ab extremis.
units.tr: 8. Jupiter bestows temperance, since virtues, good morals and natural strength consist in moderation. Therefore Jupiter will signify all these things, and at the same time riches and honours, for such things come from moderate actions and never from extremes.

units.la: 9. Causæ universales effectuum sunt potentiores singularibus, & generaliores minus generalibus.
units.tr: 9. The universal causes of effects are more powerful than particular ones, and more general than less general ones.

units.la: 10. Causa debilis universalis non potest vincere validam propriam.
units.tr: 10. A weak universal cause cannot overcome a strong particular one.

units.la: 11. Causa universalis vincit propriam, ubi par est magnitudo effectuum significatorum.
units.tr: 11. A universal cause overcomes a particular one when the magnitude of the effects signified is equal.

units.la: 12. Conjunctiones in signis aqueis, quia est trigonus Martis, significant multa bella, inventionesq; operum mechanicorum propter Martem, morbosq; malignos, contagiosos, propter scorpionem & cancrum, mixtionemq; Martis cum Venere & Luna: tum graves hæreses Mahumeticas, lex enim & religio sub hoc trigono habuit initium.
units.tr: 12. Conjunctions in watery signs, because it is the trigon of Mars, signify many wars and the inventions of mechanical works on account of Mars; malignant and contagious diseases on account of the Scorpion and Cancer, and the mixture of Mars with Venus and the Moon; and then grave Mahometan heresies, for law and religion began under this trigon.

units.la: 13. Conjunctiones in signis igneis si fiant, tunc mundi Imperia & Monarchiæ constituuntur propter Solem & Jovem, hujus triplicitatis Dominos, qui significant tranquillitatem in mundo, hominumq; sapientiam & industriam, sed sterilitates insignes, propter dominium calidorum & Planetarum & signorum.
units.tr: 13. If conjunctions occur in fiery signs, then empires and monarchies of the world are established, on account of the Sun and Jupiter, the lords of this triplicity, who signify tranquillity in the world and the wisdom and industry of men; but they signify notable barrenness, on account of the dominion of the hot planets and signs.

units.la: 14. Conjunctiones in trigoni terrei signis terræ motus significant, & inundationes, nec non Cometas propter capricornum, in quo dominantur Mars & Saturnus, significant quoque dissipationem eorum, quæ parta sunt & conquisita sub trigono aqueo.
units.tr: 14. Conjunctions in the earthly trigon signify earthquakes and floods, and likewise comets, on account of Capricorn, in which Mars and Saturn rule. They also signify the dissipation of those things that have been acquired and gathered under the watery trigon.

units.la: 15. Conjunctiones in signis aereis dissipatione Monarchiarum, per trigonum igneum institutarum portendunt, vel traductionem Monarchiæ in aliam mundi partem, & propter dominium Saturni & Mercurii vigebunt artes, & viri sapientes pariter atq; improbissimi, vitia, libidines, apparebuntq; propter Mercurium multi Planetæ.
units.tr: 15. Conjunctions in airy signs portend the dissolution of monarchies established under the fiery trigon, or the transfer of a monarchy to another part of the world. On account of the dominion of Saturn and Mercury, the arts will flourish, and wise men and most wicked men alike, vices and lusts; and many planets will appear on account of Mercury.

units.la: 16. Stellæ verticales magnam habent vim, suntq; illæ, quæ tantam habent declinationem ab æquatore, quanta est elevatio poli illius regionis.
units.tr: 16. Vertical stars have great power, and they are those which have as great a declination from the equator as the elevation of the pole of that region.

units.la: 17. Stellæ, quæ simul in eadem regione ascendunt, aut medium cœli obtinent, aut descendunt, plurimum eodem possunt tempore, quia vires inter se commiscent.
units.tr: 17. Stars which rise together in the same region, or hold the middle of heaven, or set together, for the most part have power at the same time, because they mingle their powers with one another.

units.la: 18. Stellæ, quæ in communi sunt circulo positionis, multum possunt, quia singulis diebus vires suas invicem commiscent.
units.tr: 18. Stars which lie in the common circle of position have great power, because they mingle their powers with one another every day.

units.la: 19. Siquis singularium rerum prædictionibus operam daturus est,non poterit, nisi comprehensione generaliorum ad illas pervenire.
units.tr: 19. If anyone intends to work on predictions of particular things, he will not be able to arrive at them except by grasping the more general things.

units.la: 20. Trigonus igneus est Christianorum, terreus idololatriæ, aerius Judæorum, aqueus Mahumetarum.
units.tr: 20. The fiery trigon belongs to the Christians, the earthly to idolatry, the airy to the Jews, the watery to the Mahometans.

units.la: 21. Stellæ, quæ disponunt loca Eclipsium, si noviter e-mergunt,aut occultantur, aut stationem ingrediuntur, vel noctu emicant, augent, minuuntve effectus: augent, dum è Solis radiis emergunt, & in stationibus sunt, licet enim ibi sint debiliores, quia tamen firmi manent uno in loco, plus operantur, nam debilis assiduè assistens, plus operatur, quàm validus vagans: minuunt vero effectus, cum occultantur, & sunt retrogradi.
units.tr: 21. Stars which govern the places of eclipses increase or diminish their effects if they newly emerge, or are hidden, or enter a station, or shine at night. They increase them while they emerge from the rays of the Sun and are in stations; for although they are weaker there, yet because they remain firm in one place, they act more, for a weak thing that is constantly present acts more than a strong thing that wanders. They diminish the effects, however, when they are hidden and are retrograde.

units.la: 22. Effectus Eclipsium incoati augentur vel minuuntur, aut per novilunia, aut per plenilunia, aut radiaturas quadratas luminarium, cùm inciderint in loca eclipsium, aut illa irradiârint ex trigono, si enim concordant, augebunt, sin minus, minuunt.
units.tr: 22. The effects of begun eclipses are increased or diminished either by new moons, or by full moons, or by the square aspects of the luminaries, when these fall upon the places of the eclipses, or when they have irradiated them from a trigon. For if they agree, they will increase them; if not, they diminish them.

units.la: 23. Quotiescunq; fuerit unus locus tantùm significator alicujus rei, potentior in illo loco pro dispositore accipiendus: si verò duo aut plura loca fuerint significatores, principalis erit potentior, inde ex ordine ei adjungentur, qui proximam ab eo sunt dignitatem adepti.
units.tr: 23. Whenever there is only one place signifying a certain thing, the more powerful planet in that place is to be taken as the disposer. But if two or more places are signifiers, the principal one will be the more powerful, and then those will be joined to it in order which have attained the dignity next to it.

units.la: 24. Si verò ambigua fuerit dominii ratio, præponetur ille, qui extiterit in angulo, vel qui potentior in domo vel exaltatione fuerit, directus item retrogrado, orientalis occidentali.
units.tr: 24. If, however, the reason for lordship is doubtful, he is to be preferred who stands in an angle, or who is more powerful by domicile or exaltation; likewise the direct over the retrograde, and the oriental over the occidental.

units.la: 25. Regiones, quæ æquatori sunt proximæ, magis afficiuntur à Planetis, quæ verò remotiores, minus afficiuntur ab eclipsibus, sed magis à stellis fixis.
units.tr: 25. Regions nearest the equator are more affected by the planets, but those more remote are less affected by eclipses, and more by the fixed stars.

units.la: 26. Planeta levior sæpiùs revertens ad congressus alterius, qui tardius movetur, seu per conjunctionem, seu per aspe-ctus stus applicet, quod pollicitus est ab initio, sæpius repetendo, confirmat & auget.
units.tr: 26. A lighter planet, returning often to the meetings of another which moves more slowly, whether it applies by conjunction or by aspect, confirms and increases by repeating often what it promised from the beginning.

units.la: 27. Aëris qualitates difficulter cognoscuntur, quia con-gressus & configurationes stellarum non revertuntur, & confi-gurationes cœlorum nostris temporibus non sunt similes, qua-rum similitudine ars ipsa confecta est.
units.tr: 27. The qualities of the air are known with difficulty, because the meetings and configurations of the stars do not recur, and the configurations of the heavens in our times are not similar; and it is from the similarity of these that the art itself was made.

units.la: 28. Major est astrorum vis, quàm ut quisquam eam æsti-mare possit, nam legum & Imperiorum mutationes, naturæq; miracula (non illa, quæ divina fiunt providentiâ) ab his promanant.
units.tr: 28. The power of the stars is greater than anyone can estimate, for changes of laws and empires, and miracles of nature (not those which are done by divine providence), come forth from them.

units.la: 29. Astrorum promissa minuuntur, augentur, & per-vertuntur multis de causis; quales sunt, natura seminis, patria, educatio, consuetudo, & ea quæ hæc consequuntur, atq; ex his pendent.
units.tr: 29. The promises of the stars are diminished, increased and perverted for many reasons, such as the nature of the seed, country, education, custom, and those things which follow from these and depend on them.

units.la: 30. Per Astrologiam præcognoscere possumus mutationes, quæ fiunt per aëris transmutationem, & in ipso aëre ambiente mutato, simul corpora nostra primis qualitatibus immutantur, inde & animus, unde temperaturæ, sanitas, morbus, vitæ brevitas & longitudo, & quæ unicuique horum sunt conjuncta, ut corpori res familiaris atq; convictus, animo, existimatio & dignitas.
units.tr: 30. Through astrology we can foreknow the changes that occur through a transmutation of the air; and when the surrounding air itself is changed, our bodies are at the same time changed in their primary qualities, and thence the mind also: whence come temperaments, health, sickness, shortness and length of life, and whatever is joined to each of these, as to the body, household affairs and way of life; to the mind, esteem and dignity.

units.la: 31. Mars cum Sole in leone siccitates auget, unde febres acutæ.
units.tr: 31. Mars with the Sun in Leo increases dryness, whence come acute fevers.

units.la: 32. Maximè illustres sunt effectus Lunæ & stellarum fixarum illustrium, quæ proximè accedunt ad viam Solis.
units.tr: 32. The effects of the Moon and of the bright fixed stars that lie closest to the path of the Sun are most conspicuous.

units.la: 34. Omnis Planeta, omneq; sidus talem habet virtutem, qualem habet impressionem.
units.tr: 34. Every planet and every star has such a virtue as it has impression [of its own].

units.la: 35. Quæ aqualiter moventur, substantiam alterant, quæ vero nunc velociter, nunc tardè, qualitates magis excitant, quàm substantiam mutant.
units.tr: 35. Those which move uniformly alter the substance; but those which move now swiftly, now slowly, rather stir up the qualities than change the substance.

units.la: 36. Sol secundum substantiam calidissimus est, secundum vero qualitatem impressam moderatè calidus, paululumque siccus.
units.tr: 36. The Sun is in its substance the hottest, but in its impressed quality it is moderately hot and somewhat dry.

units.la: 37. Virtus omnium siderum consequitur luminis magnitudinem, quæ consistit in magnitudine corporis, luminis claritate & densitate.
units.tr: 37. The power of all the stars follows the magnitude of their light, which consists in the size of the body, the brightness of the light, and its density.

units.la: 38. Uniuscujusq; sideris proprium lumen est diversum ab aliis, magnitudine, multitudine, tenuitate, & celeritate, quod vero reflectitur, Solis est, purissimum, tenuissimum, & densissimum.
units.tr: 38. The light proper to each star differs from the others in magnitude, quantity, fineness, and speed. The light that is reflected belongs to the Sun, and it is the purest, finest, and densest.

units.la: 39. Velocitas motus in Luna maximè consideranda est, postea in Mercurio & Venere, nam motus velocitas in superioribus non tantum facit, quantum in inferioribus.
units.tr: 39. The speed of motion should be considered chiefly in the Moon, then in Mercury and Venus, for speed of motion does not have as great an effect in the higher planets as in the lower.

units.la: 40. Jupiter cum Sole & Luna fœcunditatis omnis autor est.
units.tr: 40. Jupiter, together with the Sun and the Moon, is the author of all fruitfulness.

units.la: 41. Nullus superiorum Planetarum potest esse valdè humidus, nec ullus inferiorum valdè siccus.
units.tr: 41. None of the higher planets can be very moist, nor any of the lower very dry.

units.la: 42. Lunæ motus, quia est perpetuò manifestus, ideò Lunaticorum instabilitas omnibus est cognita, unde etiam stultitia nominatur.
units.tr: 42. Because the Moon's motion is always visible, the lunatics' instability is known to everyone, and for this reason it is also called foolishness.

units.la: 43. Mercurii instabilitas dubia est, & non adeò manifesta, iccirco calliditas appellatur, habetque speciem prudentiæ, quamvis verè prudentia non sit, sed natura quædam instabilis & dolosa.
units.tr: 43. The instability of Mercury is doubtful and not so evident, and therefore it is called cleverness. It has the appearance of prudence, although it is not truly prudence but a certain unstable and deceitful nature.

units.la: 44. Luna luminibus plena maximas inducit felicitates, quoniam satis calida pro luminis ratione, vacua verò debiliter nobis benefacit.
units.tr: 44. The Moon, full of light, brings the greatest happinesses, since it is warm enough for the amount of its light; but when empty, it benefits us only weakly.

units.la: 45. Mercurius Orientalis & remotus à Sole, Lunæque propinquus, aut in illius configurationibus, humectat.
units.tr: 45. Mercury, when eastern and far from the Sun, and near the Moon, or in its configurations with it, makes things moist.

units.la: 46. Jupiter temperamentum habet supremum, & maximè beneficus est, quia calor humido dominatur perfectè.
units.tr: 46. Jupiter has the highest temperament and is most beneficent, because its heat perfectly governs the moisture.

units.la: 47. Venus mediocriter temperata est, propter humidi-vitalis abundantiam, & caloris mediocritatem.
units.tr: 47. Venus is moderately tempered, on account of the abundance of vital moisture and the moderation of its heat.

units.la: 48. Luna minus temperata propter caloris paucitatem, parum enim dominatur humido.
units.tr: 48. The Moon is less tempered, because of the scarcity of its heat, for it governs the moisture only slightly.

units.la: 49. Luminis magnitudo prima est in Sole, postea in Jove, quo ad robur, inde in Luna, quo ad densitatem, terræq; propinquitatem, tandem Venere, Marte, Mercurio, Saturno.
units.tr: 49. The greatest magnitude of light is in the Sun, then in Jupiter as regards strength; next in the Moon as regards density and nearness to the earth; and finally Venus, Mars, Mercury, and Saturn.

units.la: 50. Orientales Planetæ humidiores sunt occidentalibus, quantitate luminis, non qualitate.
units.tr: 50. Eastern planets are moister than western ones, by the quantity of their light, not by its quality.

units.la: 51. Stellæ fixæ, quia plurimum à terra absunt, motuque proprio feruntur tardissimè, ideò vis illarum ad terram non pervenit, sed mixta aliis Planetis ad terras defertur.
units.tr: 51. The fixed stars, because they are very far from the earth and move with their own motion most slowly, their force does not reach the earth directly, but it is carried down to the earth mixed with the other planets.

units.la: 52. Stella fixa cum Planeta simili, id est, ejusdem naturæ, evidentissimos habet effectus, cum contrario obscurissimos, cum dissimili incertos, & qui fere non nisi post eventum dignosci possunt.
units.tr: 52. A fixed star conjoined with a planet of like kind, that is, of the same nature, has the most evident effects; with a contrary planet, the most obscure; with an unlike one, uncertain effects, which can scarcely be recognised except after the event.

units.la: 53. Stellæ fixæ propiores ecliptice beneficio Planetarum, qui illis junguntur, vires suas ad nos transmittunt.
units.tr: 53. Fixed stars nearer the ecliptic transmit their powers to us by the help of the planets that join them.

units.la: 54. Stellæ fixæ cum Sole magnos habent effectus circa honores & vitam, cum Luna circa fortunam, postea cum Jove, Venere, Marte, Saturno, Mercurio.
units.tr: 54. Fixed stars with the Sun have great effects concerning honours and life; with the Moon, concerning fortune; afterwards with Jupiter, Venus, Mars, Saturn, and Mercury.

units.la: 55. Robur stellæ bona & mala auget, sicut imbecillitas minuit.
units.tr: 55. The strength of a star increases good and evil, just as weakness diminishes them.

units.la: 56. Benefica si fuerit domina Eclipsis & cardinis, domi-neturq; civitati aut provinciæ, in quam significata incidunt, & à maleficis non impediatur, plurimum illis locis benefaciet, quod si aliqua harum conditionum defecerit, juvabit minus.
units.tr: 56. If a benefic is lord of the eclipse and of the cardine, and rules the city or province into which the significators fall, and is not hindered by malefics, it will greatly benefit those places; but if any of these conditions is lacking, it will help less.

units.la: 57. Malefica, si præfuerit Eclipsi & cardini, locisq; per Eclipsin affectis, & vincatur à beneficis, parum oberit.
units.tr: 57. A malefic, if it is over the eclipse and the cardine, and over the places affected by the eclipse, and is overcome by benefics, will do little harm.

units.la: 58. Maleficæ, si regionibus, civitatibus, provinciis, vel locis affectis non dominentur, nec à beneficis impediantur, deterius afficient, ac quanto validiores, tanto pejus.
units.tr: 58. Malefics that do not rule over regions, cities, provinces, or the affected places, and are not hindered by benefics, will afflict more badly; and the stronger they are, the worse.

units.la: 59. Omnes effectus significatorum generaliter reducuntur ad tres dispositiones, naturam significatoris bonam, malam, aut mediam, ad debilitatem vel robur, & ad qualitatem, an sit scilicet felix vel infelix: ut ita optimi contingant effectus, si benefica est robustissima, & fortunatissima, pessimi, cum malefica fuerit robustissima, & infortunatissima, mediocres effectus ex his cognoscuntur.
units.tr: 59. All the effects of the significators are generally reduced to three dispositions: the nature of the significator is good, bad, or middling; as to weakness or strength; and as to quality, that is, whether it is fortunate or unfortunate. Thus the best effects come about if the benefic is very strong and very fortunate; the worst, when the malefic is very strong and very unfortunate; and middling effects are known from these.

units.la: 60. In unaquaque genitura eligendus est locus in coelo pro vita, honoribus, divitiis, morte, & ad illum locum coeli, reliquum totum coelum comparandum, juxtaq; illam comparationem judicandum.
units.tr: 60. In every nativity a place in the heavens must be chosen for life, honours, riches, and death; and the whole remainder of the heavens must be compared with that place, and judgement made according to that comparison.

units.la: 61. Nullo in loco Saturnus tantum offendit, quantum in Occidente, sicut nullo in loco Mars tantum, sicut in culmine coeli.
units.tr: 61. In no place does Saturn harm so much as in the West, just as in no place does Mars harm so much as at the midheaven.

units.la: 62. Id astrum, quod debet perimere violenter, est paratum in omnem occasionem, ideo infligit pericula & metus in-eo genere sæpius, antequam occidat.
units.tr: 62. The star that is to destroy violently is ready on every occasion, and so it inflicts dangers and fears of that kind more often before it sets.

units.la: 63. Quæ dicuntur de radiis quadrangularibus, de oppositis multò magis sunt intelligenda.
units.tr: 63. What is said about square rays should be understood much more of opposition.

units.la: 64. Violentâ morte decedunt, cùm aut uterq; malefi-cus interemptorio loco imperat, aut per congressum, aut per radios quadrangulos, oppositósve: aut alteruter eorum, aut etiam ambo Solem, aut Lunam, aut utrumq; luminare infesto radio pulsârint.
units.tr: 64. They die a violent death when either malefic holds rule over the place of destruction, whether by conjunction, or by square rays, or by opposition; or when one or both of them strike the Sun, or the Moon, or both luminaries, with a hostile ray.

units.la: 65. Genus mortis sumitur ab astrorum reliquorum intuitu, & signis, quæ à maleficis occupantur, tum etiam stellis fixis violentis.
units.tr: 65. The kind of death is taken from the aspect of the remaining stars and from the signs occupied by the malefics, and also from violent fixed stars.

units.la: 66. Saturnus Solem quadrangularibus radiis feriens in signis fixis, lapidationem, strangulationem, & læsionem per ignem nunciat.
units.tr: 66. Saturn, striking the Sun with square rays in the fixed signs, announces stoning, strangling, and injury by fire.

units.la: 67. In ferialibus à feris dilaniandos.
units.tr: 67. In the beast-signs, they are to be torn apart by wild beasts.

units.la: 68. Soli aut Marti junctus in tropicis, aut etiam oppositus, ruina opprimendos.
units.tr: 68. Joined to the Sun or to Mars in the tropical signs, or also in opposition, they are to be overwhelmed by a collapse.

units.la: 69. Soli aut Marti junctus in tropicis, aut oppositus in medio cœli, ab alto præcipitandos.
units.tr: 69. Joined to the Sun or to Mars in the tropical signs, or in opposition in the midheaven, they are to be thrown down from a height.

units.la: 70. Idem junctus Mercurio, eiq; vel oppositus, vel per quadratum consociatus, serpentum aut terrestrium venenatorum ictu.
units.tr: 70. The same, joined to Mercury, and either in opposition to it or associated with it by a square, by the bite of serpents or of poisonous land creatures.

units.la: 71. Cum Mercurio & Venere congrediens, ex veneficio, fœminarumq; dolis.
units.tr: 71. Meeting with Mercury and Venus, by poisoning and the deceits of women.

units.la: 72. Saturnus occidens, & Lunam sequens, aquâ suffocandos: Idem in aqueis signis Lunæ configuratus portendit, necnon in Argo, ubi naufragio mergendos denunciat. Priori modo Saturnum cum Luna constitutum habet inter chelas, Magnus quidam Princeps, & quidem in signo scorpionis, quare non tam pericula per aquas, quàm venena minatur. (Deus id clementer prohibeat.)
units.tr: 72. Saturn setting and following the Moon: to be suffocated by water. The same, configured with the Moon in watery signs, portends it, and also in Argo, where it announces they are to be drowned in shipwreck. In the former way, Saturn is placed with the Moon between the Claws, a certain great Prince, and indeed in the sign of Scorpio; wherefore it threatens not so much dangers through waters as poisons. (May God mercifully prohibit this.)

units.la: 73. Sed in Occidente Soli vel Lunæ oppositus carceribus opprimendos.
units.tr: 73. But in the West, the Moon or Sun in opposition means they are to be crushed in prisons.

units.la: 74. Mars Soli vel Lunæ, corpore, tetragonis, vel oppositis radiis configuratus, seditione, bello, aut propria manu interficiendos: cum testimonio Veneris fœminarum causâ, cum testimonio Mercurii, à latronibus occidendos, cum capite Medusæ capite truncandos vel mutilandos: in scorpione vel sagittario, ustionibus, sectionibus, & chirurgorum revulsionibus: cum Cepheo & Andromeda, inq; medio vel imo cœli crucibus affigendos: in occasu vivos comburendos, quadrupedibus distrahendos, aut ruina opprimendos: cum Jovis tamen testimonio omnia mitigantur, itaque locus Jovis diligenter examinandus.
units.tr: 74. Mars configured with the Sun or Moon by body, by squares, or by opposing rays: to be killed in sedition, in war, or by one's own hand. With Venus as witness, on account of women; with Mercury as witness, to be slain by robbers; with the head of Medusa, to be beheaded or mutilated; in Scorpio or Sagittarius, by burns, cuttings, and the tearing out by surgeons; with Cepheus and Andromeda, to be fastened to crosses at the midheaven or the nadir; in the West, to be burned alive, to be torn apart by four-footed beasts, or to be crushed by a fall. Yet with the testimony of Jupiter all these things are mitigated, so the place of Jupiter must be carefully examined.

units.la: 75. In universum semper considerare oportet constitutiones generales, veluti si quis iturus sit ad bellum valde exitiale, ex minima occasione judicari potest, facile illum in ista expeditione moriturum: similiter cum transituri ex Gallia in Angliam tempore tempestatis ingruentis, suffocantur, ob tempestatem scilicet, quae est generalis clades in certa parte maris, si plures naves submergantur. Et quae evadunt, evadunt ob constitutionem navis & nauclerj bonam. Sed si casu contingat, unam navim tantum perire multis evadentibus, erit hoc ex prava constitutione navis & gubernatoris ejus, non ex calamitate universali.
units.tr: 75. In general, one must always consider the general constitutions. For example, if someone is about to go to a very deadly war, it may be judged from the slightest occasion that he will easily die on that expedition; similarly, those who are about to cross from Gaul to England at a time of approaching storm are suffocated, namely on account of the storm, which is a general disaster in a certain part of the sea, if many ships are sunk. And those who escape, escape on account of the good constitution of the ship and the pilot. But if by chance it happens that only one ship perishes while many escape, this will come from the bad constitution of that ship and its steersman, not from a universal calamity.

units.la: 76. Virtus geminata habet plus roboris, quàm separatæ & dispersa. Malefici igitur juncti, & luminare alterū vel utrumque oppugnantes, vel etiam Anaræta & locum mortis, duplicatis agunt viribus. Tales igitur morte violenta peribunt, nisi beneficus aspectus auxilietur; adest enim pravi influxus magnitudo: exempla sunt in promtu plus quàm illustria.
units.tr: 76. A doubled power has more strength than separate and scattered ones. Therefore malefics joined together, and attacking one or both luminaries, or also the anaretae and the place of death, act with doubled forces. Such people will therefore perish by violent death, unless a benefic aspect comes to help; for the magnitude of the evil influence is present. Examples are at hand, more than illustrious.

units.la: 78. Idem significator multa genera mortis denotare potest, quæ nobis videntur diversa quidem, sed tamen inter se affinia, ut strangulatio, suffocatio in aquis, & a ruina, & a catarrho: sic ruina & casus ab alto sunt inter se affinia, sicut etiam cum his ictus per tormentum bellicum: similiter venenum, morsus canis rabidi, serpentis ictus.
units.tr: 78. The same significator can denote many kinds of death, which seem to us indeed different, but nevertheless are related to one another: such as strangling, suffocation in water, and from a fall, and from catarrh; thus a fall and collapse from a height are related to one another, as also a blow from a siege engine along with these; similarly poison, the bite of a mad dog, the sting of a serpent.

units.la: 79. Per Anaræta non intelligendus hic secundum alios, Planeta interficiens, sed locus, in quem radii interficientes cadunt: ut, si alicui locus mortis sit in 10. gradu cancri, in eum autem gradum cadant trigonus Lunæ, quadratus Solis, & quadratus Saturni, hic non appellandus Anaræta est Saturnus aut Sol, sed 10. gradus cancri, qui tenet cuspidem mortis.
units.tr: 79. Here, according to others, Anaræta is not to be understood as the injuring planet but as the place onto which the injuring rays fall. For example, if the place of death is at the tenth degree of Cancer, and the trine of the Moon, the square of the Sun and the square of Saturn fall upon that degree, then the one to be called Anaræta is not Saturn or the Sun but the tenth degree of Cancer, which holds the cusp of death.

units.la: 80. Quo igitur tempore Anaræta attingit Aphetam, id est, principalem vitæ gubernatorem & significatorem, homo vel moritur, vel acuto morbo corripitur.
units.tr: 80. Therefore, at the time when the Anaræta reaches the Aphetes, that is, the principal governor and signifier of life, a person either dies or is seized by an acute illness.

units.la: 81. Quod si illo momento luminaria vel ascendens sint conjuncta cum Planetis angulo cadentibus, significant mortem extra patriam, ita tamen, ut Planeta cadens vel occupet locum interemptorium, vel adsit principali vitæ significatori.
units.tr: 81. But if at that moment the luminaries or the ascendant are conjoined with planets falling in the angles, they signify death away from one's homeland, provided that the falling planet either occupies the place of destruction or is present with the principal signifier of life.

units.la: 82. Benefica si non adsit, & maleficæ fuerint in signis quadrupedum, vel etiam volatilium, ut corvi in hydra, devorandos ab ejusmodi animalibus portendunt: in signo vero piscium, vel cancri, benefica supra terram non respiciente, submergendos.
units.tr: 82. If a benefic is not present, and malefics are in signs of quadrupeds, or also of birds, as the Raven in Hydra, they portend being devoured by animals of that kind; but in the sign of Pisces or Cancer, with no benefic looking upon the land, they portend drowning.

units.la: 83. Mars cum stellis fixis regiis violentis, alteroq; nodorum, vivos comburendos, dirisq; cruciatibus lacerandos: semper enim Martis cum stellis violentis, nodisq; positus (præsertim si ipse significator sit mortis) ut & cum luminaribus, funestus deprehensus est.
units.tr: 83. Mars with the violent royal fixed stars, and with the other node, portends being burned alive and torn by dreadful torments. For Mars placed with violent stars and nodes (especially if he himself is the signifier of death), as also with the luminaries, has always been found to be fatal.

units.la: 84. Luminaria, si mortis fuerint significatores, & bene affecta, maleficiq; in mortis loco testimonium non habuerint, mors erit naturalis & placida.
units.tr: 84. If the luminaries are signifiers of death, well disposed, and have no testimony of malefics in the place of death, the death will be natural and peaceful.

units.la: 85. In arte prædicendi non sunt prædictiones redigendæ ac restringendæ ad certa loca seu capita, ut recentiores quidam conati sunt, cum scribunt: Saturnū in hoc loco illud, in illo hoc significare, &c. (nō secus ac ædificaturus domum omnia ligna in uno loco disponit per ordinem, alio tabulas omnes, alio totam calcem, alio sabulum, alio lapides, alio clavos, & vincula ferrea ligneaq;, quæ tamen omnia ad ipsam domus ædificationem plane nihil conferunt) sed commiscenda significata sunt in singulis, radixq; tempus, modus, ordo & locus commixtionis omnium cognoscenda sunt. Saturnus enim in ariete & ascendente quandoque significat statum corporis, quandoque animi mores, & quandoq; vitæ spacium, quandoq; fortunam, quandōq;[?] amicos, statum uxoris, dignitatis peregrinationem, & mortis genus. Sic Saturnus in scorpione & sexta, & Jupiter in-piscibus & undecima significat prudentem animo, & corpore ægrum. Idem Saturnus in ascendente, si fuerit dispositor morum, facit tardum, malevolum, invidum, gravem. Mercurius vero celerem, acutum, instabilem: & si Saturno fuerit junctus, faciet dolosos, invidos & avaros: sed dignitatibus eundem superans medium quiddam inter tarditatem & velocitatem præstat, & quandam inducit mediocritatem. Sic igitur in qualibet genitura scligendus locus est in cœlo pro vita, divitiis, vel honoribus, addq; illa loca totum cœlum dirigendum, & juxta illam directionem judicandum: ut sit Sol in alicujus genitura in 24. gradu Aquarii, & quidem ascendente, hic vigesimus quartus gradus est dirigendus ad totum cœlum, & diligenter inquirendum, an à Saturni vel Martis radiis malis sit liber, nec ne? Si enim Mars vel Saturnus respexerit per quadratum, significatur tertio ætatis anno morbus, vel vitæ nocumentum, sin per oppositum, sexto ætatis suæ anno natum, periclitaturum indicatur, estq; quadrati illius, vel oppositi Saturni aut Martis, reditus & progressio per totius vitæ decursum observanda.
units.tr: 85. In the art of prediction, predictions should not be confined and restricted to fixed places or heads, as some recent writers have tried to do when they write: "Saturn in this place signifies that, in that place this," and so on. This is no different from a man who is about to build a house and arranges all the timber in one place in order, all the boards in another, all the lime in another, the sand, the stones, the nails, and the iron and wooden fastenings in yet others, though none of these contributes anything to the actual building of the house. Rather, the things signified must be mixed together in each case, and the root, time, manner, order and place of the mixing of all of them must be learned. For Saturn in Aries and the ascendant sometimes signifies the state of the body, sometimes the moral character, sometimes the span of life, sometimes fortune, sometimes friends, the state of the wife, dignity, travel, and the manner of death. So Saturn in Scorpio in the sixth house, and Jupiter in Pisces in the eleventh, signify a man prudent in mind and sick in body. Likewise, Saturn in the ascendant, if he is the disposer of the character, makes a person slow, malevolent, envious and heavy. Mercury, on the other hand, makes one quick, sharp and unstable; and if he is joined with Saturn, he will make people deceitful, envious and greedy; but when he surpasses Saturn in dignities, he produces something in between slowness and quickness, and brings in a certain mediocrity. Thus, in any nativity, a place in the heavens must be chosen for life, riches or honours, and those places must be added so that the whole heaven is directed, and judgement is made according to that direction. For example, if in someone's nativity the Sun is at the twenty-fourth degree of Aquarius, and indeed in the ascendant, this twenty-fourth degree is to be directed through the whole heaven, and it must be carefully inquired whether it is free from the evil rays of Saturn or Mars or not. For if Mars or Saturn look at it by square, an illness or harm to life is signified in the third year of age; but if by opposition, it is indicated that he will be in danger in the sixth year of his age. The return and progression of that square or opposition of Saturn or Mars must be observed over the whole course of life.

units.la: 86. Luna in ventre draconis, id est, in maxima latitudine boreali vel australi, ubi mox est ascendens, mox descendens, & à via Solis remotior, significat cerebri debilitatem & rationem corruptam, unde varietas, inconstantia & dolus, quæ ab imbecillitate intellectus proveniunt: in extremitatibus vero nodorum acutum intellectum præstat & industriam, ingenioque promptissimos, præsertim si Mercurius respexerit, sed plerumque gibbos, claudos, vel corpore læsos, quod oritur à commixtione ipsius Lunæ cum maleficis.
units.tr: 86.
