The Moon in the belly of the dragon, that is, at its greatest northern or southern latitude, where she is soon ascending, soon descending, and further removed from the path of the Sun, signifies weakness of the brain and a corrupted reason, whence come variability, inconstancy and deceit, which arise from weakness of the intellect. But at the extremities of the nodes she gives a sharp intellect, diligence and very ready wit, especially if Mercury looks upon her; yet for the most part such people are hunchbacked, lame, or injured in body, which arises from the mixture of the Moon herself with malefics.

units.la: 87. Diligenter hic pensitandum, quid sit Luna ascendens, cum scilicet dicit Ptolomæus l. 3. de judic. astrorum, text.
units.tr: 87. Here we must carefully weigh what the Moon ascending is, namely as Ptolemy says in the third book of his Judgements of the Stars, text:

units.la: 74. Ascendens & aucta lumine animum nobiliorem, illustriorem ac liberaliorem reddit: aucta enim lumine dicitur, cùm plus habet luminis, ut circa oppositionem, quo etiam tempore optimè Luna est disposita, abundat enim lumine copioso, lumen in dies & horas augetur, superavit longitudinem mediam, est in parte superiore eccentrici, inq; dies & horas apogæo fit propior. Pessimè autem est disposita in ultima quadra, & maximè 4.diebus conjunctionem præcedentibus.
units.tr: 74. "The Moon ascending and increased in light makes the mind nobler, more illustrious and more generous. For she is said to be increased in light when she has more light, as around opposition, which is also the time when the Moon is best disposed; for then she is abundant with copious light. Her light increases day by day and hour by hour; she has passed her mean longitude, is in the upper part of the eccentric, and becomes nearer to apogee day by day and hour by hour. She is worst disposed, however, in the last quarter, and especially in the four days preceding conjunction."

units.la: Ascendens verò Luna dicitur quinque modis: 1. cùm ascendit in latitudinem, id est, à meridie in Septentriones. 2. ab ascendente ad medium cœli, vel etiam ab imo cœli usq; ad cardinem Orientis. 3. cùm est in angulo, tunc enim semper ascendit ad centrum seu lineam, quæ describit anguli seu cardinis initium. 4. cùm ascendit ad apogæum epicycli, id est, movetur versus ipsum. 5. cùm ascendit ad apsidem eccentrici, qui ascensionis modus cæteris ideò verior existimatur, quia fit à prima post conjunctionem quadra usq; ad oppositionem, tunc enim luminibus est plena, inq; singulas horas crescit, donec ad veram venerit oppositionem, ascenditque versus apsidem eccentrici, cùm enim est in media quadratura, semper est in opposito apsidis eccentrici sui, id est, perigæo.
units.tr: The Moon is said to ascend in five ways: (1) when she ascends in latitude, that is, moves from the south towards the north; (2) from the ascendant to the midheaven, or even from the lower heaven up to the cardinal point of the East; (3) when she is in an angle, for then she always ascends towards the centre or line that describes the beginning of the angle or cardinal point; (4) when she ascends to the apogee of the epicycle, that is, moves towards it; (5) when she ascends to the apsis of the eccentric. This last mode of ascension is considered truer than the others, because it occurs from the first quarter after conjunction up to opposition; for then she is full of light and grows every hour until she comes to the true opposition, and she ascends towards the apsis of the eccentric. For when she is in the middle of the quadrature, she is always opposite to her own apsis of the eccentric, that is, at perigee.

units.la: 88. Omnes Planetæ juxta apogæum eccentrici & epicycli sunt puriores, fortunatiores, & meliores, sed non validiores, at in opposito sunt robustiores & deteriores, præter Lunam ratione epicycli, quæ in opposito apsidis illius non solùm est robustior, sed etiam purioris & melioris influxus.
units.tr: 88. All the planets near the apogee of the eccentric and epicycle are purer, more fortunate and better, but not stronger; at opposition, however, they are more robust and worse, except the Moon, who by reason of her epicycle is not only stronger at opposition to her apsis, but also of purer and better influence.

units.la: 89. In mentis, animi, intellectusq; dispositione & qualitatibus ante omnia expedit observare Mercurium & Lunam, an scilicet & quomodo invicem conjungantur, apudq; Orientalem finitorem à maleficis aut supplodantur, aut obsideantur, aut circumdentur, aut ex opposito feriantur, tunc enim multorum ruin[?]æ animi morborū sunt autores, sensitivam, intellectivamq; potentiam depravantes, idq; eo magis, cum inconjuncta maximè in angulo Orientis à maleficis opprimuntur, deinde in Occidentali, vel tandem in sexta. Si quis igitur dixerit, astra inclinare homines quandoq; ad virtutes, quandoq; ad vitia, non errabit, dummodò nō credat homines cogi necessariò, quia voluntas, quæ principium est humanarum operationum, astris non subjicitur, voluntas, inquam, potest & debet frenare inclinationes, nam inclinationes, quæ à stellis oriuntur & imprimuntur, integræ actionum causæ esse non possunt. Itaq; valere jubemus argumentum Basilii in enarratione capitis de rerum creatione, quo siderum effectiones tollit. Si à sideribus vitiosæ inclinationes aut scelera orirentur, Deus causa effet vitiorum & furorum. Hæc ratiocinatio plausibilis videri posset Ethnico. Nobis in Ecclesia dolorem augere debet, quòd homo, Deo non volente, in tantas se ipse ærumnas conjecerit. Si hominum natura mansisset integra, fulsisset in nobis lux divina, gubernatrix omnium motuum, & stellæ in materia non contaminata alias habuissent actiones: at verò nunc in his sordibus infeliciores sunt actiones, & extincta est illa lux, quæ rexisset omnes motus humanos. Hæc deploranda sunt in Basilii ratiocinatione[?], non dejicienda de cœlo sidera. Non enim fatalem necessitatem constituimus, nec cogi aliquem à stellis ad scelera & vitia dicimus, multò minus, Deum non posse cœlo & astris imperare, eademq; à proprio cursu revocare. Procul certè absit Stoicorum delira necef-sitas, quâ illi & Deo imperium naturæ eripiunt, & pecuino[?] vitio premi voluntatem volunt. Chaldæorum & Ægyptiorum omnia commenta, quibus & artem ipsam & cœlum impleverunt, rejicio, nec quicquam cum ejusmodi deliramentis mihi est commune. Nam est hæc divinatio ex astris eruditæ Physices pars, aliena ab omni superstitione, quoniam est aspectio divinorum operum, causarum, signorum, & effectuum naturalium. Nec pugnat cum hac religio Christiana, nec damnant has exa-stris prædictiones sacræ literæ, quia oriuntur è causis naturali-bus. Et licèt solus Deus in sua sibi potestate temporū momenta reservaverit, præscius quoq; solus sit ipse futurorū eventuum, ac nemo omnium in hoc existat mundo, qui diem possit crasti-num polliceri, & quid in ea futurum sit prædicere, nihilominus tamen idem Deus exliberalissima sua bonitate plurima in creaturas effudit dona, quibus ea, quæ futura & procul sunt, videre & præscire permittit, præscire, inquam, non certò, ut ipse, sed conjecturali quodam ac discursivo judicio. Nec obstat dictum Aristotelis, ajentis futurorum eventuum non esse determinatam veritatem, cùm idem affirmet vicissim, omne futurum de necessitate evenire. Si eventurū est de necessitate, aliunde etiam causam ejus oportebit præcedere, hanc verò determinatam & præcisam causam solus Deus omniū novit perfectissimè, dedit tamen homini rationem & intellectum, seu potentiam judicativam & discursivam, quibus ex præteritis futura conjecturare, dedit & scientiā astrorum, quibus plures effectus, ad quos astra inclinant, adhuc futuros prædicere possit. Et ut rem paucissimis attingam atq; concludam. dedit Deus homini triplicem futura prædicendi viam. ¹· est communior, ac consistit in vita longa, qua scilicet per longam experientiā, rerum omniū Magistram, ex dudum præteritis per similitudinem & conjecturam quandam prædicere futura homo potest, & hanc prædicendi viam norunt senes. ²· habetur ex astris, causas enim rerum rimaturi, primò cœlestia debent contemplari corpora, quia mundus in-ferior à superioribus gubernatur, teste Aristotele ipso. Homines enim per astra moribus informantur, inquit Ptol. quandamꝫ;[?] inclinationem astra ipsa præstant corporibus humanis, necessi-tatem verò nullam, unde homines eorum inclinationes præcaverspossunt, vel mitigare saltem ratione & consilio. Tertia est via revelationum. Etsi enim solus Deus futurorum scientiam posuerit in sua potestate, tamen eam nonnullis revelare voluit, vel in spiritu, vel visione, vel per angelos palàm missos, vel aliis occultis modis, quæ futura sunt, certis hominibus ingerit, ut verè futura prænuncient. Huc pertinet, cùm accenditur David, ut prælietur cum Goliath, quæ actio & similes non cientur stellarum viribus & inclinationibus, sed sunt motus divini, quos ideò diligenter considerari prodest, ut nos assuefaciamus ad petendam à Deo gubernationem, ut videlicet mentes hominum ad prava inclinantes flectat ad salutaria consilia, ambulentq; in via ejus. Ex dictis autē tribus modis futura prædicendi, primus, & secundus potissimùm concessi sunt, cùm astrologia sit verè scientia, futurorumq; cognitio, imò fructus scientiæ magnitu-dinis motuum & affectionum cœlestium, qua ad futura bona tutius licet nobis accedere, mala verò vitare, declinare, minue-re,infringere. Procedit namq; per causas nobilissimas, & futura docet per signa prædicere,non secus ac in medica arte ex cogni-tione causarum, signorum & effectuum ars extitit, tum judi-candi, tum prædicendi multas corporum mutationes, in morbis verò futuras crises, per signa etiam salutis vel mortis, salutem vel mortem prænunciandi, quæ certè prædictiones, quia physicæ sunt, nulla ratione damnari possunt, nec debent. Si igitur Medico licet ex arte divinare, nautis ex Luna & aere, agricolis ex seminibus, cur naturali Philosopho ex astrorum motu & positu conjecturare non licebit? Quid est, quaeso, quòd filius ex duobus parentibus honestissimis prognatus, & probè etiam educatus, nequissimus tamen sæpè evadat? Non enim à parentibus hoc contraxit, neq; etiam à Deo quicquam mali hausit. Si igitur neq; ex Deo, neq; ex parentibus id habet, aut fortuito id eveniet, aut quod solum est reliquum, ex astris. Atq; hoc uno
units.tr: 89. In regard to the disposition and qualities of mind, soul and intellect, it is above all useful to observe Mercury and the Moon: whether and how they are conjoined with each other, and whether, in the eastern horizon, they are struck, besieged, surrounded, or attacked from opposition by malefics. For then they are the authors of many ruins of the mind and diseases of the soul, corrupting the sensitive and intellectual powers; and this all the more when, not conjoined, they are oppressed by malefics especially in the eastern angle, then in the western, or finally in the sixth house. If someone therefore says that the stars sometimes incline men to virtues and sometimes to vices, he will not be wrong, provided he does not believe that men are necessarily compelled, because the will, which is the source of human actions, is not subject to the stars. The will, I say, can and should restrain the inclinations, for inclinations arising and imprinted from the stars cannot be complete causes of actions. And so we bid farewell to Basil's argument in his exposition of the chapter on the creation of things, by which he removes the effects of the stars. If wicked inclinations or crimes arose from the stars, God would be the cause of vices and madness. This reasoning might seem plausible to a pagan. For us in the Church, the grief should increase that man, against God's will, has cast himself into such miseries. If human nature had remained intact, the divine light, governing all motions, would have shone in us, and the stars in an uncontaminated matter would have had other actions; but now, in these filths, actions are more unhappy, and that light which would have ruled all human motions is extinguished. These things are to be lamented in Basil's reasoning, not the stars to be cast down from heaven. For we do not establish a fatal necessity, nor do we say that anyone is compelled by the stars to crimes and vices, much less that God cannot command heaven and the stars and recall them from their proper course. Far be from us the mad necessity of the Stoics, by which they snatch from God the rule over nature and want the will pressed down by brutish vice. I reject all the fictions of the Chaldeans and Egyptians, with which they filled both the art itself and the heavens, and I have nothing in common with such follies. For this divination from the stars is a part of learned physics, alien to all superstition, since it is the observation of divine works, causes, signs and natural effects. Nor does the Christian religion fight against it, nor do the Holy Scriptures condemn these predictions from the stars, because they arise from natural causes. And although God alone has reserved the moments of times in his own power, and he alone foreknows future events, and no one in this world can promise tomorrow or foretell what will be in it, nevertheless the same God, in his most generous goodness, has poured many gifts upon creatures, by which he permits them to see and foreknow things that are future and remote: foreknow, I say, not with certainty as he does, but by a certain conjectural and discursive judgment. Nor does the saying of Aristotle stand in the way, who says that there is no determinate truth of future events, since he likewise affirms that every future thing happens of necessity. If it is going to happen of necessity, its cause must also precede from elsewhere; but God alone knows this determinate and precise cause most perfectly. Yet he gave man reason and understanding, that is, the judgmental and discursive power, by which from past things man may conjecture future ones; he gave also the science of the stars, by which he can foretell the many effects, still future, to which the stars incline. To touch on the matter in very few words and conclude: God has given man a threefold way of foretelling the future. The first is more common, and consists in long life, by which, through long experience, the teacher of all things, a man can foretell future things from past ones by likeness and a certain conjecture; and the old men know this way of foretelling. The second is derived from the stars: for those who wish to search out causes must first contemplate the heavenly bodies, because the lower world is governed by the higher, as Aristotle himself testifies. For men are shaped in their morals by the stars, says Ptolemy; the stars furnish to human bodies a certain inclination, but no necessity, whence men can take precautions against their inclinations, or at least mitigate them by reason and counsel. The third is the way of revelations. For although God alone has placed the knowledge of future things in his own power, yet he has willed to reveal it to some: either in spirit, or in vision, or through angels plainly sent, or by other hidden means he impresses upon certain men what is to come, so that they foretell truly what will be. To this belongs the time when David is kindled to fight with Goliath; such an action and similar ones are not stirred by the powers and inclinations of the stars, but are divine movements, which it is profitable to consider carefully, so that we may accustom ourselves to asking God for governance, namely that he may turn the minds of men inclining to evil toward salutary counsels, and that they may walk in his way. Of the three ways of foretelling the future, the first and second have been chiefly conceded, since astrology is truly a science and a knowledge of future things; indeed its fruit is the knowledge of the magnitude of the celestial motions and affections, by which we may more safely approach good future things and avoid, decline, diminish and break the evil ones. For it proceeds through the most noble causes, and teaches how to predict future things through signs, just as in the medical art the art arose from knowledge of causes, signs and effects, both for judging and for predicting the many changes of bodies, and in diseases the coming crises, also foretelling health or death by signs of health or death; which predictions, since they are physical, can by no means be condemned, nor ought they to be. If therefore it is lawful for the physician to divine by his art, for sailors from the Moon and the air, for farmers from seeds, why should it not be lawful for the natural philosopher to conjecture from the motion and position of the stars? What is it, I ask, that a son born of two most honourable parents, and well educated too, often turns out most wicked? For he did not contract this from his parents, nor did he draw anything evil from God. If therefore he has it neither from God nor from his parents, it will either happen by chance or, which is the only thing left, it comes from the stars. And on this one point...

units.la: Astronomiam esse artem verissimam, utpote quæ divina etiam constet providentia, demonstratur. Et licet artifices in judiciis quandoq; aberrent, non tamen id arti derogat quicquam, cùm vitia artificum aberrantium in ipsam artem non sint rejicienda. Constat enim magnam esse infirmitatem humanarum mentium, & facilem hallucinationem, & errata multa, propter quæ certè ipsæ artes, circa quam ejusmodi errata contingunt, non sunt abjiciendæ. Nec etiam quicquam habet virium, quod objicitur, à civilibus legibus eam esse explosam. Olim Romana severitate, Medici, Rhetores, Philosophi, & Mathematici, imò omnia liberalia studia à civitate arcebantur. An ob id etiam nunc odisse Medicos & Philosophos decet, quòd illi oderint? At, inquiunt, lex illa de Medicis, Philosophis & Rhetoribus abdicata est. Astrologorum manet. Ego, quòd hæc lex non sit de Astrologis, sed Mathematicis, & illis quidem, qui per puncta, numeros, notasq; divinabant, & characteres, quod divinandi genus ut insulsum penitùs, ita & impium, est abominandum, legibusq; coërcendum. Omne enim quod est extra publicam utilitatem, & nullius usus, explodi debet atq; puniri. Per Solem autem, Lunam, ortusq; & occasus siderum divinare nemini unquam prohibitum fuit, imò publicam secum hoc divinandi genus affert utilitatem. Ergo, quæ damnata fuit sub Tyberio & aliis, vera Astrologia non erat, sed scientia mille superstitionibus referta, atq; vanitatibus contaminata.
units.tr: That astronomy is a most true art, since it also rests on divine providence, is demonstrated. And although practitioners sometimes err in their judgments, this does not take anything from the art, since the faults of erring practitioners are not to be imputed to the art itself. For it is established that the human mind is very weak and easily deceived, and makes many errors; on account of these, the arts in which such errors occur are certainly not to be abandoned. Nor does it have any force, what is objected, that astrology has been banished by civil laws. In former times, under Roman severity, physicians, rhetoricians, philosophers and mathematicians, indeed all the liberal studies, were kept out of the city. Ought we therefore now to hate physicians and philosophers because those men hated them? But, they say, that law about physicians, philosophers and rhetoricians has been abrogated; that of the astrologers remains. I answer that this law was not about astrologers but about mathematicians, and indeed those who divined by points, numbers, marks and characters; this kind of divination, being utterly foolish and also impious, is to be abominated and restrained by laws. For everything outside public utility, and of no use, ought to be rejected and punished. But to divine by the Sun, the Moon, and the risings and settings of the stars has never been forbidden to anyone; indeed this kind of divination brings public utility with it. Therefore the astrology which was condemned under Tiberius and others was not true astrology, but a science filled with a thousand superstitions and contaminated by vanities.
